Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

Surah (Ya-Sin)

It is authentically reported from the hadith of Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, al-Tabarani and others, on the authority of Ma'qil ibn Yasar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ya-Sin is the heart of the Qur'an." He counted this among its names. Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali (may Allah have mercy on him) explained the reason this name is applied to it: the basis of faith and its soundness lies in acknowledging the Gathering and the Resurrection, and this is established in the surah in the most eloquent and excellent manner. For this reason it was likened to the heart, on which the health and sustenance of the body depend. Imam al-Razi approved of this and presented it in its apparent sense: every matter that must be believed in is one whose faith is not valid without it, so there is no reason to single out the Gathering and the Resurrection for this.

It is answered that what is meant by "soundness" in the words of the Hujjah is that which is the opposite of sickness and disease. There is no doubt that whoever's faith in the Gathering is sound fears the Fire and desires Paradise, the abode of the righteous, and so he refrains from sins, which are like the illnesses of faith, since by them faith is disordered, weakened and corrupted, and he occupies himself with acts of obedience, which are like the preservation of health. Whoever's faith is not strong in this respect is in the opposite condition. Thus, acknowledging it resembles the heart, for by its soundness the body becomes sound and by its corruption the body is corrupted.

It is also permitted to say that the point of resemblance to the heart is that the body's soundness and corruption depend on it, and that it is not observed by the senses. It is the locus where realities and hidden matters are revealed. Likewise the Gathering is among the unseen matters, and in it the disclosure of matters occurs and one comes to stand on the realities of what has been decreed. By attending to it and rectifying its causes, eternal happiness is attained, and by turning away from it and corrupting its causes, one is afflicted with everlasting wretchedness.

In al-Kashf: perhaps the indication in naming this surah "the heart" is prophetic. The heart of everything is its core and origin, that to which everything else is either a preliminary or a completion. This is as we have explained regarding the naming of al-Fatiha as "the Mother of the Qur'an," namely that the purpose of sending the messengers and revealing the scriptures is to guide the servants to their perfect goal in the Hereafter. This is achieved through realization (tahaqquq) and character-formation (takhalluq), which were mentioned there, and which is expressed as following the Straight Path. The subject of this noble surah is the most complete explanation of this. End of quotation.

From this the reason for singling out the Gathering with what was mentioned in the words of the Hujjah becomes known, so there is no reason for the statement of some in objecting to it, "there is no reason..." etc. Later, if Allah the Exalted wills, at the end of the commentary on the surah, there will be an indication of the fundamental matters of the science of usul al-fiqh (principles of jurisprudence) and the well-regarded issues among the great scholars that it contains, and its establishing them in the most eloquent and complete manner. Perhaps this is the secret behind the command reported in the authentic reports to recite it over the dead, that is, over the dying.

It is also called "the Great One with Allah the Exalted." Abu Nasr al-Sijzi reported in al-Ibana and graded it as good, on the authority of A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Indeed in the Qur'an there is a surah called 'the Great One with Allah the Exalted,' and its reciter is called 'the Noble One with Allah the Exalted.' Its reciter will intercede on the Day of Resurrection for more than the tribes of Rabi'a and Mudar. It is Surah Ya-Sin." He mentioned that it is also called "the Sustainer" and "the Averter, the Fulfiller."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Bayhaqi reported on the authority of Hassan ibn Atiyya that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Surah Ya-Sin is called in the Torah 'the Sustainer' (al-mu'imma). It encompasses its reciter with the good of this world and the Hereafter, bears from him the afflictions of this world and the Hereafter, and repels from him the terrors of this world and the Hereafter. It is called 'the Averter, the Fulfiller': it repels from its companion every evil and fulfills for him every need." The report continues. Al-Bayhaqi criticized it, saying: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Ju'dani narrated it alone, from Sulayman ibn Difa', and it is munkar (rejected).

According to what Ibn al-Darris, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi reported on the authority of Ibn Abbas, it is Meccan. Some have excepted from this His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed We bring the dead to life﴾ (36:12), claiming that it was revealed in Medina when the tribe of Banu Salama wished to move closer to the Mosque of the Prophet (ﷺ), as they were in a remote part of Medina. The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "Your footprints are being recorded," and so they did not move. What has been said about this will come later, if Allah the Exalted wills. As for His saying, the Glorified: ﴿And when it is said to them, spend from what Allah has provided you﴾ (36:47), it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, and therefore it would be Medinan. But this has been criticized on the grounds that there is no soundness to it.

Its number of verses is eighty-three according to the Kufan count, and eighty-two according to other counts.

Among what attests to its excellence and the elevation of its rank are a number of reports and narrations, some of which have already passed. And it is authentically reported from the hadith of Ma'qil ibn Yasar: "No servant recites it seeking Allah the Exalted and the Last Abode except that his past sins are forgiven."

Al-Tirmidhi and al-Darimi reported from the hadith of Anas: "Whoever recites Ya-Sin, Allah the Exalted records for him, for his recitation of it, the reward of reciting the Qur'an ten times." This does not necessitate preferring a thing over itself, since what is meant by "the recitation of the Qur'an" is reciting it other than Ya-Sin. Al-Khafaji said: This does not necessitate that, for the stated preference suffices with a conceptual (i'tibari) difference. Ya-Sin, considered in terms of its being recited individually, is not the same as its being recited as part of the whole, as when you say: "The beautiful woman in the red dress is more beautiful than her in the white one." And sometimes a thing in isolation has what it does not have when combined with something else, as is observed in some medicines. He hoped that this would be closer to what we have presented, though I do not hope for that. The apparent meaning is that the stated reward is recorded for him multiplied, i.e., each letter counts as ten good deeds. There is nothing strange in preferring a small deed over a large one, for Allah the Exalted may bestow favor upon whom He wills with what He wills. Do you not see that it is authentically reported that this Ummah has the shortest lifespans among the nations, yet the greatest reward, and is the most stubborn in denying special privileges? And how well did one say:

"Though you surpass mankind while being one of them,
Musk is nonetheless but a part of the gazelle's blood."

Some have mentioned that whoever recites it is given the reward of one who recites the Qur'an twenty-two times.

Al-Bayhaqi reported in Shu'ab al-Iman on the authority of Abu Qilaba, who was among the senior Successors, that whoever recites it is as if he recited the Qur'an eleven times.

And on the authority of Abu Sa'id, he said: Whoever recites Ya-Sin once, it is as if he recited the Qur'an twice.

The hadith of the ten times is traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) through Ibn Abbas, Ma'qil ibn Yasar, Uqba ibn Amir, Abu Hurayra and Anas (may Allah be pleased with them all), so it is relied upon.

As for the connection of this surah with what precedes it, according to what al-Jalal al-Suyuti said: when, in Surah Fatir (35:37, 42), He mentioned the words: ﴿And there came to you the warner﴾ and His words: ﴿And they swore by Allah their most emphatic oaths that if a warner came to them...﴾ up to His words: ﴿But when there came to them a warner﴾, and what was meant was Muhammad (ﷺ), and they had turned away from him and denied him, He opened this surah with an oath affirming the truth of his prophethood (peace and blessings be upon him), and that he is upon a Straight Path, in order to warn a people whose forefathers were not warned. And He said, in Surah Fatir (35:13): ﴿He has subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term﴾, and in this surah: ﴿And the sun runs toward its resting place﴾ (36:38), and ﴿And the moon, We have determined for it phases﴾ (36:39), and so on. It is not hidden that the matter of this correspondence is complete even if "the warner" is interpreted as someone other than the Prophet (ﷺ) as well. So consider this.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ya-Sin﴾ (36:1). The discussion of it is like the discussion of Alif-Lam-Mim and similar disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs, both grammatically (i'rab) and in meaning, according to many. Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported through various chains from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Ya-Sin" means "O man." In another report from him there is an addition, in Abyssinian (Ethiopic). In yet another report from him, also, it is in the dialect of Tayy.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If this is authentic, its explanation is that its origin is "Ya Unaisin" (diminutive of insan, "man"), and the calling of it was so frequent on their tongues that they confined themselves to half of it, as in the oath "m-Allah" in "aymun Allah." Abu Hayyan criticized him, saying: What is transmitted from the Arabs in the diminutive of insan is "unaisiyan," with a yaa' before the alif, and this is evidence that insan is derived from nisyan (forgetfulness), and its origin is "unsiyan." When it was made diminutive, the diminutive returned it to its origin. We do not know that they said its diminutive as "unaisin." And even supposing it is a remnant of "unaisin," it would not be permissible except to build it on damma and not leave it in pause, because it is a vocative addressed directly. Moreover, the diminutive is not permissible in the names of the prophets (peace be upon them), just as it is not permissible in the names of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. As for what he mentioned, that Mim in "aym" is a half of "aymun," this is an opinion; and some grammarians say that Mim is a particle of oath, not a part of "aymun." End of quotation.

Al-Khafaji said: That it must be built on damma is not in dispute, so perhaps whoever explained it that way reads it with damma, which is the preferred view in it. As for the other two objections, they have no force at all. As for the first, whoever says "unaisiyan" holds that it is contrary to analogy, and this is the more correct view. He is not obliged, regarding what has been altered from it, to presume it to be as such, since he has not uttered it, so that it could be said to him: "You have spoken what the Arabs did not speak." Rather, it is a presumed matter. So if he says: "The presumed form is, in my view, according to analogy," would the objection apply to him? As for the last: diminutive in such cases is prohibited for us, but as for Allah the Exalted, He may apply to Himself, the Mighty and Majestic, and to the great ones of His creation whatever He wills, and in that case it is interpreted as befits, such as glorification, affection and the like, of the meanings of the diminutive, just as Ibn al-Farid said:

"I did not say 'my beloved little one' out of belittling,
Rather, the name of a thing grows sweet through diminutive."

What Abu Hayyan said in explaining this is that they say "iysan" with the meaning of "insan," and they make the plural "ayasin." So this is from it. It is not hidden that this needs proof, and how remote it is is not hidden, and what is wrong with the derivation upon it.

Another group said: Ya is a vocative particle, and the sin is standing in place of insan, from which a letter was removed and another put in its place. Its parallel is what came in the hadith: "Sufficient is the sword as a sha," meaning "shahidan" (as a witness). It was reinforced by what Ibn Abbas held concerning "Ha-Mim," "Ayn-Sin-Qaf" and similar, that they are letters from among the names of Allah the Exalted, namely al-Rahim, al-Alim, al-Sami', al-Qadir and similar. The apparent sense of some scholars, such as Ibn Jubayr, is that "Ya-Sin" as a whole is one of the names of the Prophet (peace be upon him). This is the apparent meaning of the words of al-Sayyid al-Himyari:

"O soul, do not devote yourself wholly to love, striving
For affection, except the family of Yasin."

For his (ﷺ) being named with these two noble letters there is a sublime secret known to those who are acquainted with the secrets of the letters. I spoke, praise be to Allah the Exalted, on what relates to this noble word for three days, beginning each day after the afternoon prayer and concluding shortly before the sunset prayer, in a session of exhortation in the Dawudi Congregational Mosque. Today I cannot recall a word of that; indeed I do not remember from it anything but a trace, over which the devastating wind of the oppressive time has blown, and scattered it. Allah is sufficient for me against whatever is other than Him; there is no lord but Him, and none is hoped for except His goodness.

It was read with a fatha on the ya' (Yā' with fatḥa), with imāla (fronting of the vowel) in its pure form and in the intermediate form (bayna bayn). A group read the nūn with sukūn, assimilated into the wāw (idgham), and others read it with sukūn made clear (iẓhār). Both readings are sab'iyya (among the seven canonical readings). Ibn Abī Isḥāq and ʿĪsā read the nūn with fatḥa. Abū Ḥātim said: "According to the view of Qatāda, analogically it is an oath, and it may be in the manner of ﴿Wallāhi la-afʿalanna﴾ (By Allah, I will surely do it), in the accusative." It is also permissible that it be in the genitive, by supposing the implied particle of oath (bāʾ al-qasam), and it is then prohibited from tanwīn (diptotic, not declined). Al-Zajjāj said: the accusative is by the supposition of "Iqra' Yā-Sīn" (recite Yā-Sīn). This is according to the view of Sībawayh that it is a name for the sūrah. It has been said that it is indeclinable (mabnī), and the movement is for the sake of seriousness in fleeing from the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqā' al-sākinayn), and the fatḥa is for lightness, as in ayna. The reason for indeclinability is not hidden from you if you have comprehensively grasped what they established concerning "Alif-Lām-Mīm" at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqara. Do not neglect what they said regarding the accusative by supposing the verb of oath, that it is not permissible because it involves gathering two oaths upon one sworn matter, and that is disliked. There is no way to make the wāw after it a conjunction rather than an oath-particle, because of the difference in grammatical case (iʿrāb).

Kalbī read the nūn with ḍamma. It is interpreted as a called-upon, specified vocative (munādā maqṣūd), on the basis that it means "a human being" (insān), or as the predicate of an omitted subject, or as a subject whose predicate is omitted. This is to be estimated if it is a name for the sūrah. This applies if it is a name for the Qur'an, and it is applied to a part as it is applied to the whole. Making it an omitted-predicate subject that is an oath, meaning "Yā-Sīn is my oath," like "amānatu Allāh la-afʿalanna" with nominative case, its condition is not hidden. It has also been said that the ḍamma in it is a ḍamma of indeclinability, as in ḥaythu.

Abū al-Sammāl and Ibn Abī Isḥāq also read it with kasra, and it is interpreted as the movement for seriousness in fleeing from the two unvocalized letters with what is the original (vowel). So reflect and remember.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 2:

﴿Wa-l-Qur'ani﴾ is the beginning of an oath (qasam). It is also permissible that it be a conjunction (ʿatf) with "Ya-Sin," on the basis that it is in the genitive case by the implied particle of oath (bi); not that it is an oath after an oath, because of what you have heard of their speech.

﴿al-Hakim﴾ means "possessing wisdom" (dhu hikmatin), on the basis that it is a form of attribution (sighat nisbah), like laban (possessing milk) and tamir (possessing dates), meaning it includes wisdom. Or it means "the one who speaks with wisdom," like "the living" (al-hayy), on the basis that it is a metaphor by implicit comparison (al-istiʿarah al-makniyyah). Or it means "the one characterised by wisdom," on the basis that the attribution is figurative (majaz), and its true meaning is the attribution to God Most High, the One who speaks it.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit by Abu Hayyan), it is said: it is either a form on the pattern fa'il with the meaning of maf'al, like "aqadtu al-ʿasal" (I made the honey thick), so it is ʿaqid, meaning muʿqad (thickened); or it is for intensification (mubalaghah) from hakim (one who judges/decrees).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 3:

﴿Indeed, you are among the messengers.﴾ This is the response (jawab) to the oath, and the sentence serves to refute the denial of the disbelievers concerning his messengership, peace and blessings be upon him. For they said: ﴿You are not a messenger﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43]. What has already been mentioned indicates that they were in a great state of denial, namely His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿But when a warner came to them, it increased them only in aversion﴾ [Fatir: 42], out of arrogance in the land and evil scheming. This verse is among what was alluded to by His, may He be exalted, saying in reply to their denial: ﴿Say: Allah is sufficient as a witness between me and you﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43].

And specifying the Qur'an as the subject of the oath first, and describing it as "the wise" (al-hakim) second, is an honouring of its status in the most complete manner.

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on surah 36, verse 4:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿on a straight path﴾ is a second predicate (khabar thani) of inna (indeed). Al-Zajjaj chose this, saying: "It is the best in Arabic." Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in it, referring to him, peace and blessings be upon him, which is hidden in the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur), or it is what occurs as the subject of inna (ism inna), based on the opinion of those who permit a hal from the subject (mubtada'). It is also permitted that it be connected to "the messengers," and the intended meaning is not a hal or a future sense; that is, "you are among those who were sent on a straight path." It is also permitted that it be a hal from the returning pronoun of the relative clause hidden in the active participle, or a hal from "the messengers" itself.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned from these possibilities only that it is a predicate and that it is a relative complement (silah) to "the messengers." In any case, the intended meaning of "the straight path" is what encompasses the true beliefs and laws. The purpose of the statement is not to inform by distinguishing the one who was sent on a straight path from others who are not described by this, so that it could be said that this is already established before him, since everyone knows that the messengers are only on a straight path. Rather, the purpose is to inform that he is described by such-and-such, and that what the one so described has brought is such-and-such, glorifying the status of both of them. They took this course as a way of brevity.

Also, the indefiniteness in ﴿a path﴾ is for magnification. It indicates that he was sent from among the straight paths on a path whose description cannot be fully grasped, and this is something not known before. It is not objected that the straight path is one only. Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So follow it, and do not follow the other ways﴾? For each prophet who legislates has a method that is straight, and with respect to its return to the Sender, Exalted is His majesty, all is unified, and with respect to the particularity of the one sent and the laws, it differs. Thus it is correct that he was sent from among the straight paths, etc. Also, it is a supposition, and the supposition is the exaltation of this path, that there is no path more upright than it, actually or hypothetically, and no consideration is given to the possibility that another exists first. This is close to the style of "someone like you does not do such-and-such." So understand, and do not be heedless.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 5:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful﴾ is in the accusative (*nasb*) either as a praise (*madh*) or as a verbal noun (*maṣdariyya*) for a deleted verb, meaning: "It was sent down as a sending down."

A group of the Seven Readers, along with Abu Bakr, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, al-Hasan, al-A'raj and al-A'mash, read it in the nominative (*raf'*), as the predicate (*khabar*) of a deleted subject (*mubtada'*). The verbal noun is then used in the sense of the passive participle (*maf'ul*), meaning: "It is a revelation," that is, "something sent down by the Mighty, the Merciful." The pronoun refers to the Qur'an. It is also permissible to keep it in its original sense by taking it to be the very act of sending down.

It has been permitted that it be the predicate of *Yā Sīn*, if the intended meaning is the surah. The clause containing the oath is then a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*), and the oath serves to emphasise both the thing sworn to and the thing sworn by, as a matter of importance. It should not be objected that the unbelievers deny the Qur'an, so how can it be sworn by in order to bind them to it.

Abu Haywa, al-Yazidi and al-Qūrḍī, on the authority of Abu Ja'far and Shayba, read it in the genitive (*khafḍ*), either as an apposition (*badaliyya*) to "the Qur'an" or as an attributive (*wasfiyya*) qualifying it.

In any case, there is in this a display of the Qur'an's magnificence in relation to others, after the declaration of its intrinsic magnificence through its description as wise. In the specifying of the two noble names, which denote complete dominance and abundant mercy, there is an exhortation to belief in it, by both warning and encouragement, and an indication that its sending down arises from the utmost mercy, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107].

[p. 213]

**Lित** — "*li-tundhira*" (in order that you may warn) is connected to *tanzil* (revelation) or to its implied verb in the second grammatical reading. The meaning is: it was sent down as the revelation of the Mighty, the Merciful, *in order that you may warn* with it or with what indicates it. ﴿*Indeed you are among the messengers*﴾, that is: you have been sent, or: "Indeed you are a messenger, in order that you may warn ﴿a people whose forefathers were not warned﴾". That is, their forefathers were not warned, according to what is narrated from Qatadah. Here *ma* is a negation, and the clause is a qualifier of ﴿a people﴾, explaining the extent of their need for warning. By *indhar* (warning) is meant informing or frightening, and its second object is omitted, meaning "a punishment", in line with the Almighty's words: ﴿Indeed We have warned you of a near punishment﴾ [al-Naba': 40]. By "their forefathers" is meant their nearer forefathers; otherwise the more distant ones were warned by Isma'il, peace be upon him, who conveyed to them the law of Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

Some of them did hold fast to his law in its most complete form, then the matter slackened and the periods lengthened, so that nothing remained of his law, peace be upon him, except the name. In al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) it is said: the call to God the Exalted has not ceased among any nation, either through direct contact with their prophets or through transmission until the time of the sending of our Prophet ﷺ. The verses which indicate that Quraysh had not been reached by any warner mean that no warner had directly reached them or their nearer forefathers. As for the claim that warning ceased, this is not so; and when its traces were established, we know the sending of the Prophet ﷺ. What the theologians mention about the condition of the people of the intervals (*ahl al-fatarat*) is on the basis of supposition. End.

In light of this, the meaning is: no messenger warned their forefathers; that is, no one directly warned them, not that no warner had warned them at all. Thus it is permissible that some who was not a prophet had warned them, such as Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl and Qass ibn Sa'idah. There is therefore no contradiction between this and the Almighty's words: ﴿And there was no nation but that a warner had passed among them﴾ [Fatir: 24]. Nor does this deny the interval mentioned in the Almighty's words: ﴿after an interval in the messengers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 19], because that is an interval in sending, and its cessation for a time, not a complete interval of warning.

According to 'Ikrimah, *ma* means *alladhi* (that which). It is also permitted that it be a qualifying (descriptive) *ma*. In both readings it is the second object of *(tundhira)*, meaning: "in order that you may warn a people with that which was warned of by the messengers to their more distant forefathers, or with something the messengers had warned their forefathers of." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is possible that *ma* is a verbal noun (*masdariyyah*), so it is an adjective of an emphatic verbal noun, meaning: "in order that you may warn a people with a warning like the warning of the messengers to their more distant forefathers." It has also been said that it is redundant, but this is not correct.

﴿So they are heedless﴾: on the first reading this is a consequence of and results from the negation of warning, and the pronoun refers to both groups, meaning: their forefathers were not warned, so they all are heedless because of that. On the remaining readings it is connected to the Almighty's words ﴿in order that you may warn﴾, or to what is implied by ﴿indeed you are among the messengers﴾, coming to explain his warning, peace and blessings be upon him, or his sending, by their heedlessness which makes it necessary, like the phrase "give him water, for he is thirsty." This is on the basis that the pronoun refers to the people specifically. The meaning is: "so they are heedless of it," that is, of what their forefathers were warned of.

Al-Khafaji said: it is permissible that it be connected to this (clause) even on the first reading, and connected to the Almighty's words ﴿in order that you may warn﴾ on the readings, with *fa* taken as causal and the pronoun referring to them or to their forefathers. End. But it is not hidden from you that what comes first to the mind is what was established first.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 36, verse 7:**

"Indeed the Word has come to be fulfilled" (*laqad haqqa*) is the answer to an implied oath, meaning: by Allah, the Word that I spoke to Iblis (Satan) on the day he said, "I will surely mislead them all" (Q. 15:39), has indeed been established and become binding. That Word is, "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and humankind, all of them" (Q. 11:119; Q. 32:13). "Against most of them" (*ʿala aktharihim*) is connected to *haqqa*. The meaning is: it was decreed in My knowledge that most of them would enter among those whom I will fill Hell with, and they are the followers of Iblis. This is indicated by the mention of the jinn before humankind, and it is made explicit by the verse, "I will surely fill Hell with you and with those among them who follow you, all of them" (Q. 38:85).

There is no objection to taking "the Word" to mean something else, but the well-known view is what was mentioned above. The apparent sense of al-Raghib al-Isfahani's statement is that "the Word" refers to Allah's knowledge of them, and there is no need to commit to this. It has also been said that the prepositional phrase is connected to "the Word," and it is said *qala ʿalayhi* when one speaks evil about someone. The meaning would then be: My punishment of them was established in eternity. There is much to say about this. Its connection to *haqqa* is supported by the verse, "Indeed, those against whom the Word of your Lord has been fulfilled will not believe" (Q. 10:96). Abu Hayyan reported that the meaning is: the Word which Allah spoke through the tongues of the messengers, peace be upon them, concerning tawhid and other matters, has been fulfilled, and that its proof is such-and-such. This, as you see, is far-fetched.

"So they do not believe" (*fahum la yu'minun*): that is, most of them do not believe in your warning to them. The *fa'* is a *fa'* of consequence, attached to a judgment that is caused by what precedes it. It therefore indicates that the establishment of the Word against them is a cause of their denial and disbelief, and that it is a cause in the sense that Allah's foreknowledge concerns their bad choice and their actual condition in reality. Allah's knowledge does not relate to things except as they are in themselves. The result is that their bad choice and their actual condition in reality are the cause of their denial and their failure to believe after the warning. Thus there is no absolute compulsion, nor is it that the known thing follows the knowledge.

Some have said: the *fa'* may be a *fa'* of consequence, and the establishment of the Word being a cause of their non-belief is based on the view that the known thing follows the knowledge. Or it may be a *fa'* of causation, indicating that their non-belief is the cause of the establishment of the Word, based on the view that knowledge follows the known thing. Compulsion does not follow on either view. On the second it is obvious. On the first, it is because knowledge is not, according to the one who holds this view, an independent cause; rather, their choice and their acquisition (*kasb*) have a part in it. So consider this carefully. The *fa'* of consequence is the view I incline to.

[p. 214]

﴿Indeed, We have placed upon their necks﴾: *'a'nāq* is the plural of *'unuq* (with a *ḍamma*, or with two *ḍammas*), meaning the neck. It is also said *'anīq* on the pattern of *amīr*, and *'unaq* on the pattern of *ṣurad*.

﴿shackles﴾: *aghlāl* is the plural of *ghull* (with a *ḍamma*). It is, according to what has been said, that by which the hand is bound to the neck for torment and tightening. In *al-Baḥr* it is said that the *ghull* is that which surrounds the neck, for the sake of restraint, constriction, torment and captivity; and along with the neck, the two hands, or one hand, are included.

Al-Rāghib mentioned that it is that by which something is restrained, so that the limbs are placed in its midst. Its root is from *ghalal*, meaning to be enveloped by a thing and to be in its midst; from this comes *ghalal* for water flowing between trees, which may also be called *ghayl*. It seems that there is an inversion (*qalb*) in the speech regarding it, meaning: We have placed their necks in shackles, just as you say, "I placed the ring on my finger," meaning, "I placed my finger in the ring." It is also permitted that it be in the manner of His saying: ﴿And I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 71]. The *tanwīn* (indefinite ending) is for magnification and awe, meaning: great, terrifying shackles. The attribution of the verb to the pronoun of majesty supports this.

﴿so they are﴾: that is, the shackles, as is the apparent meaning, ﴿up to the chins﴾. *Adhqān* is the plural of *dhaqan* (with a *taḥrīk*, i.e. vowel), meaning the place where the two jaws meet from below. The *alif-lām* is for specific reference or is a substitute for the genitive complement. The adverbial phrase is connected to a special, complete predicate (*kawn khāṣṣ*), which is the predicate of *hiya* ("they are"). That is, they reach or end at their chins. The *fā'* is for consequence (*tafrī'*). It is also said that it is merely for sequence (*ta'qīb*), based on not taking the *tanwīn* to mean magnification and awe.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so they are lowering their heads﴾ is a result of ﴿so they are up to the chins﴾; thus the *fā'* is also for consequence. *Muqmaḥ*, according to *al-Nihāyah*, is one who raises his head and lowers his gaze, as if he intended the unknown, in a way that he raises... etc. Abū 'Ubayda said: it is said *qamaḥa al-ba'īr qumūḥan* when the camel raises its head from the water trough without drinking. The plural is *qimāḥ*. From it is the saying of Bishr describing a ship in which seasickness seized them:

"And we, upon its sides, sit, lowering our gaze like camels that refuse to drink."

Al-Layth said: it is the camel's raising its head when it drinks foul water and then returns. From it is named the two *Kānūn*s (months) *Qumāḥ*, with a *ḍamma* or *kasra* on the *qāf*, because camels, when they come to the water, raise their heads because of its intense cold. Al-Rāghib said: *qamḥ* is raising the head for the sipping of something made from *qamḥ*, that is, wheat, when it runs in the ear from the time of ripening until it becomes firm. Then the raising of the head, however it occurs, is called *qamḥ*. *Qamaḥa al-ba'īr* means the camel raised its head, and *aqmaḥtu al-ba'īr* means I tied its head backward. It is also said: the *muqmiḥ* is one whose chin is pulled until it reaches his chest and then he raises it. Mujāhid said: the *qāmiḥ* is one who raises his head and places his hand over his mouth. Al-Ḥasan said: it is one who raises his gaze toward the place of his foot. Its apparent meaning requires that there be a downward movement of the head there, whereas what is known in *qamḥ* is raising.

The point of the consequence [is this]: the collar of the shackle that is on the neck of the one who is shackled lies, at the junction of its two ends beneath the chin, as a ring in which the head of the post sits, projecting from the ring up to the chin. So it does not let him lower his head or press his nape; he remains always raising his head, especially if the shackle is large.

Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: the *ighlāl* is a wide [collar] whose edges reach the chins, so that *qamḥ* results. The speech of Ibn al-Athīr suggests that the *qamḥ* is due to the narrowness of the shackle. If it is intended that We placed in each of their necks shackles, the matter of *qamḥ* becomes clearer and clearer.

Al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj and al-Ṭabrisī said: the pronoun in *hiya* refers to the hands, even though no mention of them has preceded, because their place in meaning is clear, since the shackle includes the neck and the hand. For this reason it is called *jāmi'a* (a binding). What is in the neck alone, or in the hand alone, is not called a *ghull*. So when it is mentioned with the neck, the hand is also intended; and when it is mentioned with the hand, as in the reading of Ibn 'Abbās "*fī aydīhim aghlālan*" and in the reading of Ibn Mas'ūd "*fī aymānihim aghlālan*," the neck is also intended. This is a kind of conciseness and brevity. A parallel to this is the saying of the poet:

"And I do not know, when I head toward a land, desiring good, which of the two will befall me:
Is it the good that I seek, or the evil that does not leave me alone?"

Here he mentioned only the good, and said *ayyuhumā* ("which of the two"), meaning good and evil; and it is known that good and evil both come upon a human being.

Al-Zamakhsharī chose what has been mentioned, then said: The evidence for it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so they are lowering their heads﴾. Do you not see how He made the raising of the head a result of ﴿so they are up to the chins﴾? If the pronoun referred to the hands, the meaning of causation in the raising of the head would not be apparent. Moreover, this supposition contains a kind of artificiality, and leaving the apparent meaning, which the sense itself calls for, in favor of the hidden one, which is remote, is leaving the clear truth for the confused falsehood. End.

The author of *al-Intiṣāf* wished to support the Jamā'a, and said: It is possible that the *fā'* in ﴿so they are lowering their heads﴾ is for sequence, like the preceding one, or for causation, since the pressing of the hand together with the neck necessitates the raising of the head, because the hand remains holding the shackle beneath the chin, raising it. And because if the hand were free, it would be a relief to the one shackled, for he might thereby devise a way to free himself from the shackle; so it indicates the closing of the door of stratagem. End.

The author of *al-Kashf* said: The answer is that there is no grandeur in mere sequence. Moreover, what al-Zamakhsharī mentioned, which we have also alluded to earlier, is independent in bringing about the raising of the head, so where is the sequence? And with this the answer regarding causation is complete. His saying, "and because the hand, etc.," cannot stand as an answer without the first two. End.

In any case, returning the pronoun to the shackle is the more worthy of consideration, and the eloquence of the Noble Book requires it, and one hardly turns to anything else.

[Page 215]

﴿And We have placed﴾ is conjoined to the earlier ﴿We have placed﴾. ﴿Before them﴾ means in front of them, ﴿a barrier﴾ a great one. It is said it is a kind of barrier. ﴿And behind them﴾ means behind them, ﴿a barrier﴾ likewise. The "in front" and "behind" are a metonymy (kinaya) for all directions. ﴿So We have covered them﴾ means We covered their sight with what We placed as a barrier. It is reported from Mujahid that ﴿So We have covered them﴾ means We clothed their sight with a veil. ﴿So they﴾ because of that ﴿do not see﴾ means they are not able to see anything at all.

A group among the seven readers and others read "saddan" (a barrier) with a ḍamma on the sin (sudd), and this is a dialectal form of the word. It is said that what is made by people is with a fatḥa, and what is made by God the Exalted is with a ḍamma. It is also said the reverse. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Ibn Ya'mur, 'Ikrima, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Sirin, al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Zayd ibn 'Ali, Abu Hanifa, Yazid al-Barbari, Yazid ibn al-Muhallab and Ibn Muqsim read ﴿fa-a'shaynahum﴾ with the letter ʿayn, from al-ʿashā, which is weakness of sight. The combined two conjoined clauses, from His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, We have placed﴾ etc., are an emphasis and confirmation of what is indicated by His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Certainly the word has come true against most of them﴾ etc., of their bad choice and the ugliness of their state. If God the Exalted made them, by what He manifested in them of great self-admiration, arrogant against following the Messengers, peace be upon them, lifting their heads high, not submitting to what they brought, and closed off the doors of reflection on what would benefit them completely, that is only because they are of bad choice and ugly states. Their essences have loved what they are upon with an essential love, and sought it with a predisposed seeking, so there is no receptivity in them for anything else, and they do not turn to anything other than it. If their essences and what they are upon are compared with body, place, or the number three and oddness, for example, they would hardly find any difference. ﴿And God did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves﴾ [al-Nahl: 33].

So in the speech there are multiple similes (tashbihat), as we have hinted. This is the view required by what many eminent scholars hold, even if they did not mention it in the verse. In al-Intisaf, if the simile is separated, their insistence on disbelief is likened to the shackles, and their arrogance against accepting the truth and humbling themselves to hear it is likened to raising the head (iqmah), because one who is raised-headed does not lower his head.

His statement, exalted is He, ﴿so they are up to the chins﴾ completes the necessity of the raising of the head for them. The lack of reflection on the conditions of earlier nations is likened to a barrier behind them, and the lack of reflection on future consequences is likened to a barrier in front of them. In al-Taysir, joining the hands to the chins with shackles is an expression for withholding success, until they became arrogant toward the truth, because the arrogant one is described as raising the neck, and the humble one by its opposite, as in His statement, exalted is He, ﴿so their necks remained bowed to it, submitting﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 4]. The purpose of placing the barrier is not mentioned. The Imam mentioned that the obstacle to reflecting on the signs is of two kinds: one kind prevents reflection on the self, and this is likened to the shackle that makes its bearer raise his head, not seeing himself, his gaze not falling on his body. The other kind prevents reflection on the horizons, and this is likened to the encompassing barrier, for one enclosed by a barrier does not have his gaze fall on the horizons, so the signs in them do not appear to him. Whoever is afflicted with both is completely deprived of reflection.

Some chose that ﴿Indeed, We have placed﴾ etc. is an allegory (tamthil) brought to establish their insistence on disbelief and their not desisting from it. Thus their state in that is depicted by the state of those whose necks are shackled. It is permitted that His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and We have placed﴾ etc. be a completion of that and its perfection, and that it be an independent allegory, for their being confined between two terrifying barriers that have covered their sight, so that they see nothing at all, is sufficient to reveal the completeness of the horror of their state and that they are imprisoned in the dungeon of error and ignorance.

Abu Hayyan said: The apparent meaning is that His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, We have placed﴾ etc. is literal. When God the Exalted informed that they do not believe, He informed, glorified is He, about some of their states in the Hereafter when they enter the Fire. The use of the past tense is for the certainty of occurrence. This is not weakened, as Ibn 'Atiyya claimed, by His statement, exalted is He, ﴿So We have covered them, so they do not see﴾, because the sight of the disbeliever on that day is sharp, seeing the ugliness of his state. Do you not see His statement, glorified is He, ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind﴾ [al-Isra': 97], and His statement, glorified is He, ﴿He will say: My Lord, why have You gathered me blind?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 125], and His statement, glorified is He, ﴿So your sight today is sharp﴾ [Qaf: 22]? Either these are two states, or His statement, exalted is He, ﴿So your sight today is sharp﴾ is an allusion (kinaya) to his perception of what it will lead to, until it is as if he sees it. Some objected to this, saying it would make the speech extraneous in between, and that its justification, as an explanation of His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Certainly the word has come true against most of them﴾, has been criticized. The fair view is that it is contrary to the apparent meaning.

al-Dahhak and al-Farra' said regarding His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, We have placed shackles upon their necks﴾, that it is a metaphor (isti'ara) for their being prevented from spending in the way of God the Exalted, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾ [al-Isra': 29]. Perhaps he made the second clause a metaphor for their being prevented from seeing good and striving for it. It is not hidden that the speech being extraneous in between is most evident under this view.

Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite in the mosque and would raise his voice in recitation, so some people of Quraysh were harmed by it, until they stood to seize him. Then their hands were found gathered up to their necks, and they could not see. They came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: We beseech you by God the Exalted and by kinship, O Muhammad. He said: There was no clan of the clans of Quraysh without the Prophet (ﷺ) having a relative among them. So the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, supplicated until that was removed from them. Then there was revealed ﴿Ya-Sin. By the wise Qur'an﴾ up to His statement, glorified is He, ﴿Whether you warn them or do not warn them, they will not believe﴾. Not one of that group believed.

It is reported that the two verses were revealed concerning the Banu Makhzum. That is because Abu Jahl carried a stone to strike the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with it while he was praying. His hand became fixed to his neck until he returned to his companions, and the stone was stuck to his hand, and they did not free it except with difficulty. Then another Makhzumi took it, and when he approached the Messenger (ﷺ), God the Exalted obliterated his sight. He returned to his companions and did not see them until they called out to him. Then a third rose and said: I will surely crush his head. Then he took the stone and set off, but he returned backwards, retreating on his heels, until he fell on his back unconscious. It was said to him: What is your condition? He said: I saw a great thing. When I came close to him, there was a stallion I had never seen larger than it, standing between me and him. By al-Lat and al-'Uzza, if I had come close to him, it would have devoured me.

So making the shackle a metaphor for preventing whoever intended to harm him, peace be upon him, and making the barrier a metaphor for stripping away the strength of sight, is as has been said.

al-Suddi said: The barrier is a darkness that came between and prevented sight. Other things close to this have come in the reports, and the linking of the verses to it is not apparent. Perhaps this is in terms of the indication of the two verses to what they are upon of insistence on disbelief and severity of obstinacy. Yet, in the view of the eloquent, the preferable course is to take the speech in a sense other than what the apparent meanings of the reports require, of what you have heard. There is nothing in them that contradicts it upon careful examination. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 10:

﴿And it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe.﴾ That is: your warning them and not warning them are equal in their sight, as has been verified above at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah. The apparent view is that the conjunction (ʿatf) is upon ﴿Indā jaʿalnā﴾ (﴿Indeed, We have placed﴾), and it seems it was brought in to make explicit what they are in themselves, after the allusion to it earlier, on the basis that it is among the things that follow from the aforementioned placing. Close to this is the view that what came before explains their state as something placed (upon them), while this explains their state without consideration of any placing, and in it there is a preparation for His Exalted saying: ﴿You only warn﴾, etc.

In Irshad al-ʿAql al-Salim (Abu al-Suʿud's commentary): it is an explanation of their condition by way of explicit statement, following its explanation by way of metaphor. In al-Hawashi al-Khafajiyyah: it was not introduced with the particle fa (so, therefore), although it follows from what precedes it, either by leaving it to the mind of the hearer, or because it is not intended here. End of quote. Consider whether you find any obstacle to the conjunction being upon ﴿Lā yubṣirūn﴾ (﴿they do not see﴾), so that it would be a predicate for them too, falling within the scope of the fa, and the derivation from what came before would be as if it were said: "So they are equal in respect to them, etc." The difference between the two sentences, nominal and verbal, is not, I think, something you would consider an obstacle.

As for His Exalted saying: ﴿They will not believe﴾, it is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming what precedes it and clarifying what is implied in it of the ambiguity regarding that in which equality holds; or it is an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal) for it; or it is a substitute (badal) for it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 11:

Since the warning's effect on them was equated with its absence, he followed this with an explanation of who is affected by it. So He, glorified is He, said: ﴿You can only warn﴾, meaning, a warning that is followed by an effect.

﴿Those who follow the Reminder﴾, that is, the Qur'an. This is what was narrated from Qatadah: by reflecting upon it and acting upon it. It was also said: [the Reminder is] the admonition. "Ittaba'a" here means "yattabi'u" (follows), and the use of the past tense indicates that the act is certain to occur. Alternatively, the meaning is: your warning benefits only the believers who have followed (the Reminder). In that case, "those who follow" refers to the believers, and "warning" refers to warning them against what may slip from them after they have followed, so there is no requirement of obtaining what is already obtained. It was also said: "those who follow" refers to those who are so in the knowledge of God, Exalted is He, and they are the few who the Word has not become due against.

﴿And fear the Most Merciful﴾, that is, His punishment, and who are not deceived by His mercy, Mighty and Majestic is He. For He, glorified is He, despite the immensity of His mercy, is severe in punishment, as His saying, Exalted is He, expresses: ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Most Forgiving, the Most Merciful, and that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾ [al-Hijr: 49]. From what has been established, the reason for mentioning "the Most Merciful" together with fear, rather than "the Subduer" or the like, becomes known.

﴿In the unseen﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the omitted noun that is implied in the structure of the sentence, as we have indicated. That is: he feared the punishment of the Most Merciful while the punishment was unseen, meaning absent from him; its essence is that he feared the punishment before it descended and before witnessing its terrors. It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause relating to the subject of "khashiya" (feared), meaning: he feared the punishment of the Most Merciful while being absent from the punishment, not witnessing it; or he feared while being absent from the eyes of people, not displaying his fear to them, since open display is rarely free from showing off. Some have interpreted "al-ghayb" as "the heart," and made the preposition relate to "khashiya," meaning: he feared in his heart and did not display fear, and he is not one who fears. It was said: it is also permissible to make it a circumstantial clause relating to "al-Rahman," and its status is not hidden. The discussion of "khashiya" follows the same pattern as the discussion of "ittaba'a."

﴿So give him good tidings of forgiveness﴾, great for what has passed, and it was said: for what may slip from him; ﴿and a generous reward﴾, good, whose worth cannot be measured, for what he has advanced. The "fa" (so) indicates that the glad tidings, or the command to give them, follow from what precedes it, namely following the Reminder and fearing (the Most Merciful). In al-Bahr: since the warning has proven effective in him, "so give him good tidings," etc. So do not be heedless.

It is narrated from Qatadah that the generous reward is interpreted as Paradise, and the intended meaning is its bliss, which encompasses what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human being. The greatest of all of that is the sight of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 12:

And His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life﴾ and so on, is a general conclusion (tadhyil) addressed to both groups who are set upon disbelief and who are reinforced by the warning, by way of intimidation and encouragement, threat and promise. The repetition of the pronoun (inna nahnu) serves either to give exclusivity (hasr) or to emphasize. How subtle is this pronoun, whose reverse is like its direct form here. The pronoun of majesty (nahnu) indicates the greatness of the act, and the emphasis (inna) is either for attending to the matter of the report or for refuting denial, for the disbelievers used to say: ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world; we die and we live, and we shall not be raised again﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 37]. That is: indeed it is We who bring the dead, all of them, back to life by resurrecting them on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And We record what they have sent forward﴾: the deeds, good and bad, that they have sent ahead, ﴿and their traces﴾ which they have left behind them of good deeds, such as knowledge they taught, or a book they composed, or an endowment (habis) they established, or a building they erected in the way of Allah the Exalted, and other forms of righteousness; and of evil deeds, such as establishing laws of injustice and aggression, and arranging the foundations of evil and corruption among people, and other kinds of mischief which they initiated and instituted after them for the corrupters.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Jarir ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bajali, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Whoever institutes a good practice will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts by it after him, without their rewards being diminished in any way; and whoever institutes an evil practice will bear its burden and the burden of whoever acts by it after him, without their burdens being diminished in any way." Then he recited: ﴿And We record what they have sent forward and their traces.﴾" And from Anas that he said concerning the verse: "This refers to walking on Friday (to the mosque)."

Some have interpreted "traces" as the steps taken to the mosques in general, citing what 'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Tirmidhi (who graded it as hasan) related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "The Banu Salamah were in a remote part of Madinah and they wanted to move closer to the mosque, so Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Indeed, it is We who bring the dead to life, and We record what they have sent forward and their traces﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned them and said: Indeed, He records your traces. Then he recited the verse to them, and they stayed put."

Imam Ahmad in al-Zuhd, Ibn Majah, and others related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Ansar lived far from the mosque, so they wanted to move close to the mosque, and ﴿And We record what they have sent forward and their traces﴾ was revealed. They said: No, we will remain in our place."

You know that there is no indication in what has been mentioned that "traces" means only steps; the most that it indicates is that they are among the traces, so "traces" should be taken to encompass them and other things. These two reports and similar ones have been cited as evidence that the verse is Madani.

Abu Hayyan said: "That is not a sound claim," and he criticized it for what has been reported indicating it. Al-Khafaji defended it by saying that the indicating hadith is contradicted by what is in the two Sahihs, that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse to them and did not mention that it was revealed concerning them, and that his recitation to them, upon him be blessings and peace, does not preclude prior revelation. Abu Hayyan's point here was not that he denied the basic hadith. It is not hidden that the two preceding hadiths are apparent that the verse was revealed on that occasion, and there is nothing in the report of the two Sahihs that contradicts that. What is strange is how al-Khafaji failed to notice this.

It has been said: "what they sent forward" refers to intentions, and "their traces" to deeds. The apparent meaning is that the writing refers to recording in the scrolls of the noble recording angels, and because it is by His command, it is attributed to Him, glorified is He. It is mentioned later than the giving of life, though it precedes it, because its effect appears after it. On this basis, the interpretation of "what they sent forward" as intentions is weakened, in light of what some reports indicate, that the angels, peace be upon them, do not have access to intentions and are not commanded to record them.

Some have interpreted "writing" as "preservation," meaning: We preserve that and establish it in Our knowledge, not forgetting it nor neglecting it, as a written thing is established. Perhaps you may prefer that the writing of "what they sent forward and their traces" is a metaphor (kinaya) for requiting them for it: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil. In that case, the reason for mentioning it after the giving of life is clear.

It is reported from al-Hasan and al-Dahhak that Allah's giving life to the dead is His bringing them from shirk to faith, and they made death a metaphor for ignorance. The definiteness of "al-mawta" is for specific reference, and the discourse on it is an emphasis on the promised good tidings, as if it were said: your warning only benefits these people because We give them life and record their righteous deeds and traces. The distance of this is not hidden. Zarr and Masruq read "wayuktabu" with the yā' in the passive voice, and "wa-athāruhum" in the nominative.

﴿And everything﴾ among things, whatever it may be; the accusative is by way of the verb being implied (ishtighal), meaning: and We have counted every thing ﴿We have counted﴾, that is, We have clarified and preserved it. The root of ihsa' is counting, and then it was used figuratively for what has been mentioned, because counting is for its sake.

﴿In a manifest Imam﴾, meaning a great-status origin which is followed, imitated, obeyed, and not opposed. ﴿Clear﴾: revealing what was and what will be. It is, according to what al-Bahr relates from Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd, the Preserved Tablet. The explanation of everything in it, if the generality is taken in its literal sense so that it includes the events of Paradise and what renews for its people without cessation, is like what is related about the explanation of the worldly events in al-Jafr al-Jami', but on a higher and more noble pattern. Similar to this is what many have said about the Noble Qur'an including everything, even the names of kings and the durations of their reigns. Or it may be said that the explanation of that in it is not all at once but in stages, such that a set of things, such as the events of a thousand years for example, is explained in it, then at the completion of the thousand it is erased, and another set, such as the events of another thousand, is explained, and so on. What prompts what has been mentioned is that the Tablet, according to the Muslims, is a body, and every body has finite dimensions as the proofs indicate, and the explanation of everything in it in the known manner for us all at once necessitates that the finite be a container for the infinite, which is absurd by necessity. And if by "everything" is meant the things of this present creation and the deeds of the servants and their states in it, then there is no difficulty in explaining them in the known manner all at once.

What appears to me as more probable is that what is written in the Tablet is what was and what will be until the Day of Resurrection, and that is finite. Some traditions testify to this, and the unrestricted among them is to be understood in light of the restricted. The reality of the Tablet has not been described with anything that gives certainty, and for this reason we refrain from specifying it. That one of its two faces is a red ruby and the other a green emerald has come in some traditions, but we have no certainty of its authenticity. That it is one of the immaterial beings, and that there is nothing which it does not know actually, is a view no Muslim has adopted; it is merely one of the imaginings of the philosophers and those who follow their path, so it should not be relied upon. Some have interpreted the Clear Imam as His eternal knowledge, just as they interpreted "the Mother of the Book" in His saying: ﴿And with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 39] as that. It is a principle that nothing among the rows of possible things opposes it, as al-Shafi'i's saying hints:

You created the servants according to what You knew, so in knowledge the youth and the elder proceed.

Describing it as "clear" is because it is manifest; they have said: knowledge is an attribute by which the known is revealed to whoever it subsists in. Or because the manifesting of things from the treasuries of non-existence occurs after its relation to them, for power relates to a thing only after knowledge: the thing is first known, then willed, then power relates to bringing it into being, and it comes into being. The fault in this interpretation, in departing from the apparent meaning, is not hidden. On this basis there is no discussion of generality. Yes, regarding the manner of the existence of things in His knowledge, the Exalted, there is a lengthy discussion whose place is in the books of kalam.

It is reported from al-Hasan that by it is meant the scrolls of deeds, but this is not the right view. It has been related to me from some extremist Shi'a that the intended "Clear Imam" is 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and the counting of everything in it is of the type of:

It is not a thing deemed unusual for Allah to gather the world into one (thing).

Among them are some who claim that this is in the sense of His making him, may Allah ennoble his face, a treasury of knowables, like the Preserved Tablet. What great ignorance of the glorious Book this involves is not hidden; we ask Allah the Exalted for pardon and well-being. It is possible to say that they meant by this something like what the Sufis meant when they applied "the Manifest Book" to the Perfect Man, as a term of their own convention, and thus the matter of ignorance is lightened. The perfection of 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, is denied only by one of deficient intellect and no religion.

And Abu al-Sammal read "wa-kullu" with the nominative, as the inceptive subject (mubtada').

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 13:

﴿And strike for them an example: the companions of the town,﴾ either it is a coordination (ʿatf) of the story upon the story preceding it, or it is a coordination upon something implied, meaning: "So warn them, and strike for them..." etc. The striking of an example (ḍarb al-mathal) is used at times for applying one strange state to another similar to it, as in His Exalted saying: ﴿Allah strikes an example for those who disbelieved: the wife of Noah﴾ [al-Tahrim: 10], and at other times for mentioning a strange state and clarifying it for the people without intending to match it with a counterpart, as in His saying: ﴿And We have struck for you the examples﴾ [Ibrahim: 45] in one view, meaning: We have clarified for you states that are wondrous, which in their strangeness are like examples. So the meaning on the first reading is: make the companions of the town an example for these people in exaggerating disbelief and persisting in denial, that is, apply their condition to theirs; [here] ﴿mathalan﴾ is the second object of (iḍrib), and ﴿aṣḥāba al-qaryah﴾ is its first object, which was postponed so that what explains and clarifies it would be connected to it. On the second reading: mention to them and make clear to them a story which in its strangeness is like the example.

His Glorified saying ﴿aṣḥāba al-qaryah﴾ is with an implied genitive construction, meaning "the likeness of the companions of the town," and this implied noun is a substitute (badal) for ﴿mathalan﴾, a substitute of whole for whole, or an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to it, according to the view that the two may differ in definiteness and indefiniteness. It is also permitted that the implied word be an object and this be a state (ḥāl). The town, as related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Buraydah and ʿIkrimah, is Antioch, and in al-Bahr it is said that it is definitely that, without disagreement.

﴿When the messengers came to them﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for ﴿aṣḥāba al-qaryah﴾, or an adverbial clause of time (ẓarf) for the implied verb. It is also permitted that it be a substitute of whole for ﴿aṣḥāb﴾, with the intended meaning being their story and the adverbial clause what is in it, but this is an unnecessary strain with no reason for it. It was said: "when he came to them" rather than "when he came to them" is an indication that the messengers came to them in their place of residence. The messengers, according to Qatadah and other eminent exegetes, were the messengers of ʿIsa, upon him be peace, from among the Disciples (al-Hawariyyun), whom he sent when he was raised up to heaven. The attribution of their sending to Him, in His Glorified saying:

Page 221

When We sent to them two (messengers) is based on the view that this was by His command, exalted is He, in order to complete the parable and the consolation. Ibn 'Abbas and Ka'b said they were messengers of God, exalted is He. Some eminent scholars chose this view and claimed that God, exalted is He, sent them as a supporter for 'Isa, peace be upon him, confirming his law, like Harun for Musa, peace be upon them both. It is supported by the apparent sense of "When We sent to them two" and by the statement of those to whom they were sent, "You are but humans like us," since humanity, in their opinion, is incompatible with a message from God, exalted is He, and not from someone else. Some have argued for this by the manifestation of miracles at their hands, such as healing the blind from birth and raising the dead, as is reported in some narrations. A miracle, however, is specific to a prophet, as has been established in the (science of) kalam (theology). Whoever holds the first view answers the first point with what you have heard. As for the second point, they may have addressed them in a way that they understood to mean that they were conveying from God, exalted is He, without an intermediary; or they made the messengers equal to their sender and addressed them with what would invalidate his message, treating him as present by way of taghlib (prioritizing the more prominent party), so they said what they said. As for the third point, what appeared at their hands, if the report is sound, was a karamah (a divine favour or marvel granted to a righteous person) for them, in the sense of a miracle for 'Isa, peace be upon him. It is not necessary that it be a miracle for them unless they had claimed a message from God, exalted is He, without an intermediary, and that is the very point at issue.

"Idh" (when) is a badal (substitute, i.e., apposition) for the first "idh." It is said that the two were Yuhanna and Bulus. Muqatil said Tuman and Bulus. Shu'ayb al-Jibba'i said Sham'un and Yuhanna. Wahb and Ka'b said Sadiq and Sadhuq. It was also said Nazus and Marus.

It is said that "We sent to them" (rather than "We sent to it") was used so that it would correspond with "when the messengers came to it," because sending in the strict sense is directed to people, not to a town, unlike coming. Also, the sequential connection (ta'qib) by His saying, exalted is He, "Then they denied them both," is more evident in this (wording). This is like the sequential connection in His saying, exalted is He, "Then We said, 'Strike the rock with your staff,' and it burst forth" (al-A'raf 160). The fa' is called al-fa' al-fasihah (the eloquent fa', i.e., the fa' that reveals a omitted action), because it reveals a deleted verb. At that time, the people of the town were worshippers of idols.

"Then We strengthened" means We reinforced and fortified the two. This is what Mujahid and Ibn Qutaybah said. It is said: "ta'azzaza lahmu al-naqah" when the flesh of the camel became firm. Others said: "'azzaza al-matar al-ard" when the rain packed and firmed the ground, and "al-izaz" is used for hard ground, and from this comes "al-'izz" (honour) in its well-known meaning. The object of the verb is omitted, meaning "so We strengthened them both" with a third, since what precedes indicates it, and because the intent is to mention that by which they were strengthened. According to what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, it is Sham'un al-Safa; it is also said Sam'an. Wahb and Ka'b said Shalum. According to Shu'ayb al-Jubba'i, it is Bulis with a sad; some transmit it with a sin.

Al-Hasan, Abu Hayah, Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal and Aban read "fa'azaznā" with a light (unshaddah) pronunciation. The light and the heavy forms are two dialects, like "shiddah" and "shaddadah," so the meaning is the same. Abu 'Ali said the light form comes from "'azzahu," meaning to overpower him, and from it comes the saying "man 'azza yasulab" (whoever overpowers is plundered). The meaning on this view is: "so We overpowered them with the proof of a third." 'Abdullah read "bi-al-thalith" (with the third).

"Then they said" is coordinated with "they denied them both, so We strengthened," and the fa' indicates sequence: that is, after the denial of the two and their strengthening by a third, the three said, "Indeed, we are sent to you." Attributing the statement to the three is not harmed by the silence of some of them, since agreement suffices. Rather, the Arabic manner of speaking in the plural, where the speaker is one and the others agree with him, is customary.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 15:

﴿Qālū﴾ — i.e., the people of the town, addressing the three messengers: ﴿You are nothing but humans like us﴾, with no superiority over us that would necessitate your being singled out for what you claim. The raising of ﴿basharun﴾ (human) is due to the negation being annulled by ʾillā (except), for (mā) functioned in the manner of laysa (is not) by analogy; when its negation is annulled by the entry of ʾillā upon the predicate, its resemblance to laysa weakens and so its governing power is nullified, contrary to the view of Yūnus (Yunus al-Nahwi). And mithl (like) is an attribute of basharun, and it did not acquire definiteness through being put in construct form, as is known in grammar.

﴿And the Most Merciful has not sent down anything﴾ of what you claim of revelation to anyone. The apparent meaning of this statement implies their acknowledgment of divinity, but they deny prophethood and seek intercession through idols. The specification of this glorious Name among His names, exalted and majestic is He, is due to their supposition that mercy precludes the sending down of revelation, since it demands an obligation from which no benefit returns to Him, glory be to Him, and the bestowal of reward by Him, exalted is He, upon the servant does not depend on it. It has also been said that the mention of "the Most Merciful" belongs to the quoted speech, not to the reported speech itself. And they said: there is no god and no prophethood. This is due to what is in some reports, that they said: "Has a god other than our gods been made?" The expression by this Name is for His forbearance toward them and His mercy, glory be to Him, toward them in not hastening punishment at the time of their denial. And perhaps what has preceded is more preferable and clearer, and there is no certainty regarding the soundness of the report that contradicts it.

﴿You are nothing but liars﴾ in what you claim. This is an explicit statement of what they intended by the two preceding sentences. The choice of ﴿takdhibūna﴾ (you lie) over ﴿kādhibūna﴾ (liars) is to indicate renewal (tajaddud).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 16:

﴿Qālū﴾ (They said), that is, the messengers, ﴿Rabbunā yaʿlamu innā ilaykum la-mursalūn﴾ (Our Lord knows that we are indeed sent to you). They invoked the knowledge of God, Exalted is He, and this serves as an oath in emphasis and as a response in the manner in which an oath is answered. It has been mentioned that whoever invokes it falsely becomes a disbeliever, and this is not the case with an oath made upon a falsehood. In it is a warning to them against opposing the knowledge of God, Exalted is He. In the choice of the title of Lordship (al-Rububiyyah) there is an allusion to the wisdom of the sending, just as the disbelievers alluded to what contradicts it according to their claim.

The addition of "Rabb" (Lord) to the pronoun of the messengers does not preclude this. It is also possible that its choice was because it is more fitting to the situation in which they were, namely the manifestation of miracles at their hands; so it is as if they said: "Our Helper through the miracles knows that we are indeed sent to you." The placing of the predicate-subject (the subject before the predicate, al-musnad ilayh) first serves either to strengthen the judgment or to restrict it, meaning: "Our Lord knows, not you," because you have no regard for the signs.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 17:

﴿And upon us is only the clear conveyance.﴾ That is, only conveying His message (ta'ligh risalatihi, ta'ala) in a manifest, clear manner, such that it is not hidden from its hearer and does not admit of interpretation or of being taken to mean other than what is intended at all. We have thereby discharged our obligation, so there is no blame upon us from the side of our Lord. Thus it is said. However, the better view is that "the clear conveyance" is explained as that which is accompanied by the signs that testify to the truth, and they had conveyed in this manner, based on what has been related: that they healed the blind-born and the leper and revived the dead, or that they performed some other marvel besides what has been mentioned. This has not been transmitted to us, nor is it required in the Glorious Book or in the reports to mention the marvel of every messenger, as is not hidden. Then, that [marvel] is either a miracle (mu'jizah) for them, on the view that they were messengers of God, the Exalted, without an intermediary, or a karamah (act of honour) for them and a miracle for their sender, Jesus, peace be upon him, on the view that they were his messengers, peace be upon him. The meaning is: "Upon us, from the side of our Lord, is only the clear conveyance by means of the signs, and we have done it, so there is no blame upon us." Or: "Upon us is nothing that we are held to account for from your side except conveying the message in the manner mentioned, and he has conveyed it to us thus. So what is it that you demand of us, that you should believe our claim?" And because their conveyance was clear in this sense, it was fitting for them to cite knowledge, so do not be heedless. The words of the messengers came secondly in the utmost emphasis, because of the great insistence of the unbelievers in denial, for they brought three sentences, and each of them indicates the intensity of denial, as is not hidden from one who has the least reflection.

Al-Sakkaki said: They emphasized the first time because the denial of the two is a denial of the third, given the unity of the statement. So when they exaggerated in denying them, they increased the emphasis. Al-Zamakhshari said: The first utterance is the beginning of an informative statement, and the second is a reply to a denial. Al-Sayyid al-Sanad justified this by saying that the first is the beginning of an informative statement in view of the fact that the whole of the three had not preceded by any information, so there is no denial of them the first time; the emphasis in it is therefore taken as their care and concern for the matter of the news. End. But in this there is [the objection] that the three were aware of their denial, and a statement addressed to a denier is not called the beginning of an informative statement. Sahib al-Kashf said: He meant that it was not preceded by a prior informing, and he did not mean that it was a statement addressed to one with an empty mind, nor that the beginning is taken with regard to the statement of the third or of the group. Al-Jalabi said: Perhaps his meaning is that it is in the position of the beginning of an informative statement with respect to their second denial, in that it does not need such emphases, so their first denial is not counted as a denial with respect to their second denial, not that it is truly a beginning of information. The weakness of this is not hidden. Al-Fadil al-Yamani said: The first statement was emphasized only because they were placed in the position of one who denies the sending of the three, since this appeared from the denial of the two. On this basis, it is the beginning of an informative statement with regard to bringing the speech in accordance with the apparent requirement, and a denial-type statement with regard to bringing the speech not in accordance with the apparent requirement. So al-Zamakhshari's view is more subtle than al-Sakkaki's, although al-Sayyid al-Sanad said the reverse. Its flaw, from what has preceded, is known with slight reflection.

Al-Fadil Abd al-Hakim al-Sialkoti, the greatest of the later scholars, said: In my view, what al-Sakkaki mentioned is based on the conjunction of ﴿فَقالُوا إنّا إلَيْكم مُرْسَلُونَ﴾ upon ﴿فَكَذَّبُوهُما فَعَزَّزْنا﴾, and the fa' denotes sequence, so the speech issues from the three after the denial of the two and the strengthening by a third, so it was a speech with deniers, hence it came emphasized.

The statement of al-Zamakhshari
Page 223
is based on its being a conjunction upon ﴿إذْ جاءَها المُرْسَلُونَ﴾, and that it is an elaboration of the story mentioned in summary by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿إذْ جاءَها المُرْسَلُونَ﴾ up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿فَعَزَّزْنا بِثالِثٍ﴾. So the fa' is for elaboration, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿فَقالُوا إنّا إلَيْكم مُرْسَلُونَ﴾ is an explanation of His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿إذْ أرْسَلْنا إلَيْهِمُ اثْنَيْنِ﴾, so it is a beginning of an informative statement issued by the two, who spoke in the plural form to affirm the importance of the news.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿قالُوا ما أنْتُمْ إلا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُنا﴾ etc. is an explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿فَكَذَّبُوهُما﴾.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿رَبُّنا يَعْلَمُ إنّا إلَيْكم لَمُرْسَلُونَ﴾ ﴿وما عَلَيْنا إلا البَلاغُ المُبِينُ﴾ is an explanation of His saying, majestic is His affair: ﴿فَعَزَّزْنا بِثالِثٍ﴾, for the clear conveyance is their establishing the messengership by means of the miracles, and this is the strengthening and the victory.
