Then he said: The excellence of this explanation is not hidden, since it agrees with the story mentioned in the tafsir books and fits the flow of the verse, for it was first mentioned in summary by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿واضْرِبْ لَهم مَثَلا أصْحابَ القَرْيَةِ﴾, then elaborated in part by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إذْ جاءَها المُرْسَلُونَ﴾ up to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿فَعَزَّزْنا بِثالِثٍ﴾, then elaborated in full by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿فَقالُوا إنّا إلَيْكم مُرْسَلُونَ﴾ up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿خامِدُونَ﴾. And there is no need to make the fa' in ﴿فَكَذَّبُوهُما﴾ an explanatory fa', unlike al-Sakkaki's explanation, which requires an assumed element. So they called to monotheism. End.

It is not hidden from the fair-minded that this is an interpretation in the extreme of remoteness, and its discussion reaches the level of riddles, and despite this there is much in it. I say: It is not far-fetched that al-Zamakhshari intended by his words one of the possibilities mentioned in its explanation, except that what al-Sakkaki held is further from artificiality and safer from disputation.

They said, when their stratagems were exhausted and their excuses had failed them: **"Indeed, we take an omen from you"** (*tatayyur*, taking omens). That is, we consider you a bad omen, following the practice of the ignorant, who regard as auspicious everything that accords with their desires even when it brings every evil, and regard as inauspicious what does not accord with them even when it brings every good. Or it is based on the fact that the call is never free of a warning of what they dislike, namely that harm will befall them if they do not believe, so they used to flee from it. Muqatil said: rain was withheld from them. Another said: leprosy (*judham*) spread among them when they denied the messengers, peace be upon them. Ibn Atiyya said: their taking omens was due to the discord that entered among them and the people being led into temptation.

The origin of *tatayyur* is optimism or pessimism drawn from birds, from the bird flying to the right (*sanih*) and the bird flying to the left (*barih*), and then it became general. The basis of their taking omens from the messengers was their saying, as indicated by the words of Exalted God: **"If you do not desist"**, that is, from this your saying.

**"We will surely stone you"** with stones. This was said by Qatada, who mentioned two possibilities: that stoning means killing, i.e., "we will surely kill you by stoning with stones"; and that it means harming, i.e., "we will surely hurt you thereby." Abd ibn Humayd related from Mujahid that he said: that is, "we will surely revile you." Then he said: stoning in the whole Qur'an means reviling.

**"And a painful punishment will surely touch you from us."** Al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) said: it is burning. It was said: it is a punishment other than that by which life remains. The meaning is: "we will surely kill you by stones, or, if we do not kill you, we will punish you with a painful punishment whose extent cannot be measured, with which you will wish for death." It was said: by the painful punishment is meant the spiritual punishment, and by stoning is meant a specific type of bodily harm; so they made the matter hover between bodily harm and spiritual harm. It was said: by the painful punishment is meant bodily punishment, and by stoning is meant spiritual punishment and harm, based on the view that by it is meant reviling. It was also said other than that.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 19:**

﴿They said﴾, that is, the Messengers, responding to them: ﴿Your omen is with you﴾, that is, the cause of your ill omen is with you, ﴿not from us, as you claim﴾, and it is your evil belief and the ugliness of your deeds.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas that he interpreted "the omen" (al-ta'ir) as the ill omen itself, meaning: your ill omen is with you, namely remaining in disbelief. ﴿As for us, there is no ill omen with us﴾, because we call to monotheism and the worship of God Most High, and in that lies the ultimate of religion, goodness and blessing. From Abu Ubayda and al-Mubarrad: ﴿Your omen﴾ means your share and portion of good and evil, which is with you from your own actions; if it is good, then it is good, and if it is evil, then it is evil.

Al-Hasan, Ibn Hurmuz, Amr ibn Ubayd and Zurr ibn Hubaysh read "ṭayrukum" (with a silent yā' after the ṭā'). Al-Zajjaj said: al-ṭā'ir and al-ṭayr have the same meaning. In al-Qamus (the dictionary), al-ṭayr is the plural of ṭā'ir and may be used for the singular; it mentions that al-ṭayr does not occur in the Noble Qur'an except in the plural, as in God Most High's saying ﴿and the birds spreading their wings in ranks﴾ [al-Nur: 41]. If in this reading it is so, then ṭā'ir (in the singular) is in its sense of the plural, since, although it is singular, it encompasses by its annexation everything by which omens are taken, and so it has the meaning of the plural. Thus the two readings agree.

From al-Hasan that he read "iṭṭayyurukum", the verbal noun of iṭṭayyara, whose origin is taṭayyara; the tā' was assimilated into the ṭā', and so a hamzat al-waṣl (connecting hamza) was introduced in the past tense and in the verbal noun.

﴿A-in dhukkirtum﴾ with two hamzas: the first is the hamzat al-istifham (interrogative hamza), and the second is the hamza of in (the conditional particle). The Kufans and Ibn Amir made both clearly pronounced, while the rest of the Seven softened the second. Sibawayh and Yunus differed concerning when an interrogative and a conditional occur together, which of them is answered. Sibawayh held that the interrogative is answered, meaning the thing being asked about is supplied, and as if one dispenses thereby with supplying an answer to the conditional. The meaning according to him is: "Is it that you are reminded and admonished with that in which is your happiness, you take omens (tataṭayyarūna), or you threaten, or the like?" Either a present-tense verb in the nominative is supplied, or, if you wish, you may supply a past-tense verb such as (taṭayyartum). Yunus held that the conditional is answered, as if one dispenses thereby with answering the interrogative and supplying a target for it. So the supplied sense is: "Is it that you are reminded, you will take omens or the like of what is indicated by what precedes?" Here a jussive present-tense verb is supplied, or, if you wish, a past-tense verb in the jussive position.

Zurr read with two open hamzas, and this is the reading of Abu Ja'far and Talha, except that they softened the second between-between (bayn bayn, an intermediate sound between hamza and the vowel). On the full pronunciation of both, the verse of the poet comes:

*"Are you, son of Dawud, the son of Ahwa, combed and anointed? You are not a shepherd for your cousin, one who keeps him from harm."*

The first hamza is the interrogative, and the second is the hamza of an (the verbal particle), and the sentence is supplied with the preposition lām, meaning: "Is it because you are reminded that you have taken omens?"

Al-Majishun, Yusuf ibn Ya'qub al-Madani, read with a single open hamza. It may be taken that the interrogative hamza is supplied, so this reading and the previous one agree in meaning; or it may be that it is not supplied, so the sentence takes the form of a statement. This, it is said, is directed toward wonder and reproach, and the preposition remains as it is, and the prepositional phrase is attached to something omitted, as what the Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari's commentary) indicates. That is: "You took omens because you were reminded." Ibn Jinni said: "(an dhukkirtum) in this reading is the object governed by ﴿your omen is with you﴾, for when they said ﴿We take omen from you﴾, they were answered: ﴿Nay, your omen is with you, because you were reminded﴾; that is, it is with you because you were reminded, but you did not remember and did not desist. So the cause, which is the reminding, is used instead of the effect, which is desisting, just as they described the bird in the place of its effect, which is ill omen, because they were accustomed to it from their aversion to the cawing of the crow or to its spirit."

Al-Hasan read with a single hamza, kasra-vowelled. In this there are two possibilities: if the hamza is supplied, this reading and the reading of the majority agree; if it is not supplied, the sentence takes the form of a statement, and the answer is omitted, its indication being what precedes, and its supplied form is as stated above. Abu Amr, in the transmission of Zurr as well, read with two open hamzas with a madda between them, as if he found their juxtaposition burdensome, so he separated them with an alif. Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, and likewise Qatada, al-A'mash and others read "ayna" with an open hamza, a silent yā', and an open nūn, and "dhakartum" with the kāf lightened. On this reading, ayna is an adverb functioning as a conditional particle, and its answer is omitted, its indication being "your omen" (ṭā'irukum), according to what has been said: "Wherever you were reminded, your omen accompanies you." The meaning is that your ill omen is with you wherever your mention occurs. In this there is an exaggeration of their ill omen that is not hidden.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, Abu Hayyan's commentary): whoever permits placing the consequent before the condition, namely the Kufans and Abu Zayd, and al-Mubarrad permits that the answer be ﴿your omen is with you﴾, and its original form was "wherever you were reminded, then your omen is with you"; when the answer was placed first, the fa' was omitted.

﴿Nay, you are a people who exceed the bounds﴾, that is: your custom is excess and transgressing the limit in disobedience, and you persist in it; therefore the ill omen has come to you, not from the Messengers of God Most High and their admonition. This is a turning away from what his saying, God Most High, ﴿Is it because you are reminded﴾ requires, namely the denial that what is the cause of all happiness should be the cause of ill omen, because it is an alert and a stirring toward firmly binding the ill omen upon them and affirming excess, which is more eloquent and is what brings all ill omen. Or it means ﴿Nay, you are a people who exceed the bounds﴾ in your error, persisting in your deviation, in that you take omens from those whom one must seek blessing from, the guides to the religion of God Most High. So it is a turning away from the whole speech: they answered them by making them causes of happiness, embedding in this the warning of their bad conduct in being deprived of it; then they turned away from it to what the people did of reversing things, contrary to what right reasoning requires. So consider this carefully.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 20:

﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city a man﴾, meaning a man from its most distant places. "A man" means a man in the sight of Allah, the Exalted. The tanwin (nunation, the indefinite ending) on رَجُلٌ is for glorification. It is also permitted that the indefiniteness serves to indicate that the messengers did not know him, so that they would not collude with him. His name, according to what is narrated from Ibn Abbas, Abu Mijlaz, Ka'b al-Ahbar, Mujahid and Muqatil, is Habib, and he is the son of Isra'il, as it has been said. It has also been said that he was the son of Murri. According to the well-known view he was a carpenter. It has been said that he was a farmer, a launderer, a cobbler, or a carver of idols. It is possible that he combined all these attributes. Some have mentioned that he was a believer who worshipped his Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, in a cave, and when he heard that his people had denied the messengers, he came running (يَسْعى), that is, he hastened and quickened his walk, eager to advise his people. It has also been said that he heard that his people had resolved to kill the messengers, so he intended, for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, to defend them. Here سَعى (sa'a, "to strive/run") has the same sense as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿and strives for it its striving﴾ [al-Isra': 19], and this is a well-known metaphor (majaz). His being in a cave does not contradict his coming from the farthest part of the city, since it is possible that there was a cave in its farthest part. Indeed, this view clearly indicates that he was a believer, and it contradicts the claim that he was a carver of idols.

It has been answered that what is meant is that he carved images that were not for worship, and such carving was permitted in that law. The view that he was a believer has been reported from Ibn Abi Layla, and in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) it is quoted from him that he said: "The foremost of the nations were three, who never disbelieved for the blink of an eye: Ali ibn Abi Talib, the companion of Ya-Sin, and the believer of the family of Pharaoh."

al-Zamakhshari and a group of scholars mention this as a ḥadīth from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They also mention that he was among those who believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as Tubba' al-Akbar, Waraqah ibn Nawfal and others did. No one believed in any prophet other than him, peace and blessings be upon him, before his appearance. It has also been said that he had leprosy, and that his dwelling was at the farthest of the city's gates. He worshipped idols for seventy years, asking them to remove his affliction, but it was not removed. When the messengers invited him to worship Allah, the Exalted, he said: "Is there a sign?" They said: "Yes. We call upon our Lord, the All-Powerful, who will relieve you of what you have." He said: "This is indeed strange! For seventy years I have called upon these gods, and they have not been able to relieve it. How then will your Lord relieve it in a single morning?" They said: "Our Lord is capable of whatever He wills, while these do neither benefit nor harm." So he believed, and they called upon their Lord, glory be to Him, and He, the Mighty and Majestic, removed what was on him, as if there had never been any affliction. He then turned to earning a living. When evening came, he gave half of his earnings in charity and spent the other half on himself and his dependants. When his people resolved to kill the messengers, he came from the farthest part of the city running (يَسْعى). According to this view, his carving of idols is not problematic and does not need that distant answer. However, there is a contradiction between this report and the report "The foremost of the nations are three," and that he was among those who believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as Tubba' did. The fact that his belief in him, peace and blessings be upon him, came through the messengers, though this is contrary to the apparent meaning, removes the contradiction between him and the latter report. The contradiction then remains between him and the first report, unless it is said that what is meant by "the foremost of the nations" is the foremost to believe after the call, three of whom never disbelieved after it for the blink of an eye. Among the things whose apparent meaning indicates that the man was not a believer before this is what is related: when the two messengers who were first sent drew near the city, they saw him tending sheep. They asked him, and he informed them. He said: "Do you have a sign?" They said: "We heal the sick, and we cure the blind and the leper." He had a sick son, so they wiped over him and he was healed, and he believed. Taking "believed" (āmana) to mean the manifest form of belief is contrary to the apparent meaning. What seems preponderant to me is that he was a believer in the messengers before his coming and his advising of his people, though I am not certain whether he was a believer or not before the sending of the messengers. The reports on this are contradictory, and even so, the soundness of none of them has been established for me. And Allah, the Exalted, knows best the reality of the matter.

﴿And there came from the farthest part of the city﴾: here the prepositional phrase precedes رَجُلٌ (a man), the reverse of what occurs in the narrative of the story. Abu Hayyan regarded this as a variation (tafannun) in eloquence.

al-Khafaji said: The prepositional phrase has been placed before the agent (فاعل), which by rule should come first, to demonstrate his excellence, for Allah guided him despite his distance from them, and his distance did not prevent him from that. For this reason the word "city" (al-madīna) is used here after the word "town" (al-qarya) was used, as an indication of breadth, and that Allah guides whom He wills, whether near or far. It has also been said that it was placed first for emphasis, since it implies that their warning had reached the farthest part of the city, which suggests that they had delivered the clear message. It has also been said that if it were delayed, it could be thought to be connected to يَسْعى (running), and then it would not convey that he was from the people of the city, his dwelling being at its edge, and that is the intended meaning. The clause يَسْعى (running) is a description of رَجُلٌ (a man). Whoever permits the occurrence of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from an indefinite noun has permitted it to be a ḥāl from him. The words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿He said⦆ are an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), as if it were said: "What did he say when he came?" So it was said: ﴿He said: "O my people, follow the messengers."﴾ It is also permitted that this be an explanation of "running", meaning he intended the face of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The problem with this is not hidden. Mentioning the title of their mission is to urge them to follow them, just as addressing them as "O my people" is to win over their hearts and incline them toward accepting his advice.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 21:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Follow those who do not ask you for a reward﴾ is a repetition for emphasis, and a means of reaching, through this, a description of them by what implies the removal of any obstacle to following them, after the indication that the cause (of following) is established. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and they are guided﴾, i.e., steadfast upon the guidance by what they are upon, to the good of this world and the Hereafter, is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya) containing what confirms that they do not ask for a reward, nor for what follows it of seeking status and exaltation. For this reason it has been regarded as an ighal hasan (a graceful elaboration, i.e., adding a phrase that reinforces the meaning), like the saying of al-Khansa':

"Indeed Sakhr, the guided ones take him as their leader, as if he were a banner with a fire at its top."

The apparent meaning is that the man did not say that except after his faith had preceded. It is narrated that when the call reached him, he came running, heard their speech and understood it, then said to them: "Do you ask a reward for this call of yours?" They said: "No." Thereupon he called his people to follow them and to believe in them, saying: "O my people," etc.

Among the grammarians, regarding such a construction there are two views. The first: that "min" (in "man") is a substitute (badal) for "al-mursalin," with the governing element repeated, as it is repeated when it is a preposition, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We would surely have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful roofs for their houses﴾; and this view was taken by some. The second, to which the majority went, is that it is not a substitute, for the substitution is specific to the case where the repeated governing element is a preposition; as for when it is a governing element in the nominative or accusative, they call that tatbi' (apposition in following), not badal. The verse has been cited as evidence for the deficiency of one who takes a wage for any of the acts of the Sharia. The discussion is treated fully in the books of jurisprudence (al-furu').

**[Commentary of al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on surah 36, verse 22]**

﴿وما لِيَ لا أعْبُدُ الَّذِي فَطَرَنِي﴾ ﴿And why should I not worship He who originated me?﴾ This is a gentle way of guiding his people. He presents the matter as counsel for himself, and it is sincere advice, for he shows them that he chooses for them what he would choose for himself. The purpose is to rebuke them for abandoning the worship of their Creator in favour of worshipping others, as indicated by His words: ﴿وإلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾. This is an intensified threat, frightening them with the prospect of returning to severe punishment, openly and directly. Had he said, "And to Him I will be returned" (wa-ilayhi ur'ja'u), there would have been a threat by way of allusion (ta'ridh). The expression ﴿وإلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ after "ma li la a'budu" is, by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), a shift to address the listeners directly, because the allusion in "ma li la a'budu" etc. is aimed at them. Thus the thing referred to in both expressions is one and the same, according to what al-Khatib (al-Qazwini) and Sa'd al-Din al-Taftazani held, namely that allusion (ta'ridh) is either metaphor (majaz) or metonymy (kinaya). Here it is metaphor, because the literal subject is impossible to intend, so the word is used in a sense other than that for which it was coined, and the thing referred to is therefore one.

Al-Sayyid al-Sanad verified that the allusive meaning is one of the implications of the arrangement (tartib), and that the word is not used for it; rather, relative to the meaning it is used for, it is either a literal expression (haqiqa), a metaphor, or a metonymy. Accordingly, the speaker's pronoun in "ma li" etc. is not used to refer to the listeners, so the thing referred to in the two expressions is not one, and there is therefore no iltifat.

Some have allowed that the verse is an instance of ihtibak (a device in which elements mentioned in one part are omitted from another and vice versa). The original would be: "And why should I not worship He who originated me, and to Him I will be returned; and why do you not worship He who originated you, and to Him you will be returned." The first clause omits the counterpart of what is mentioned in the second, and vice versa. This, however, forfeits what you have heard.

The apparent sense of al-Wahidi's words is that there is no allusion in the verse, for he said: When the man said, "O my people, follow the messengers," etc., they took him to the king. The king said to him, "Do you then follow them?" He said, "And why should I not worship He who originated me?" That is: what is it for me if I do not worship my Creator? ﴿وإلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ ﴿and to Him you will be returned﴾ means you will be brought back at the resurrection, and He will repay you for your disbelief. This has been rejected on the ground that if the denial returns to him alone and not to the people, then the address "you will be returned" has no meaning. The apparent wording would have been "I will be returned" (ur'ja'u).

It may be answered that the man was in intense rage at their denial of the messengers and their threats against them, so he seized the opportunity for retribution. When he was able to threaten them, he inserted his words ﴿وإلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ﴾ in the midst of his speech. That is: why should I not worship He who has favoured me with the blessing of creation and the blessing of avenging myself upon you and satisfying my anger against you, since you will be returned to Him and He will repay you for your disbelief, your denial of the messengers, and your obstinacy? You know that the sublime composition does not support this reading, and this is evident from what preceded.

Al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah Ya-Sin, verses 23–25:

He has returned to the first line of argument, which is gentle guidance, and said: ﴿Shall I take besides Him gods?﴾ This is a denial and a negation of taking any kind of god at all. It also contains a great deal of mocking the folly of those who worship idols.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿If the Most Merciful wills me harm, their intercession will avail me nothing﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnaf) brought to give the reason for the negation mentioned. Making it a qualifier (ṣifa) of "gods," as some have held, may give the impression that there are gods which are not like this. The meaning of "will avail me nothing..." is: it will not benefit me in any way at all. This may be in the manner of the saying "you do not see the lizard entering its hole," meaning that they have no intercession that could benefit me. Or it may be on the supposition that intercession occurs, meaning: their intercession, even if it were to occur, would avail me nothing. ﴿Nor can they rescue me﴾ means they cannot deliver me from that harm by help and support. This is an ascent from the lower to the higher: he began by negating their standing (jāh), and then mentioned the absence of power, expressing it through the absence of rescue, because rescue is its result.

Ṭalḥa al-Sammān read the ya' of the first person in "yuridnī" with a fatḥa, according to what Ibn ʿAṭiyya said. Ibn Khālawayh said: Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif, ʿĪsā al-Hamadhānī and Abū Jaʿfar also read it, and it is reported from Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim and Abū ʿAmr. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it was also read, "in yuridnī al-Raḥmānu bi-ḍurrin," meaning: "if He makes me reach harm" (yūridunī ḍurran), i.e., makes me a place of arrival for harm. End of quotation.

Abū Ḥayyān said: it seems, and Allah knows best, that he saw in the books of readings "yaridnī" with a fatḥa on the ya', so he thought it was the ya' of the present tense (muḍāraʿa), and so he made the verb transitive by means of the ya' that causes transitivity, like the hamza (hamzat al-taʿdiya, the causative hamza). Therefore he added to it the hamza of transitivity and governed two objects by it. What is found in the books of irregular readings (shādhdh) is that it is the ya' of possession (ya' al-iḍāfa), which is omitted in writing and in pronunciation because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. In Ibn Khālawayh's book: with a fatḥa on the ya', the ya' of possession. In al-Lawāmiḥ: "an yaridnī al-Raḥmānu" with a fatḥa, and this is the origin of the visible ya' (the ya' that is seen by the eye), that is, the one written in the script, but this one is omitted. End of his words. Good opinion of al-Zamakhsharī requires the opposite of what he mentioned.

﴿Indeed, then I would be in clear error﴾: that is, if I were to take besides Him gods. Associating with Him what does not create, and whose nature is not to benefit or to repel harm, with the Creator, the Mighty, besides whom there is no one able, and in whom alone is all good, is error and manifest mistake, which is not hidden from anyone who has even the slightest discernment.

﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord﴾. The apparent meaning is that the address is to his people; he addressed them with this directly, and proclaimed the truth openly, showing firmness in religion and indifference to what might come from them. The sentence is declarative in both form and meaning, and the emphasis (taʾkīd) is because it is said that they did not know from his speech that he had believed, but they hesitated about it when they heard what they heard from him.

The addition of the Lord to their pronoun is to establish the truth and to alert them to the falsehood of what they hold, namely taking idols as lords. That is: "Indeed I have believed in your Lord who created you, so listen to me," that is, listen to my words, for I do not care what you do in response to that. It has also been said that he meant: I invited them to the good which he had chosen for himself. It has also been said that he intended by this statement nothing but to anger them and to distract them from the messengers by himself, when he saw that admonition was not taking effect on them and they had resolved to destroy him; but this is not correct. Some have taken the omitted mudāf (the implied governed noun) as general, and have interpreted listening as acceptance, as in "Allah hears him who praises Him" (samiʿa Allāhu li-man ḥamidah). That is: listen to all that I have said and accept it, and it is of what can be heard.

Making the address in both sentences directed to the people is what is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Kaʿb and Wahb. al-Ḥākim reported from Ibn Masʿūd that he said: when the companion of Yā-Sīn said: ﴿O my people, follow the messengers﴾, they choked him so that he would die. So he turned to the prophets and said: ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me﴾, that is, bear witness. In that case the address in both is to the messengers by way of shifting of address (talwīn). He emphasized the report to show that it came from him with complete eagerness and vigor, and he added the Lord to their pronoun, with the intention of adding confirmation and to show special relation and following of them, as if he had said: "your Lord who sent you," or "the One to whom you call us to believe." He asked them to listen so that they would bear witness for him before Allah, mighty and majestic, as the words of Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, indicate. It has also been said: the first address is to his people, and the second to the messengers; he addressed them by way of seeking their testimony and entrusting the matter to them. It has also been said: both addresses are to all people.

It is reported from ʿĀṣim that he read "fasmaʿūna" with a fatḥa on the nūn. Abū Ḥātim said: this is an error that is not permissible, because it is an imperative; so either the nūn is omitted, as the nūn of grammatical inflection (nūn al-iʿrāb) is omitted, and one says "fasmaʿū," or it remains and is given a kasra. Some people have given it a reading by saying that the original was "fasmaʿūnā," that is, "listen to our speech," meaning my speech and their speech, so that you may bear witness to what came from me and from them.

Or it may be on the supposition that intercession occurs, meaning: their intercession, even if it were to occur, would avail me nothing. ﴿Nor can they rescue me﴾ means they cannot deliver me from that harm by help and support. This is an ascent from the lower to the higher: he began by negating their standing (jāh), and then mentioned the absence of power, expressing it through the absence of rescue, because rescue is its result.

Ṭalḥa al-Sammān read the ya' of the first person in "yuridnī" with a fatḥa, according to what Ibn ʿAṭiyya said. Ibn Khālawayh said: Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif, ʿĪsā al-Hamadhānī and Abū Jaʿfar also read it, and it is reported from Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim and Abū ʿAmr. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it was also read, "in yuridnī al-Raḥmānu bi-ḍurrin," meaning: "if He makes me reach harm" (yūridunī ḍurran), i.e., makes me a place of arrival for harm. End of quotation.

Abū Ḥayyān said: it seems, and Allah knows best, that he saw in the books of readings "yaridnī" with a fatḥa on the ya', so he thought it was the ya' of the present tense (muḍāraʿa), and so he made the verb transitive by means of the ya' that causes transitivity, like the hamza (hamzat al-taʿdiya, the causative hamza). Therefore he added to it the hamza of transitivity and governed two objects by it. What is found in the books of irregular readings (shādhdh) is that it is the ya' of possession (ya' al-iḍāfa), which is omitted in writing and in pronunciation because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. In Ibn Khālawayh's book: with a fatḥa on the ya', the ya' of possession. In al-Lawāmiḥ: "an yaridnī al-Raḥmānu" with a fatḥa, and this is the origin of the visible ya' (the ya' that is seen by the eye), that is, the one written in the script, but this one is omitted. End of his words. Good opinion of al-Zamakhsharī requires the opposite of what he mentioned.

﴿Indeed, then I would be in clear error﴾: that is, if I were to take besides Him gods. Associating with Him what does not create, and whose nature is not to benefit or to repel harm, with the Creator, the Mighty, besides whom there is no one able, and in whom alone is all good, is error and manifest mistake, which is not hidden from anyone who has even the slightest discernment.

﴿Indeed, I have believed in your Lord﴾. The apparent meaning is that the address is to his people; he addressed them with this directly, and proclaimed the truth openly, showing firmness in religion and indifference to what might come from them. The sentence is declarative in both form and meaning, and the emphasis (taʾkīd) is because it is said that they did not know from his speech that he had believed, but they hesitated about it when they heard what they heard from him.

The addition of the Lord to their pronoun is to establish the truth and to alert them to the falsehood of what they hold, namely taking idols as lords. That is: "Indeed I have believed in your Lord who created you, so listen to me," that is, listen to my words, for I do not care what you do in response to that. It has also been said that he meant: I invited them to the good which he had chosen for himself. It has also been said that he intended by this statement nothing but to anger them and to distract them from the messengers by himself, when he saw that admonition was not taking effect on them and they had resolved to destroy him; but this is not correct. Some have taken the omitted mudāf (the implied governed noun) as general, and have interpreted listening as acceptance, as in "Allah hears him who praises Him" (samiʿa Allāhu li-man ḥamidah). That is: listen to all that I have said and accept it, and it is of what can be heard.

Making the address in both sentences directed to the people is what is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Kaʿb and Wahb. al-Ḥākim reported from Ibn Masʿūd that he said: when the companion of Yā-Sīn said: ﴿O my people, follow the messengers﴾, they choked him so that he would die. So he turned to the prophets and said: ﴿Indeed I have believed in your Lord, so listen to me﴾, that is, bear witness. In that case the address in both is to the messengers by way of shifting of address (talwīn). He emphasized the report to show that it came from him with complete eagerness and vigor, and he added the Lord to their pronoun, with the intention of adding confirmation and to show special relation and following of them, as if he had said: "your Lord who sent you," or "the One to whom you call us to believe." He asked them to listen so that they would bear witness for him before Allah, mighty and majestic, as the words of Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, indicate. It has also been said: the first address is to his people, and the second to the messengers; he addressed them by way of seeking their testimony and entrusting the matter to them. It has also been said: both addresses are to all people.

It is reported from ʿĀṣim that he read "fasmaʿūna" with a fatḥa on the nūn. Abū Ḥātim said: this is an error that is not permissible, because it is an imperative; so either the nūn is omitted, as the nūn of grammatical inflection (nūn al-iʿrāb) is omitted, and one says "fasmaʿū," or it remains and is given a kasra. Some people have given it a reading by saying that the original was "fasmaʿūnā," that is, "listen to our speech," meaning my speech and their speech, so that you may bear witness to what came from me and from them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 26–27:

﴿It was said: "Enter Paradise."﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining what befell him after his saying that. The apparent meaning is that the command is a permission for him to enter Paradise in actuality, and this indicates that the man had already departed the world. According to Ibn Mas'ud, after he said what he said, they trampled him with their feet until his intestines came out from his anus, and he was thrown into a well, which is the Rass. Al-Suddi said: they stoned him while he was saying, "O Allah, guide my people," until he died. Al-Kalbi said: they threw him into a pit and piled earth over him, and he died. Al-Hasan said: they burned him until he died, hanged him on the outskirts of the city, and his grave is at the wall of Antioch. It was also said: they sawed him with a saw until it came out between his legs.

His entry into Paradise after death is the entry of his spirit and its roaming within it, like the entry of all the martyrs. It was also said: the command is for good news, not for permission to enter in actuality. The angels of death said this to him as good tidings that he is among the people of Paradise, who will enter it when the believers enter it after resurrection. Something similar is reported from Mujahid.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said, concerning the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿It was said: "Enter Paradise,"﴾ that Paradise became obligatory for him. And it came in a narration from al-Hasan that he said: when his people wanted to kill him, Allah the Exalted raised him alive into the heavens, just as Jesus, peace be upon him, was raised into the heavens. So he is in Paradise and will not die except with the perishing of the heavens and the destruction of Paradise. When Allah the Exalted restores Paradise, its entry will be restored for him; so the matter is as it was at first. The majority hold that he was killed. Ibn 'Atiyyah claimed that the reports and narrations concerning this are mutually transmitted (mutawatir). The saying of Qatadah, "Allah the Exalted made him enter Paradise while he is in it alive and provided with sustenance," is not an explicit text negating killing. In al-Bahr it is said that by his saying "while he is in it alive and provided with sustenance" he intended the Exalted's saying: ﴿Rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for﴾ [Al 'Imran: 169]. Some have said: the clause answers an implied question, as if it were said: what is his state when he meets his Lord the Mighty and Majestic after that steadfastness in his religion? So it was said: "It was said: Enter Paradise." The expression in the past tense is for the certainty of its occurrence. Perhaps the preferable view is what we pointed to at first. The reason he did not say "It was said to him" is that the important purpose is to explain what was said, not the speaker and the one addressed.

* * *

And the saying of the Exalted: ﴿He said: "Would that my people knew﴾ ﴿of what my Lord has forgiven me, and made me among the honored."﴾ This is also a clarifying resumptive clause, as if it were said after informing about him what has been informed: then what did he say upon attaining that noble honor? He said, etc. He wished that his people would know his state so that this would move them to acquire the like of it through repentance from disbelief and entry into faith and obedience, following the way of the friends of Allah in restraining anger and showing mercy to enemies. In the hadith is the counsel of his people, both living and dead.

It was also said: his wish for this may be so that they would know that they had been in great error regarding his matter, that he had been upon rectitude, counsel and compassion, and that their enmity had gained him nothing but success and brought him nothing but happiness; for in that is increased delight for him and multiplied pleasure and joy. The first view is preferable. The apparent reading is that "mā" is a verbal-noun (masdariyyah) particle; it may also be a relative (mawsulah) with an implied returning pronoun, i.e., "Would that my people knew with that by which my Lord forgave me," meaning by its cause, or "with that which He forgave," i.e., with the forgiveness that my Lord granted me. The intent is to magnify Allah's forgiveness toward him, so it returns to the masdariyyah reading. Al-Zamakhshari said: i.e., with that which my Lord forgave me of sins. This was criticized as not good, since it would amount to wishing that they know of his forgiven sins, which is not fitting; likewise the coordination of "and made me among the honored" with it does not fit. As for what is said, that the purpose is to inform of the greatness of Allah's forgiveness, His abundant generosity and vast mercy, then it is not far-fetched in that case to intend the meaning of being made aware of them for that reason; indeed it is more striking to the soul than mentioning forgiveness alone without mention of what is forgiven, since the possibility of its lowliness makes it strained. Al-Farra' permitted that "mā" be interrogative, with the preposition governing "ghafara," i.e., "with what has my Lord forgiven me?" He means by this his emigration from their religion and his patience under their harm until he was killed. Al-Kisa'i objected that if this were correct it would be said "bi-mah" without alif, since the eloquent usage is to delete it when the interrogative "mā" is preceded by a preposition, as in: ﴿About what do they question one another?﴾ and the poet's saying:

"ʿAlāma uqūlu ar-rumḥa athqala ʿātiqī / idhā anā lam aṭʿan idhā al-khaylu karrat"
("Why do I say the spear has weighed on my shoulder, if I do not thrust when the horses charge?")

— to distinguish it from the relative, and retaining it is rare. It was also said that it is specific to poetic necessity, as in his saying:

"ʿalā mā qāma yashtumunī laʾīmun / kakhinzīrin tamarragha fī ramādi"
("Because a base man stood up reviling me, like a pig rolling in ash")

and his saying:

"Innā qatalnā biqatlānā sarātakum / ahla al-liwāʾi fa-fīmā yakthuru al-qatlu"
("We have slain your chiefs with our slain, the people of the banner; so, in what does killing increase?")

The reading of ʿIkrimah and ʿĪsā is "ʿammā yatasāʾalūna." And he read "min al-mukarramīn" with the rāʾ doubled, fatḥa on it, and fatḥa on the kāf.

Completed. Praise be to Allah: the twenty-second part; and following it, God willing, the twenty-third part, whose beginning is: ﴿And We did not send down upon his people﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 28–29:

Page 2
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿And We did not send down upon his people﴾ — that is, the people of the man to whom it was said, ﴿Enter Paradise﴾ — ﴿after him﴾, that is, after his killing; and it was said: after his being raised up to the heaven alive. ﴿Any host﴾, that is, any host (jundan), so (min) is redundant, for emphasis of the negation. It was also said that it may be partitive, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. Al-jund (host) means soldiery because of the harshness in it, as if it were from al-janad, that is, hard ground in which there are stones. The apparent meaning is that by this host is meant the host of angels; that is: We did not send down angels from heaven to destroy them. ﴿And We were not going to send down﴾. And it was not fitting in Our wisdom to send down a host to destroy them, since We have appointed a cause for everything; for We destroyed some of the nations by the hāṣib (a storm of stones), some by the blast (ṣayḥa), some by the sinking into the earth (khasf), and some by drowning. We made the sending down of a host one of your special features in victory for you against your people. We dealt with the matter of these people by a single cry from an angel who cried out at them, and they perished, as He—glorified is He—said: ﴿It was but one cry, and behold, they were extinguished﴾. In this there is belittling of them and of their destruction, and an indication of the magnifying of the station of the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Hayyan explained the host as encompassing the angels, saying: like the stones, the wind, and other things. The more immediate meaning is what preceded. It was also said: the host are the angels of revelation who descend upon the prophets (peace be upon them); that is, We cut off the message from them when they did what they did, and We did not regard them, and We destroyed them. It is related from al-Hasan and Mujahid that they said: Allah—exalted is He—cut off the message from them when they killed His messengers. This interpretation is very far-fetched. The killing of the three messengers is reported in al-Bahr with "it was said" (qil), and this is the apparent meaning of this narration, but what is known is that they were not killed; rather only Habib was killed. A group went to the view that "ma" in His saying—exalted is He—﴿and We were not going to send down﴾ is a relative pronoun conjoined to (jund), and the meaning is: We did not send down upon his people after him a host from heaven, and We did not send down what We were going to send down upon those before them, of stones, wind, and other things.

Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that it entails the addition of (min) before a definite noun, and for this reason it was said that it is better to make it an indefinite qualified noun. It was answered that what is tolerated in the follower is not tolerated in the followed. It is not hidden that this does not remove its remoteness. Among the most remote is the saying of Abu al-Baqa': "ma" may be redundant, meaning "and We had indeed been sending down upon others a host from heaven"; rather it is nothing at all. And "in" is negating, and "kana" is defective, its subject is pronominal hidden, and (ṣayḥatan) is its predicate, meaning: it was not (that is, the seizure or the punishment) except one cry. It is narrated that Allah—exalted is He—sent Gabriel—peace be upon him—against them until he took hold of the two posts of the city gate and cried at them one cry, and they all died. "Idha" is sudden (fuja'iyya), and in it is an indication of the speed of their destruction, such that it was with the cry. They have been likened to fire by way of implicit metaphor (isti'ara makniyya), and "extinguished" is an imaginative image (takhyil). In this there is a symbol that the living is like the flame of fire and the dead like ash, as Labid said:

"Man is nothing but like a meteor and its light, which turns to ash after it was blazing."

It is permissible that the metaphor be an explicit subsidiary metaphor (isti'ara tasrihiyya tab'iyya) in "extinguished" in the sense of coldness and stillness; because the spirit, from its fright at the cry, is pushed into the interior at once, then it becomes confined, and so the innate heat is extinguished due to its confinement. Perhaps in the deviation from

Page 3
"hamidun" (still) to "khamidun" (extinguished) there is a hidden symbol of resurrection after death. The apparent meaning is that none of them believed except Habib, and that they all perished to the last of them. In some reports it is stated that the king believed and a group of his courtiers believed, and whoever did not believe perished by the cry; but this is far-fetched. For if that were so, it would have been apparent that those believers would have supported the messengers as Habib did, and there would have been some mention of them in the glorious Qur'an in some way. Unless it is said that they believed secretly and had an excuse for not supporting openly; yet even with this, it is not free from remoteness.

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and Mu'adh ibn al-Harith al-Qari read "ṣayḥatun" with a nominative case, on the basis that "kana" is complete, meaning: there happened and occurred only one cry. It should not be that the feminine marker attaches to the verb in such a construction, so one does not say "ma qamat illa Hind," but rather "ma qama illa Hind"; because the sense is: no one stood except Hind, and the agent in it is masculine. Many grammarians did not permit the attaching of the feminine marker except in poetry, like the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"Pass the nahz and al-ajraz of what was in their ṣurūd, and there remained only the ribs, the jarāshi'"

and the saying of another:

"They were not cleared of doubt and blame in our war, except the daughters of the paternal uncle."

Hence many, as Abu Hatim said, denied this reading. Some permitted it in speech but rarely, as in the reading of al-Hasan, Malik ibn Dinar, Abu Raja', al-Jahdari, Qatada, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi 'Abla, and Abu Bahriyya: ﴿la turā illā masākinuhum﴾ with the upper "t", and its justification is consideration of the expressed agent. As if I see you inclining to this view. Ibn Mas'ud read "illā zaqyatan", from zaqā al-ta'ir yazqū, yazqī, zaqwan and zuqā'an when it cries out, and from it the proverb "heavier than the zawaqi", which are the roosters, because they used to stay up talking until they crowed, and when they crowed they dispersed.

It is permissible that the metaphor be an explicit subsidiary metaphor (isti'ara tasrihiyya tab'iyya) in "extinguished" in the sense of coldness and stillness; because the spirit, from its fright at the cry, is pushed into the interior at once, then it becomes confined, and so the innate heat is extinguished due to its confinement. Perhaps in the deviation from

Page 3
"hamidun" (still) to "khamidun" (extinguished) there is a hidden symbol of resurrection after death. The apparent meaning is that none of them believed except Habib, and that they all perished to the last of them. In some reports it is stated that the king believed and a group of his courtiers believed, and whoever did not believe perished by the cry; but this is far-fetched. For if that were so, it would have been apparent that those believers would have supported the messengers as Habib did, and there would have been some mention of them in the glorious Qur'an in some way. Unless it is said that they believed secretly and had an excuse for not supporting openly; yet even with this, it is not free from remoteness.

Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and Mu'adh ibn al-Harith al-Qari read "ṣayḥatun" with a nominative case, on the basis that "kana" is complete, meaning: there happened and occurred only one cry. It should not be that the feminine marker attaches to the verb in such a construction, so one does not say "ma qamat illa Hind," but rather "ma qama illa Hind"; because the sense is: no one stood except Hind, and the agent in it is masculine. Many grammarians did not permit the attaching of the feminine marker except in poetry, like the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"Pass the nahz and al-ajraz of what was in their ṣurūd, and there remained only the ribs, the jarāshi'"

and the saying of another:

"They were not cleared of doubt and blame in our war, except the daughters of the paternal uncle."

Hence many, as Abu Hatim said, denied this reading. Some permitted it in speech but rarely, as in the reading of al-Hasan, Malik ibn Dinar, Abu Raja', al-Jahdari, Qatada, Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi 'Abla, and Abu Bahriyya: ﴿la turā illā masākinuhum﴾ with the upper "t", and its justification is consideration of the expressed agent. As if I see you inclining to this view. Ibn Mas'ud read "illā zaqyatan", from zaqā al-ta'ir yazqū, yazqī, zaqwan and zuqā'an when it cries out, and from it the proverb "heavier than the zawaqi", which are the roosters, because they used to stay up talking until they crowed, and when they crowed they dispersed.

*Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 30:*

﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ *Al-hasrah* (regret) is, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said, grief over what has been lost together with remorse for it, as though the one who feels *hasrah* is left without strength (*yanhasiru*) because of its intensity, or is overcome by exhaustion (*i'ya'*) from being unable to make up for what he has neglected. In *al-Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit* of Abu Hayyan), it says: *hasrah* is when a person experiences, from the intensity of remorse, a degree of regret with no end after it, until he remains *hasir* (worn out). The apparent reading is that *ya* (*ya*, the vocative particle) is for address, and *hasrah* is the one addressed (*al-munada*). Its being addressed is a figurative usage, treating it as though it were rational, as if it were said: "O regret, be present, for this is one of the states in which you ought to be present," and this is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There never came to them a messenger but they used to mock him.﴾ By *al-ibad* (the servants) is meant those who denied the messengers, and it includes, in the first instance, those destroyed earlier. It has also been said that they are the intended meaning, but that is not the case. By *hasrah*, the addressed one, is meant their regret. Those who mock the sincere advisers, whose advice concerns the good of both abodes, are deserving of regretting themselves, since they forfeited for themselves eternal happiness and took in its place the lasting punishment. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abbas, Ubayy, Ali ibn al-Husayn, al-Dahhak, Mujahid and al-Hasan: "*ya hasrata al-ibad*" with the *idafa* (genitive construction). That the intended meaning is the regret of others over them, with the *idafa* used for the slightest connection, is contrary to the apparent sense. Ibn Jarir and others related from Qatada that he said, in some of the readings: "*ya hasrata al-ibad ala anfusiha ma ya'tihim*," and so on.

It is permitted that it be the regret of the angels, upon them be peace, and of the believers among the two species (jinn and humankind). It is related from al-Dahhak that he restricted it to the regret of the angels, upon them be peace, and he claimed that by the servants is meant the three messengers. Abu al-Aliyah also explained "*al-ibad*" in this way, but he took the regret to be the regret of the destroyed unbelievers. He said: They felt regret when they saw the punishment of God, exalted is He, and they lamented over what had escaped them. It has also been said that by the servants are meant those who were destroyed, and the one who felt regret is the man who came from the farthest part of the city; he felt regret when the people leapt upon him to kill him. It has also been said that by the servants are meant those (the people who killed the man), and the one who felt regret is the messengers, when they killed that man and the punishment descended upon them while they had not believed. The condition of these sayings is not hidden. The intention of the one who said that the one who felt regret is the man, and the one who said that the one who felt regret is the messengers, was that the statement mentioned is the statement of the man or the statement of the messengers. In the words of Abu Hayyan there is something clear on this. Nevertheless, nothing that has been mentioned should be relied upon. It is also permitted that the regret be attributed to Him, glorified and exalted is He, metaphorically, meaning the magnifying of what they committed against themselves. It is supported by the fact that it was read: "*ya hasrata ala al-ibad*," for the original on this reading is "*ya hasrati*," and the *ya* was changed to an *alif*. Similar to it is the reading of Ibn Abbas, as Ibn Khalawayh said: "*ya hasrata ala al-ibad*" without *tanwin*, for the original here too is "*ya hasrati*," the *ya* was changed to an *alif*, then the *alif* was deleted and the vowel *fatha* was used in its place. Abu al-Zinad, Ibn Hurmuz and Ibn Jundub read: "*ya hasrah ala al-ibad*" with a silent *ha*. In *al-Muntaqa* it says: Pause on "*hasrah*" at length, to magnify the matter; then "*ala al-ibad*."

In *al-Lawami* it says: They paused on the *ha* for emphasis in regret, because in the *ha* there is a sound of groaning like *ta'awwuh* (a sigh of pain), then they joined it in that state.

Al-Tibi said: When the Arabs speak about a thing they regard as insignificant, they hasten through it and do not produce the full word that expresses it, as in: "You said to her, 'Stop (*qifi*),' she said to us, 'Qaf,'" meaning "I stopped," so she took from the word only one letter, out of contempt for the situation and reluctance to respond. It is not hidden that this does not suit the context. According to this reading, "*ala al-ibad*" should not be connected to *hasrah* or be its qualifier, since a pause would then not be good; rather it is made connected to an implied verb indicated by "*hasrah*," such as "he regrets" (*yatahassaru*) or "I regret" (*atahassaru*) "over the servants." The assumption "look" (*unzuru*) is not that; or it is the predicate of an omitted subject to clarify the object of regret, that is, "the regret is over the servants." The derivation of the reading "*ya hasrata*" with the *alif* according to this pattern is that one says: the pause on an accusative with *tanwin* is made with an *alif*, as in "*kana Allahu ala kulli shay'in qadiran*" (God is able over all things). "*Daraba Zaydun Amran*" (Zayd struck Amr) is not a thing; and even if it is granted that it is a thing, it does not contradict the support. It has also been said: *ya* is for address, the addressed is omitted, and *hasrah* is an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) of an implied verb, and "*ala al-ibad*" is connected to that verb, that is: "O these people, feel regret, a regret over the servants."

Perhaps what is most suited to the context and what comes first to minds is that what is meant is the summoning of the regret of everyone capable of feeling regret, and in this there is what there is of emphasis.

His saying, exalted is He: "*ma ya'tihim*" (there never came to them) and so on, is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*) explaining what the regret is about, and "*bihi*" (at him) is connected to "*yastahzi'una*" (they mock). It was placed before it for the sake of restriction in a claimed sense (*al-hasr al-idda'i*), and it is permitted that it is for the sake of observing the rhyme (*fawasil*).

[Page 5]

﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ The pronoun (the "they" in ﴿أَلَمْ يَرَوْا﴾) refers to the people of Makkah. The interrogative (istifham) is for affirmation (taqrir), that is, to make the listener acknowledge a fact. ﴿كَمْ﴾ (kam, "how many") is khabariyya (a "kam" used for stating a quantity, not asking about it) and is in the accusative position as the object of ﴿أَهْلَكْنا﴾ (ahlaknā, "We destroyed"). ﴿مِنَ القُرُونِ﴾ (min al-qurūn, "of the generations") is a clarifying specification (bayan) for ﴿كَمْ﴾. Some later scholars permitted ﴿كَمْ﴾ to be the subject (mubtada'), with the sentence after it as its predicate (khabar). This is the speech of someone who has no predicate in mind. The clause is governed by ﴿يَرَوْا﴾ (yarawā, "they see"), and its meaning takes effect within it, while ﴿كَمْ﴾ suspends (mu'allaqa) the verb from acting on it in its wording. This is because ﴿كَمْ﴾, even when khabariyya, has the front position of the sentence like the interrogative, so no governing word that comes before it acts on it in the eloquent standard usage, except when it is a preposition (harf jarr) or a noun in construct (ism mudaf). Examples: ﴿عَلى كَمْ فَقِيرٍ تَصَدَّقْتُ أرْجُو الثَّوابَ؟﴾ (On how many a poor man did I give charity, hoping for reward?) and ﴿وابْنُ كَمْ رَئِيسٍ صَحِبْتُهُ؟﴾ (And the son of how many a chief did I accompany?)

Al-Akhfash (the grammarian al-Akhfash), as reported in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), related the permissibility of a governing word coming before ﴿كَمْ﴾ other than these cases from some scholars, as in: ﴿مَلَكْتُ كَمْ غُلامٍ﴾ (malaktu kam ghulām), meaning "I owned many a slave boy", that is, "I owned many of the boys." They treated it in the manner of kathīr (many).

The seeing (al-ru'yah) here is ʿilmiyya (knowing), not basariyya (seeing with the eyes), contrary to Ibn ʿAṭiyya. This is because it is not suspended according to the well-known view, and because the people of Makkah were not present at the destruction of those before them so as to see it. Rather, they knew of it through reports and by observing the remains.

al-Qurūn (generations) is the plural of qarn, and they are the people who lived together in one time, such as ʿĀd, Thamūd and others.

﴿أَنَّهُمْ﴾ (annahum, "that they"): the pronoun refers to the meaning of ﴿كَمْ﴾, which is "the generations," meaning that the generations who were destroyed ﴿إِلَيْهِمْ﴾ (ilayhim, "to them"), that is, to the people of Makkah, ﴿لا يَرْجِعُونَ﴾ (lā yarji'ūn, "do not return"). ﴿أَنَّ﴾ and what follows it are, in interpretation, equivalent to a single noun (mufrad).

[Page 6]

It is a substitute (badal) for the whole clause ﴿كَمْ أَهْلَكْنا﴾ according to its meaning, as transmitted from Sibawayh, and followed by al-Zajjaj. That is: "Did they not see the multitude of Our destruction of those before them, and that they did not return to them?"

It was also said that the substitution is according to meaning, because the mentioned multitude and the non-return do not have a unity between them by partness, wholeness or connection, as the principle of substitution requires. But since that is in the sense of "those We destroyed" with "and that they do not return" meaning "not returning," the substitution becomes clear, and it is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) or a substitution of the whole from the whole (badal kull min kull), as said by al-Khafaji. Ṣāḥib al-Kashf benefited that it is a substitution of the whole by making their not returning the multitude of destruction, by way of metaphor (tajawwuz). In my view, this aspect, although it does not involve the substitution of a single noun for a clause and is realised in it, justifies the substitution as I have heard, but it is not free of artificiality. Sibawayh is not the prophet of grammar, so that following him would be obligatory.

al-Sīrāfī said: it is permissible to make ﴿أَنَّهُمْ﴾ ... etc. a relative clause (ṣila) of ﴿أَهْلَكْناهُمْ﴾, meaning: We destroyed them by means of their not returning, that is, by this type of destruction. Ibn Hishām, in al-Mughni, permitted that ﴿أَنَّ﴾ and its clause be the object (maʿmūl) of ﴿يَرَوْا﴾, with the clause ﴿كَمْ أَهْلَكْنا﴾ being a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) between them. He also permitted that it be suspended from ﴿كَمْ أَهْلَكْنا﴾, with ﴿أَنَّهُمْ إِلَيْهِمْ لا يَرْجِعُونَ﴾ as a object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi). al-Shumunnī said: "for they might see," and the meaning is: they knew, for the sake of the fact that they do not return, their destruction. It was rejected by saying that there is no meaningful benefit in what was mentioned of this meaning. al-Khafājī responded to this by saying: "It is not hidden that what was mentioned applies to the substitution as well, and the apparent purpose of mentioning it is either to mock them and make them look foolish, or to convey what the fronting of ﴿إِلَيْهِمْ﴾ conveys of restriction (ḥaṣr), meaning that they do not return to them but to Us, so what follows it is emphatic for it." End quote. And it is as you see. al-Jalabī said: "Perhaps the truth is that the first of the two pronouns is taken to refer to the meaning of ﴿كَمْ﴾, and the second to the messengers, and that ﴿أَنَّ﴾ and its clause is an object of purpose for ﴿أَهْلَكْناهُمْ﴾. The meaning: We destroyed them because of their persistence in not returning from their corrupt beliefs to the messengers and what they called them to. So the choice of ﴿لا يَرْجِعُونَ﴾ over ﴿لَمْ يَرْجِعُوا﴾ is to indicate the continuity of negation, while observing the verse-ending (fāṣila)." End quote. Although it is far-fetched, it is weak in meaning, and weaker than it is what was said: "The pronouns, as they seem to be, refer, the first to the meaning of ﴿كَمْ﴾ and the second to the one to whom ﴿يَرَوْا﴾ is attributed, and ﴿أَنَّ﴾ and its clause is the cause (ʿilla) of ﴿أَهْلَكْنا﴾. The meaning: they do not return to them so that they would inform them of the punishment that befell them, and the recompense for mockery is due; these people are thus restrained, therefore We destroyed them." It was reported from al-Farrāʾ that he makes ﴿يَرَوْا﴾ govern ﴿كَمْ أَهْلَكْنا﴾ and ﴿أَنَّهُمْ﴾ ... etc. without substitution, but he did not explain how this works.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya claimed that ﴿أَنَّ﴾ and its clause are a substitute for ﴿كَمْ﴾. It is not hidden that if one makes it the object of ﴿أَهْلَكْنا﴾, as is well known, this is not valid, because substitution is intended as the repetition of the governing word, and there is no meaning to your saying: "We destroyed that they do not return." Perhaps he was lenient in that. The intended meaning is a substitute for ﴿كَمْ أَهْلَكْنا﴾ according to its meaning, as reported from Sibawayh. As for making ﴿كَمْ﴾ the object of ﴿يَرَوْا﴾ and substituting from it the same ﴿كَمْ﴾ itself, its status is not hidden. Abū Ḥayyān said: "What the Arabic grammatical discipline requires is that ﴿أَنَّهُمْ﴾ ... etc. is the object of an omitted verb indicated by the meaning, and its estimate is: 'We decreed or judged that they do not return to them,' and the clause is a circumstantial (ḥāl) from the subject of ﴿أَهْلَكْنا﴾, as al-Khafājī said. I think this is further from dispute and argument; yet, in indicating the omitted word there is some obscurity. If this does not settle in your heart for that reason, then the sayings are before you, and there is no restriction on you."

It seems to me that you would choose what was reported from al-Sīrāfī, and there is no harm in it. It was also permitted, according to some views, that the pronoun in ﴿أَنَّهُمْ﴾ refers to those to whom ﴿يَرَوْا﴾ is attributed, and in ﴿إِلَيْهِمْ﴾ refers to the destroyed, meaning that the survivors do not return to the destroyed by kinship or lineage, that is, We destroyed them and cut off their offspring. Destruction together with cutting off offspring is more complete and general. This aspect makes what was reported from al-Sīrāfī good.

Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan read ﴿إِنَّهُ﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, as a resumption (isti'nāf, a new sentence), cutting the clause off from what comes before it in terms of grammatical case.

ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd) read ﴿أَلَمْ يَرَوْا مَنْ أَهْلَكْنا فَإِنَّهُمْ﴾ ... etc. according to the reading with a fatḥa, as a substitution of inclusion. It was rejected by the verse for those who hold the doctrine of return (rajʿa), as the Shīʿa have held.

[Page 6]

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Abū Isḥāq, who said: It was said to Ibn ʿAbbās: "Some people claim that ʿAlī, may God ennoble his face, will be raised before the Day of Resurrection?" He was silent for a while, then said: "What a people we would be, if we married his wives and divided up his inheritance! Do you not recite: ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, that they do not return to them?﴾"

﴿And every one of them will be assembled and brought before Us﴾. This is an explanation of the return of all to the place of gathering (al-mahshar), after the explanation that there is no return to the world (al-dunya). ﴿Wa-in﴾ is negative (nafiyah, a negating particle). ﴿Kullun﴾ is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject), and its tanwin (nunation, the "-un" ending) is a substitute ('iwad, compensation) for the genitive noun that is omitted (al-mudaf ilayhi). ﴿Lamma﴾ has the meaning of ﴿illa﴾ (except). Its use in this sense is established in the language of the Arabs by the transmission of trustworthy authorities (al-thiqat), so one should not heed the claim of al-Kisa'i (d. 189 AH, a Kufan grammarian) that this usage is not known. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: "There is a suitable meaning in its being used in this sense, namely that they are as if they were two negative particles, the first of which is emphasized by the second, and they are ﴿lam﴾ and ﴿ma﴾. Likewise ﴿illa﴾ is as if it were two negative particles, namely ﴿in﴾ (the negative) and ﴿la﴾, so one of them is used in place of the other." In my view, this is a kind of whisper of doubts (darb min al-wasawis).

﴿Jamee'un﴾ is the predicate (khabar, the grammatical predicate) of the subject. It is of the pattern ﴿fa'il﴾ in the sense of ﴿maf'ul﴾ (passive sense), and it conveys what ﴿kull﴾ does not convey, because ﴿kull﴾ conveys the encompassing of the individuals, whereas this conveys their being gathered together and the joining of some of them with others. ﴿Ladaynaa﴾ is an adverbial complement (zarf) either to it or to ﴿muhdarun﴾. ﴿Muhdarun﴾ is a second predicate (khabar thani) or an adjective (na't), and it is made plural in accordance with the meaning. The meaning is: "None of them, all of them, except that they are gathered together, brought before Us, for reckoning and recompense."

Ibn Salam said: "﴿Muhdarun﴾ means ﴿mu'adhdhabun﴾ (those who are punished)," so ﴿kull﴾ is an expression for the disbelievers (al-kafarah). It is permissible to intend this meaning according to the first interpretation as well. In the verse there is an admonition that the one who is destroyed is not left alone (al-muhlak la yutraku).

A group of the Seven (Readers) recited ﴿lamma﴾ with the light pronunciation (bi-al-takhfif), on the basis that ﴿in﴾ is a lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy ﴿inna﴾, the ﴿lam﴾ is a distinguishing particle (lam al-farq), and ﴿ma﴾ is an added particle (za'idah) for emphasis. The meaning is: "Indeed the matter is that they are all gathered together..." This is the view of the Basrans (al-Basriyyun). The Kufans held that ﴿in﴾ is negative, the ﴿lam﴾ has the meaning of ﴿illa﴾, and ﴿ma﴾ is an added particle, and the meaning is as in the heavy recitation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 33:

﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth﴾. It is read with light stress (takhfif), while Nafi' read it with emphatic stress (tashdid). ("A sign" [Arabic: āyah]) is a predicate placed before its subject for emphasis, and its indefiniteness is for magnification. ("For them" [Arabic: lahum]) may be connected to it, since it carries the meaning of a sign (ʿalāmah), or it may be connected to an implied element that is a qualifier of it. The plural pronoun refers to the disbelievers of Makkah and those who share their denial of the Resurrection. ("The earth" [Arabic: al-arḍ]) is the subject, and ("the dead" [Arabic: al-maytah]) is its qualifier. His - exalted is He - statement: ﴿We have revived it﴾ [Arabic: aḥyaynāhā] is a resumptive clause explaining how it is a sign. It has also been said that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), with the governing element being "a sign," because of the meaning of informing it contains; but this is a weak and forced analysis. It has also been said: ("A sign") is the first subject, and ("for them") is its qualifier or is connected to it; either of these two matters permits beginning with an indefinite noun. Then ("the dead earth") is a second subject with a qualifier, and the clause ("We have revived it") is the predicate of the second subject. The clause of the second subject and its predicate is the predicate of the first subject. Because it is the very same as the subject, like the predicate of the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shān), it does not need a connecting pronoun. Al-Khafaji said: "This is very good, except that the grammarians have not stated it except for the pronoun of the matter." It has also been said that it is interpreted according to the meaning of this statement, and therefore no connecting element is needed for it. Its remoteness is not hidden. It has also been said: ("A sign") is the subject and ("the earth") is its predicate, and the clause ("We have revived it") is a qualifier of "the earth," because it does not refer to a specific earth but to the genus; so there is no requirement to describe a definite noun with a clause that has the status of an indefinite. A parallel to this is the poet's verse:

And indeed I pass by the base man who reviles me, so I go on, then I say: "It does not concern me."

Abu Hayyan denied the permissibility of this, disagreeing with al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Malik in al-Tashil, and he made the clause ("who reviles me") a circumstantial clause of "the base man." You know that the meaning is about the continuity of his passing by those who revile him and his overlooking it; for this reason he said "I pass by" and joined to it "so I go on." The restriction by a circumstantial clause does not convey this meaning. Furthermore, the basis of the informative character is the intention of the genus, so there is no information about a definite noun from an indefinite one that would contradict the rules, as has been claimed. Indeed, the most preferred of the possibilities is what was established first. The meaning of the death of the earth and its revival has already passed, so reflect upon it.

﴿And We bring forth from it grain﴾ [Arabic: ḥabban], i.e., the genus of grain, such as wheat, barley, rice and others. The indefinite noun may be general, as when it occurs in the context of blessing or the like. Mentioning the bringing forth, and likewise the making (ja'l) that follows, is an indication of the perfection of the revival. ("So from it") [Arabic: famminhu], i.e., from the grain after We bring it forth. The "fa" enters upon the caused result, and "min" is either for beginning or partitive. The prepositional phrase is connected to His statement - exalted is He -: ﴿they eat﴾ [Arabic: ya'kulūn]. The fronting serves to indicate that grain is the main part of what is eaten and sustains life, because of what this implies of restriction, for the sake of emphasis on it, to the extent that it is as if there is no other food.

﴿And We placed in it gardens of palm trees﴾. *Jam'* (the plural) of *nakhl*, like *'abid*, the plural of *'abd*, as most of the scholars (*a'immah*) held, and as al-Fayruzabadi stated explicitly in *al-Qamus*. It is also said to be an *ism jam'* (collective noun). Al-Jawhari said: "*al-nakhl* and *al-nakhil* have the same meaning." The former view is the one relied upon. (**and vineyards**): the plural of *'inab*, which is applied both to the vine itself and to its fruit, as al-Raghib said. Perhaps it is a *mushtarak* (homonym) for both. It is also said that it is literally the fruit and metaphorically the tree. In any case, the intended meaning is the first, by the indication of its conjunction with *al-nakhil* (palm trees). Both were put in the plural but *al-habb* (grain) was not. It is said that the plural form indicates a multiplicity of kinds, i.e., of kinds of palm and kinds of grape, because *al-nakhl* and *al-'inab* are names for two species, so each of them is predicated of the individuals of one reality, and they do not indicate the diversity of what falls under them or the multiplicity of their kinds unless they are expressed in the plural form. This differs from *al-habb*, which is an *ism jins* (generic noun) and implies the diversity of what falls under it, because it is predicated of a multitude of differing realities by an essential predication, so it does not need the plural form to indicate diversity. The expression "the plural of *al-'alam*" in His saying ﴿Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾, where *al-'alam* is an *ism jins* in order to encompass what falls under it of the genera, does not contradict this. It is said that the purpose is to encompass in a manifest and definite way, even if the implication is obtained without it. It is also said that both were put in the plural to indicate the abundance of the blessing. As for *al-habb*, in it is the sustenance of the body, and this is achieved by the genus.

Almighty and Majestic is He, in the context of arguing for the matter of the Gathering (*al-hashr*), bestowed a favour by making the gardens from the palms and vines, meaning the trees. He, Glorified and Exalted, did not bestow a favour by making the fruits of those trees to be dates and grapes, as He bestowed a favour by bringing forth the grain, magnifying the favour, because that favour includes, along with the fruits and other benefits of those trees themselves, all their parts, for man himself without intermediary, particularly the palm. There is no indication in the statement that the outcome of the making is restricted to eating the fruit, and the benefit of specifying that among the benefits is evident. This differs from the trees of grains, for they are not in this position, and therefore He changed the style and did not treat their fruit as the grains are treated. The words of al-Baydawi, may God have mercy on him, clearly indicate that the intended meaning of *al-a'nab* (grapes) is the known fruits, not the vineyards. He explained the mention of the palms without their fruit, though that is more fitting, by what comes before and after, by their being distinguished by greater benefit and signs of craftsmanship. Interpreting *al-a'nab* as fruits rather than vineyards is, in my opinion, far-fetched, because of the conjunction, and because the prepositional phrase is in the position of an adjective to (*jannat*, gardens), and what is known is that they are of trees, not of fruits.

Al-Raghib said: *al-jannah* is every orchard with trees that covers the land with its trees, and the covering trees are sometimes called *jannah*. On this meaning is interpreted his saying:

*Of the water-camels, irrigating a garden, withered*

Moreover, in the verse after this there is what supports the intention of the fruits. So reflect!

﴿And We caused to gush forth therein﴾, i.e., We split in the earth. Janah ibn Hubaysh read *fajarna* with the light (unshaddah) form, and the meaning is one, except that the emphatic form indicates intensity and abundance.

﴿from the springs﴾, i.e., some springs. The prepositional phrase is in the position of an adjective to an elided noun, and *min* is explanatory (*bayaniyyah*). It was permitted that it be partitive (*tab'idiyyah*), but this is not so. It is said that the object is elided and (*min al-'uyun*, from the springs) is connected to (*fajjara*, caused to gush forth), and *min* is for origin (*ibtida'iyyah*), in the sense: We caused to gush forth from the sources what is benefited from in water. Al-Akhfash went to the view that *min* is additional, and he made *al-'uyun* the object of (*fajjarna*), because he holds that its additional use is permitted in affirmative sentences when its genitive is definite.

﴿So that they may eat of its fruit﴾ is related to (We made).

Its placement after (the gushing of the springs) is because the fruit's beginnings come from it. The meaning is: "We made in it gardens of palm trees and grapevines, and We arranged the beginnings of their fruit so that they might eat." The pronoun in (its fruit) refers to what was made, namely the gardens. That is why it is singular and masculine, and it was not said "of its fruit" (referring to the gardens) or "of their fruit" (referring to the palms and grapevines). A similar view is that it refers to what was mentioned, and the pronoun may function like a demonstrative, as in the verse of Ru'bah:

*In them are streaks of black and white,*
*as if on the skin is the splotching of vitiligo.*

He meant "that," as he said to Abu Ubaydah when the latter asked him about it: "as if that..." Some say it refers to the water, since the springs indicate it, or because the speech contains an omitted noun, meaning "the water of the springs." Others say it refers to the palm trees, and only they are mentioned because it is known that the grapevines share in this. Others say it refers to the gushing (tafjir) understood from (We caused to gush), and the intended meaning of (its fruit) is its benefits, as one says, "The fruit of trade is profit." Or it is its apparent meaning, and the idafa (possessive construction) is for the slightest connection. All of these are as you see.
