It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to Him, glory be to Him, and the attribution of the fruit to Him, exalted is He, is because He, glory be to Him, is its Creator. So it is as if it were said: "so that they may eat of what Allah, exalted is He, created from the fruit."

The apparent expression would have been (of Our fruit), using the royal plural pronoun, in line with what came before. However, the speech shifted (iltifat: a change of grammatical person) from the first person to the third person, because eating and living are among the things that distract from Allah, exalted is He, so the third person suits this context. Thus the iltifat is in its right place.

Some claimed that this is not its proper place, because it is more fitting to use the singular pronoun of the One who is obeyed, since He is the one intended by giving life, making, and causing to gush, and these have been attributed to Him. This was refuted: what preceded is more majestic, because those are actions of general benefit and clearly show perfect power, while fruit is of a lower rank than grain, and for this reason it was not presented in an exclusive manner, so it does not deserve that magnification. Moreover, some have made the fruit the creation of Allah, exalted is He, while its perfection is by the action of the human. With what has been mentioned, what was said above is unnecessary.

Talhah, Ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read *min thumurihi* (مِن ثُمُرِهِ) with two damma vowels, and this is a dialectal form of it, or it is the plural of *thimar*.

Al-A'mash read *min thumrihi* (مِن ثُمْرِهِ) with a damma followed by sukun.

﴿And what their hands made﴾: *ma* (ما) is a relative pronoun in the genitive position, coordinated with (its fruit). To make it accusative, coordinated with the position of (min thamarihi), is contrary to the apparent sense. The meaning is: "and so that they may eat from what they made or produced with their powers." The intended meaning is what is made from the fruit, such as juice, date syrup, and others. Al-Zamakhshari said: "That is, from what their hands made by planting, watering, and pollinating," but this is not right. It is also permissible for *ma* to be an indefinite qualified noun, meaning "and from something their hands made." The first is more apparent. It is said that *ma* is a negation particle, and the pronoun in (made it) refers to the fruit, and the clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal). The meaning of negating that their hands made it is that it is by the creation of Allah, exalted is He, not by their action, and the proponents of generation (tawlid, that causes act through natural causation) do not say this. The view that it is a negation particle is narrated from Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak. The apparent words of al-Habr (Ibn Abbas) indicate that the pronoun refers to the omitted qualified noun "shay'an" (a thing), and the clause is a circumstantial phrase from it. Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that he said: "They found it made, which their hands did not make," meaning the Euphrates, the Tigris, the river of Balkh, and the like. This is far-fetched.

The view that *ma* is relative has been supported by the reading of Talhah, Isa, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr, who read *wa-ma 'amilat* (وما عَمِلَتْ) without the final *ha'* pronoun. The basis of this support is that the relative pronoun together with its clause functions like a single noun, so it is suitable with it, because of its extension and its requirement for it, and its indication of it, so it is like what has been mentioned. The assumption of an apparent noun that is not apparent. Al-Tibi said: making it a negation particle is better than making it a relative pronoun, so as not to suggest that they independently did the work, because mention of the hands in this context is for emphasis, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not see that We created for them, from what Our hands made, livestock?﴾ The construction is like "I took it with my hand" and "I saw it with my eye." In that case, His saying, exalted is He, "(We revived it)..." etc. does not fit as an explanation of the dead earth being a sign. Al-Kashshaf responded to this, saying it is nothing, because action by servants means acquisition (kasb), and it has come in phrases such as ﴿what your hands have sent forth﴾ and ﴿what your two hands have sent forth﴾. Therefore this emphasis removes the suggestion of misunderstanding. End of quote. So do not be heedless.

It is also permissible in this reading for *ma* to be a verbal-noun particle (masdariyya), meaning "and the work of their hands," and the noun in the sense of the object is intended, meaning "the thing worked by their hands," so it returns to the meaning of the relative. What is in this is not hidden.

﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾ This is a rebuke and a censure for their lack of gratitude to the Benefactor for the blessings enumerated, through monotheism and worship. The fa' (ف) is coordinating with an implied premise required by the context, meaning: "Do they see these blessings, or do they enjoy them, and yet not thank the One who bestowed them?"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 36:

﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs﴾. This is a resumptive clause, brought to declare Him exalted above what they did in abandoning His thanks, and to magnify what was mentioned within the relative clause of the wonderful signs of His power, the secrets of His wisdom, and the marvelous bounties of His favours, which necessitate thanks to Him, the Exalted, and the singling out of worship for Him, glory be to Him, and to express wonder at their neglect of that while this is their state. The discussion of (Subhan, glory) has already been mentioned. In al-Irshad it is said here that it is a proper noun for tasbih (glorification), which is distancing from evil in belief and speech, meaning believing in His distance from it and judging Him to be so, from "sabaha fi al-ardh wa al-ma'" (he swam in land and water) when he went far into them and went to the limit. Its accusative case is as a verbal noun, meaning: "I glorify Glory be to Him," i.e., I declare Him free of what is not fitting for Him in belief and action, a declaration specific to Him and befitting His majesty, may His dignity be exalted. In it there is emphasis from the aspect of derivation, from the aspect of the shift to the form tafif'il, and from the aspect of the shift from the verbal noun that indicates the genus to the noun placed specifically for it, especially the knowledge, and from the aspect of its being put in place of the verbal noun with the verb. It is also said: it is a verbal noun like ghufran, meaning complete transcendence and total distance from evil, so there is emphasis from the aspect of attributing transcendence to the Sacred Essence. The meaning, then, is: He transcended by His essence above everything not fitting for Him, the Exalted, a transcendence specific to Him, glory be to Him. Thus, on this view, the sentence is a report from Him, the Exalted, of His transcendence and freedom from everything not fitting for Him, of what they did and what they left undone. On the first view, it is a ruling from Him, the Mighty and Majestic, to that effect and an instruction to the believers that they should say it, believe its meaning, not neglect it, and not be heedless of it.

Some have taken the governing verb to be an imperative, meaning: "Glorify Glory be to Him." By "pairs" is meant the kinds and categories. Al-Raghib said: "Azwaj" is the plural of zawj, and it is said of each of two mates and of each thing that is joined with another, either similar to it or opposite to it. Everything in the world is a pair insofar as it has some opposite, or some likeness, or some composition, indeed it never separates, in some respect, from a composition of form and matter, and of substance and accident.

﴿from what the earth produces﴾ is an explanation of "the pairs", and by it is meant everything that grows in it of the things mentioned and others.

﴿and from themselves﴾, meaning and He created the pairs from themselves, namely the male and the female.

﴿and from what they do not know﴾, meaning and the pairs of things of which Allah, the Exalted, has not informed them and has not made for them a way to know their specifics. He, glory be to Him, has informed them of that only in general terms, in the manner of ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾, for upon this depends their standing before the greatness of His power, the vastness of His dominion, and the majesty of His sovereignty, the Mighty and Majestic. Perhaps, since knowledge is among the most distinctive attributes of Lordship, it was not affirmed in its complete and encompassing form for anyone other than Him, glory be to Him, even if it is by way of overflow from Him, blessed and exalted, and because the capacity of the contingent is too narrow to encompass, so what each person does not know is far greater than what he knows. It may be said, in some respects, that what each person knows is finite and what he does not know is infinite, and there is no ratio at all between the finite and the infinite, so there is no ratio between each person's known and unknown. Reflect on this together with the claim of some of the great masters to have reached the fixed entities and to have knowledge of them, and say: "My Lord, increase me in knowledge."

**Page 10**

﴿And a sign for them is the night﴾ is an explanation of His, exalted is He, dazzling power in time, after He had explained it in space. "A sign" (*āyah*) is the predicate placed first, and "the night" (*al-layl*) is the postponed subject. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We strip from it the day﴾ is a resumptive clause (*isti'nāf*) explaining why it is a sign. There are other possible structures of the sentence, which can be understood from what has passed, but the more probable reading is what has been mentioned. That is, We uncover and remove the light from the place of the night, and from the site where its shadow and darkness fall, which is the air.

**Page 10 (continued)**

The day is an expression for the light, either by way of metaphor (*tajawwuz*) or by elision of a modifier (*ḥadhf al-muḍāf*). His saying, exalted is He, "from it" (*minhu*) involves the elision of a modifier, because the day and the night are two expressions for the time of the sun being above the horizon and below it, and there is no sense in one of them being uncovered from the other. The original sense of *salkh* is stripping the hide off something like a sheep, so it is used for uncovering the light from the place of the night and the spot where its darkness and shadow lie, as a sensory metaphor (*isti'ārah tab'iyyah*) that is explicit (*taṣrīḥiyyah*). The common element (*al-jāmi'*) is what the intellect grasps of one matter following upon another: the appearance of the flesh follows the stripping of the hide, and the appearance of darkness follows the uncovering of the light from the place of the night. It has also been permitted that there is a implicit metaphor (*isti'ārah makniyyah*) in "the day," and an imaginative metaphor (*isti'ārah takhyīliyyah*) in "stripping," but the majority hold to what we have mentioned. The "min" (*min*) is for the starting point (*ibtidā'iyyah*). It has been said that it is partitive (*tab'īḍiyyah*), but making it causal (*sababiyyah*) is worthless. This interpretation is related from al-Farrā'. Similar is interpreting *salkh* as *naz'* (pulling off).

The use of the fā' (*fa*) in His saying ﴿and then they are in darkness﴾, meaning they enter into darkness, as the *hamzah* of the causative form (*hamzat al-if'āl*) on it indicates, is clear. It occurs in the words of Shaykh Abd al-Qahir and Imam al-Sakkaki that "what is borrowed for in the verse is the appearance of the day from the darkness of the night, and what is borrowed from is the appearance of the skinned thing from its hide." According to what al-Allamah al-Tibi and al-Fadil al-Yamani said, this is taken from al-Zajjaj's saying: "The meaning of 'We strip from it the day' is 'We bring the day out of it, bringing it out in such a way that none of its light remains.'" So "appearance" (*ẓuhūr*) in their words means "coming out," and it is transitive with "min," so there is no need to make it mean "'an."

This meaning has also come in the words of Umar to Abu Ubaydah, may Allah be pleased with both of them: "Come out (*iẓhar*) with those Muslims who are with you toward it," meaning toward the land, i.e., go out to its surface. And in the hadith of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her: "The Prophet (ﷺ) would pray the 'Asr while the shadow had not yet appeared (*yaẓhar*) from the chamber," meaning it had not yet come out onto its surface. Thus the objection is dismissed, namely that if appearance were meant, it would say "then they are seeing" (*mubṣirūn*) and not "then they are in darkness" (*muẓlimūn*), because what follows the appearance of the day from the darkness of the night is seeing, not darkness. This is without need to interpret the expression by inversion (*qalb*), i.e., the appearance of the darkness of the night from the day. Some have answered this objection by saying that "day" is an expression for the whole period from the break of dawn or sunrise until sunset, not for part of it, so what follows this entire period is entering into darkness. Al-Salkuti objected to this that entering darkness is consequent upon the stripping, not upon the end of the day's duration.

Perhaps the intent of some is that stripping in the sense of the appearance of the day is not realized except by the appearance of all its parts, and once all parts of the day have appeared, its duration has ended. Al-Allamah al-Qutb mentioned that *salkh* may mean *naz'* (pulling off), as in "I stripped the skin off the sheep," and it may mean *ikhrāj* (bringing out), as in "I stripped the sheep out of its skin," so the sheep is "stripped." Shaykh Abd al-Qahir and al-Sakkaki went to the second, and others to the first. So the use of the fā' in "then they are" is clear according to the view of others. As for their view, it is valid only on the basis that it is set for what is customarily regarded as sequential without delay. This varies according to matters and customs: the time may be long while the custom in such a case does not require taking the interval into account, and it may be the reverse, as in this verse. For although the time of the day lies between bringing the day out of the night and the entry of darkness, nevertheless, because the entry of darkness after the illumination by the day is great, and because it ought to occur only after many times that duration, it counted the duration as short and made the night seem to surprise them right after the day was brought out of the night, without interval.

Then it is not hidden that the sudden *idhā* (*idhā al-mufājā'ah*) is valid only if *salkh* is taken to mean *ikhrāj*, as one says: "He brought the day out of the night, and the entry of night surprised him," which is sound. This is unlike when it is taken to mean *naz'*, for it is not correct to say: "He pulled the light of the sun off the air, and darkness surprised him," just as it is not correct to say: "I broke the jug, and breaking surprised him," because their entry into darkness is the very occurrence of darkness, so the relation of their entry into darkness to the pulling off of the day's light is like the relation of breaking to the act of breaking. For this reason the two of them took *salkh* to mean *ikhrāj* and not *naz'*. End of quotation.

**Page 11**

Al-Allamah al-Thani strengthened this by saying: "There is no doubt that a thing is a sign only if it includes a kind of strangeness and wonder, such that it requires a kind of power. What is surprising is the darkness's occurrence right after the appearance of the day, not right after the disappearance of the day's light."

Al-Salkuti said: the non-correctness of the surprise in what was mentioned is because surprise is conceivable only in what is not anticipated but happens suddenly. Then it can be answered: since the stripping of light from the night, given the complete clarity of its appearance, was anticipated to take a long period, the occurrence of darkness after it in a short period is something not anticipated. He then said: "With this, the answer to the strengthening becomes clear." It has also been said: since darkness is something that natures recoil from and souls dislike, its occurrence appears as if it were not anticipated, and the act of stripping itself suffices to indicate power. What the statements of al-Tibi and al-Yamani mentioned earlier require is that Shaykh (Abd al-Qahir) and al-Sakkaki intended bringing the day out of the night in such a way that none of its light remains, as al-Zajjaj said, and its result is the removal of the day's light from the place of the night and the site of its darkness, as al-Farra' said.

The appearance (*ẓuhūr*) has also come in their speech in the sense of disappearance (*zawāl*), as in the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

*"The slanderers reproached her that I love her, and that is a complaint whose shame has disappeared from you."*

Al-Jawhari related: "One says, 'This is a matter whose shame has disappeared from you (*ẓāhirun 'anka 'āruhu*),' i.e., it has departed." Al-Marzuqi said, regarding the verse of the Hamasi poet:

*"And that is shame, O son of Raytah, which has disappeared."*

Likewise. So there is no obstacle to its being in the words of the two shaykhs in this sense, and "appearance" may mean "making apparent." The use of this expression is a looseness (*musāhalah*), since it is evident that *nasluKh* is transitive, so the matter returns to removal, and their two statements unite with what al-Farra' said. Likewise, according to what has been said, that the intended meaning of "appearance" is "coming out in the manner of separation," because disappearance is evident in it then, and the matter of looseness remains as it is. On the view of unity, al-Allamah's objection arises, and the answer is the answer; so consider this carefully. And Allah, exalted is He, is the Guide to what is right.

In the verse, according to what many have said, there is an indication that the original state is darkness, and light is something that arrives upon it and covers it with its brightness. The hadith also hints at this. Imam Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi related from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Allah, exalted is He, created creation in darkness, then cast upon them some of His light. Whoever is struck by some of His light is guided, and whoever misses it goes astray."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 38 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And the sun﴾ is in conjunction (*'atf*) with "the night," meaning: and a sign for them is the sun.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿runs on﴾ ... etc., is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) explaining how it is a sign. It has also been said that "the sun" is the subject (*mubtada'*) and what follows it is the predicate (*khabar*), and the sentence is conjoined to "the night strips away" (*naslakh*). Other views have also been stated, so be attentive. *Al-jary* is swift passing. Its origin is the passing of water and of what moves with its flow, and the meaning is that it moves swiftly. ﴿To a fixed place for it﴾: to a specific limit at which it ends its orbit (*falak*) at the end of the year. The image is likened to the resting place of a traveler when he completes his journey, in that each ends at a specific location, even though the traveler has a resting place short of that. This is narrated from al-Kalbi, and Ibn Qutaybah preferred it. The word *mustaqarr* ("resting place") here is a noun of place, and the *lam* means "to." It is also read with *ila* ("to") in place of the *lam*. It is permissible that the *lam* be causal (*ta'lil*), or that it indicate the limit for it of the daily risings (*mashariq*) and settings (*magharib*), because it traverses them, rising point by rising point and setting point by setting point, until it reaches their furthest extent, then it returns. That is its limit and its resting place, because it does not exceed it.

This is also narrated from al-Hasan. Both views agree that *mustaqarr* is a noun of place and that the *lam* has the meaning given above, but they differ in that the first takes "resting" from the resting of a traveler, likening the completion of the cycle to the completion of the journey. The latter is with respect to the extremes of ascent and reaching its furthest point, and likewise the extremes of descent. The "resting" is with respect to not going beyond the first limit in exhausting the risings, and beyond the second in exhausting the settings. Or it is a limit for it from its course each day in the view of our eyes, which is the setting. *Mustaqarr* is also a noun of place, and the *lam* is as you have heard. Or it is for the center of the sky (*kabd al-sama'*) and the circle of midday, so *mustaqarr* and the *lam* are on the analogy of what preceded. That this is the place of its resting is either a metaphor for slow movement, or it is according to what appears. Dhu al-Rummah said, describing his horse and its running at midday and the intensity of the heat:

*Stripped bare upon the scorching pebbles, its galloping, while the sun is bewildered, spinning in the air.*

Or it is for its settling and stay in each of the twelve zodiacal signs (*burj*) in a specific manner. In that case *mustaqarr* is a mimi noun (a noun formed with *mim*), and the *lam* governs the end point or the bearer. It has been said that "it runs to its house," which is the sign of Leo, and its "resting" is an expression for the goodness of its condition therein. This is not accepted except by the astrologers, and their judgment is not hidden from the scholars of Islam. Qatadah and Muqatil said: the meaning is that it runs until a time that it does not pass. Al-Wahidi said: according to this, its *mustaqarr* is the end of its course at the conclusion of the world, and this is the preference of al-Zajjaj. As al-Nawawi said in his commentary on Sahih Muslim: "*Mustaqarr* is also a noun of time."

In more than one of the authentic collections, it is reported from Abu Dharr who said: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) in the mosque at sunset, and he said: 'O Abu Dharr, do you know where this sun goes?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best!' He said: 'It goes to prostrate, then it asks permission, and permission is granted to it. It is about to prostrate and its prostration will not be accepted, and it will ask permission and permission will not be granted. It will be told: return from where you came, and it will rise from its west.' That is His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿And the sun runs to a resting place for it﴾." In another narration: "Do you know where this sun goes?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best!" He said: "It runs until it reaches its resting place beneath the Throne, and it falls down prostrating," and the hadith continues. There are several narrations on this, and it has also been narrated in a very abridged form.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Abu Dharr who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the sun runs to a resting place for it﴾, and he said: 'Its resting place is beneath the Throne.'" So *mustaqarr* is a noun of place, and the apparent meaning is that the sun truly has a resting in it. Al-Nawawi said: a group held to the apparent meaning of the hadith. Al-Wahidi said: according to this view, whenever the sun sets each day, it rests beneath the Throne until it rises. Then al-Nawawi said: its prostration is with a discernment and perception that Allah creates in it.

Ibn Hajar al-Haytami mentioned in his *al-Fatawa al-Hadithiyyah* that its prostration beneath the Throne occurs only at its setting. He related from some of them that it rises from heaven to heaven until it prostrates beneath the Throne and says: "O Lord, indeed a people disobey You," and it is told: "Return from where you came," so it descends from heaven to heaven until it rises from the east. With its descent to the lowest heaven the dawn breaks. Also in the same vein, Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ikrimah that when it sets it enters a river beneath the Throne, and it glorifies its Lord until, when it is morning, it asks its Lord to excuse it from coming out. He, glorified is He, says: "Why?" It says: "If I come out, I will be worshipped besides You." Prostration beneath the Throne has also come in the narrations of the Imamiyyah, and they have wondrous reports about it, among them that upon the sun are seventy thousand *kullab* (rope-bearing hooks or guiding cords), and each *kullab* is drawn by seventy thousand angels from its east to its west. Then they take the light from it, and it falls prostrating beneath the Throne. Then they ask their Lord: "Shall we clothe it in the garment of light or not?" They are answered with what He, glorified is He, wills. Then they ask Him, mighty and majestic: "Shall we make it rise from its east or its west?" The call comes to them with what He, may His majesty be exalted, wills. Then they ask about the measure of the light, and the call comes to them with what creation needs regarding the shortening and lengthening of the day.

In *al-Hay'ah al-Saniyyah* of al-Jalal al-Suyuti there are reports of this kind, but the sound among the reports is few, and I have no reliance on the authenticity of the reports of the Imamiyyah, and most of what is in *al-Hay'ah al-Saniyyah* is not relied upon. Yes, what preceded from Abu Dharr is not in doubt regarding its authenticity, and what can be said about Abu Dharr and the truthfulness of his speech? The matter in this is problematic if prostration and resting beneath the Throne occur every night, whether it is said that it rises from heaven to heaven until it reaches it and then prostrates, or it is said that it rests and prostrates beneath it without rising. Imam al-Haramayn and others have stated explicitly that there is no disagreement that it sets for some people and rises for others, and the night is long for some people and short for others, and between night and day there is a difference in length and shortness at the line of equator. In the lands of Bulghar, dawn may break before the twilight of sunset has ended, and at latitude ninety, it never stops rising while it is in the northern signs and never stops setting while it is in the southern signs. So the year is half night and half day, as has been explained in its proper place. The proofs establish that it does not remain still at its setting, for otherwise it would be still at its rising, on the basis that its setting in one horizon is its rising in another. Also, the proofs establish that it does not leave its orbit, so how can it rise from heaven to heaven until it reaches the Throne? Rather, the fact that the matter is not like that is clearer than the sun and needs no explanation at all. Likewise, its being beneath the Throne always, in the sense of the Throne enclosing it, and its being within it like the rest of the spheres that are above its orbit and those below it. I have asked many of the eminent contemporaries about reconciling what I have heard of the authentic reports with what contradicts them from observation and proof, but I did not succeed in obtaining from them anything that would quench the thirst or cure the sick. What comes to mind in resolving this problem, and Allah knows best the reality of the matter, is that the sun, and likewise all the stars, are perceiving and rational, as His saying, exalted is He, that comes later indicates: ﴿Each in an orbit swims﴾, where the verb is attributed to a plural pronoun for rational beings. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾ points in the same direction. The apparent meaning of what is reported from Abu Dharr also indicates this, that it prostrates and asks permission, for what is understood from asking permission is what occurs by the tongue of speech and not by the tongue of state.

That Allah creates perception and discernment in it during prostration and asking permission, and then removes it from it, is something for which there is no need to hold, but rather it is extremely far-fetched. The evidences from the Book, the Sunnah, and the words of the Family of the Prophet (ﷺ) that it possesses perception and discernment are too numerous to count. Some of them indicate that this is specifically attributed to it, and some indicate that it is attributed to it by its inclusion in the general category or by analogy, since no one distinguishes between them. When it is like that, it is not far-fetched that it has a rational soul like the soul of a human being. Indeed, some of the Sufis explicitly stated that it has a perfect rational soul, and the philosophers established a soul for the sphere, and some of them stated that the stars also have souls. They said: everything in the upper world, of stars, universal and particular spheres, and epicycles, is living and rational. And the rational human souls, when they are holy, may strip away from bodies and depart appearing in the forms of their bodies or in other forms, as Gabriel (peace be upon him) takes form and appears in the form of Dihyah or in the form of some Bedouin, as came in the authentic reports, whenever Allah, mighty and majestic, wills, while there remains a kind of attachment for them to the original bodies by which the performance of actions from them is possible. This is as is related of some of the saints, may their secrets be sanctified, that they are seen at one time in several places, and that is only due to the strength of the detachment of their souls and the extreme of their holiness, so that they appear in one place while their original body is in another place.

*Do not say: her dwelling is in the east of Najd,*
*for all of Najd is a dwelling of the 'Amiriyyah.*

This is a very common matter among the Sufi masters, well known among them. Traveling the distance in an instant is one such matter, and the seeing of one person in two places at once is another. Whoever denies either of these about them is being obstinate, and such denial comes only from an ignorant or stubborn person. The scholar al-Taftazani (Taftazani) was astonished at some of the jurists of the Ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni community, lit. "people of the Sunna"), such as Ibn Muqatil, who ruled that one who believes what is related about Ibrahim ibn Adham (may his secret be sanctified) is an unbeliever: that his companions saw him in Basra on the Day of Tarwiyya while he was seen that same day in Mecca. His reasoning was that this is of the same kind as the great miracles (mu'jizat), and that it cannot establish a karama (a miracle granted to a saint) for a walī (saint). You know that the position we rely upon is that the saint may be granted a karama in general, except in matters for which the evidence establishes that they are impossible, such as producing a sūra like one of the sūras of the Qur'an. Many scholars have affirmed the imagining and visualizing of the soul (nafs) of our Prophet ﷺ after his death, and have claimed that he, upon him be blessings and peace, may be seen in several places at one time while he is in his noble grave praying. This has been discussed fully earlier. It is also established that the Prophet ﷺ saw Moses, upon him be peace, praying in his grave beside the red sand hill, and saw him in the heavens, and what passed between them concerning the obligatory prayers took place. As for the claim that Moses, upon him be peace, ascended to the heavens bodily, with the same body that was in the grave, after the Prophet ﷺ had seen him, no one has definitively said this, and to say it is a remote possibility. The Prophet ﷺ also saw, on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey), a group of prophets other than Moses, upon him be peace, in the heavens, although their graves are on the earth, and no one has said that they were transferred from the earth to the heavens on the analogy of what you have just heard. This is not something the philosophers (al-Hukamiyyun) claim is impossible, namely that a single soul occupies more than one body. Rather it is a matter beyond that, as will not be hidden from one whom God Most High has illumined in insight. It may therefore be said: the sun has a soul (nafs) like those holy souls, and it strips itself from the observed, familiar body while some kind of connection to it remains. It then ascends to the Throne, prostrates beneath it without intermediary, remains there, and asks permission. This does not contradict the motion of this familiar body or its non-stillness, as the astronomers (Ahl al-Hay'a) and others claim. This happens when it sets, passes beyond the true horizon, and the inhabitants of the inhabited part of the earth cease to see it. Its rising at that time at a latitude of about ninety degrees does no harm, because what we have mentioned, that the prostration and stillness are with respect to the stripped-off soul manifested in whatever form God Most High wills, does not contradict the motion of the familiar body. Indeed, even if both were at midday on the line of the equator, it would still do no harm. It is also permissible to say that its prostration is after it sets over the horizon of Medina, and its being risen at that time over another horizon does no harm, for the reason you have heard. However, what is most likely to be the case is what was mentioned first. On this same pattern is explained what is related about the Ka'ba visiting one of the saints: it may be said that the Ka'ba has a reality (haqiqa) other than what the common people know, and in terms of that reality it visits, while people see it in its place as stones built up.

The Shaykh al-Akbar (the Greatest Shaykh, Ibn al-'Arabi), may his secret be sanctified, mentioned in al-Futuhat (The Meccan Openings) a lengthy discourse clearly indicating that the Ka'ba has a reality other than what the common people know. In it he also states that during his stay there was continuous correspondence, appeals, and reproaches between him and it, and that he recorded some of this in a booklet he named Taj al-Wasa'il wa Minhaj al-Rasa'il (The Crown of Means and the Path of Epistles). Najm al-Din 'Umar al-Nasafi, the Mufti of Humans and Jinn, was asked about what is related that the Ka'ba used to visit, etc.: is it permissible to affirm this? He replied: the breaking of habitual custom (naqd al-'āda) as a karama for the people of sainthood is permissible according to the Ahl al-Sunna, and al-'Allama Sa'd (al-Taftazani) and others approved of this. However, I have not seen anyone explain its visiting in this way. The apparent meaning of some scholars' words is that this happens by the departure of the observed body from it to the one visited, and its moving from its place. In numerous fatwa collections, and in al-Walwalijiyya and others, it is stated: if the Ka'ba goes to visit some of the saints, then the prayer is toward its air. It may be that what is intended by this is other than what is related, for, God Most High knows best, it did not happen by the movement of the observed body.

[p. 15]

I have not seen anyone reconcile the hadith about the sun with what sense perception requires and with the statements of the astronomers in this way. However, I have seen in some works of our contemporary al-Rishti, head of the Imami Kashfi sect, that the sun's prostration at its setting beneath the Throne is an expression for the raising of the vessel (al-āniyya) and the removal of the cloak of quiddity (mahiyya). To me this is a kind of gibberish that no one unfamiliar with his technical terms will understand, even if he were intelligent. In another place, after mentioning the earlier hadith of the hooks (al-kalalib), he said that this does not contradict the statements of the astronomers, nor does it fall within the measure of "the eye of a needle." He did not explain how it does not contradict them, though that is clearer than the sun, excusing himself on the ground that the discussion of it is lengthy. I do not think that, had he been going to bring it, he would have brought anything except of this sort. This is my view, so let it be considered! And God Most High is the Guide to the right path.

Abdullah, Ibn 'Abbas, Zayn al-'Abidin, his son al-Baqir, 'Ikrima, and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah read لا مُسْتَقَرَّ لَها (there is no resting-place for it) with لا as the particle of absolute negation (al-nafiya lil-jins) and مُسْتَقَرَّ built on the fatha. This implies the negation of every real resting-place for its observed body, and that is in this world; that is, it runs in this world continuously and never rests. Ibn Abi 'Abla read it also with لا, but he put مُسْتَقَرٌّ in the nominative with tanwin, applying it as a functioning negation like لَيْسَ, as in the line:

Console yourself: nothing on the earth remains,
nor is there any refuge from what God has decreed.

ذَلِكَ (That) refers to the running understood from تَجْرِي, meaning: that wondrous running, comprising wise purposes whose understanding minds and intellects are bewildered by, ﴿is the decree of the Almighty﴾, who prevails by His power over every possible thing, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾, whose knowledge encompasses every object of knowledge. Some have mentioned, as the wisdom of its running so that it prostrates beneath the Throne every night, what the preceding report requires: the continual renewal of its acquisition of light from the Throne. What follows in the world of nature and the elements follows from this, and that its acquisition of light from the Throne has been stated explicitly by more than one scholar. Among the strange things is what al-Rishti mentioned: that it draws light from the outer surface of the Throne and supplies the sphere of the Moon, and from the inner surface of the Throne and supplies the sphere of Saturn; and it draws from the outer surface of the Kursi and supplies the sphere of Mercury, and from its inner surface and supplies the sphere of Jupiter; and it draws from the outer surface at the intersection of the two points of the two zones and supplies the sphere of Venus, and from its inner surface and supplies the sphere of Mars. I wonder from where he derived this and said what he said, and this is something for which we have found no transmission, nor do we think it has even passed through imagination. The Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, said: the light of the sun is not from its essence, but from a continuous manifestation of it of His Name, the Light. The light of all the other planets is from its light, and in reality it is from the manifestation of His Name, the Light, glorified be He, so there is nothing there but His light, Mighty and Majestic.

Many of the eminent verifiers (muhaqqiqun) have claimed that the light of all the stars, both fixed and wandering, is derived from the light of the sun, and that it is bestowed upon them by the Absolute Bestower, Majestic in His majesty and whose bounty is universal. In the verse there is a refutation of those who hold that the sun is at rest and is the center of the universe, while the stars and the earth are revolving spheres.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 39 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the moon — We have determined it﴾ means: We made its course, that is, its station in which it travels, ﴿into mansions﴾. Here "qaddara" is in the sense of "sayyara" (to make), which takes two objects. The sentence is elliptical: the omitted noun is the first object, and ﴿mansil﴾ (mansions) is the second. Abu Hayyan preferred to take it as a verbal noun ("taqdir") that is transitive to one object, with ﴿mansil﴾ in the accusative of place: "We determined its movement within mansions." Some scholars supplied "light" (nur) as the omitted noun: "We determined its light within the mansions," so that the amount of light increases each day in the conjunction mansions (manazil al-ijtima'iyya) and decreases in the opposition mansions (manazil al-istiqbaliyya), because its light is derived from the light of the sun, and its phases vary according to its nearness to and distance from the sun, along with its eclipse when the earth comes between it and the sun. By this, the argument is completed. The truth, however, is that there is no certainty in this matter; there is only probable opinion (ghalabat al-zann). It is also possible for "qaddara" to be transitive to two objects, with ﴿mansil﴾ taken as "possessing mansions" (dha manazil), or for it to be transitive to one object, which is ﴿mansil﴾, the original being "We determined for it mansions," by omission and attachment of the preposition. Abu al-Su'ud preferred this, and he put ﴿the moon﴾ in the accusative by a verb that the mentioned verb explains, meaning: "And We determined the moon, We determined it." In this there is the emphasis on the matter of determination that it contains, and it seems that this is because their month is reckoned by it. From this the secret of changing the style becomes known.

Al-Haramayn (Ibn Kathir and Nafi'), Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far, Ibn Muhaysin, and al-Hasan (with a variant narration from him) read ﴿wal-qamaru﴾ with the nominative. Many have said: it is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (ibtida'), and the clause ﴿qaddarnahu﴾ is its predicate. It is permissible, in my opinion, that the i'rab (grammatical inflection) of the construction proceed as it did in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿wal-shamsu tajri﴾ [And the sun runs]. Reflect!

The word ﴿manazil﴾ is the plural of ﴿manzil﴾, and what is meant by it is the distance the moon covers in one day and night. According to the people of India, this is twenty-seven, because the moon traverses the zodiacal circle in twenty-seven days and a third, so they dropped the third, since it is less than half, as is the terminology of the astrologers. According to the Arabs and the dwellers of the desert, it is twenty-eight. This is not because they completed the third to make one, as some have said, but because, since their years were reckoned by the lunar months (ahilla), whose beginnings vary, falling at times in midsummer and at other times in midwinter, and likewise their times of trade and the seasons of their festivals, they needed to fix the solar year in order to know the seasons of the year, so that at the arrival of each season they could busy themselves with what concerned them in that season, such as moving to the pastures and other things. So they devised a way to fix it. First they looked at the moon and found that it returns to a position relative to the sun in about thirty days, and it disappears at the end of the month for two nights or fewer or more. So they dropped two days from the length of the month, and twenty-eight remained. This is the period between its first appearance in the evenings, at the beginning of the month, and its last sighting in the mornings, when it is hidden at the end of the month. Then they divided the circuit of the sphere by it, so each division was twelve degrees and fifty-one minutes approximately, which is six-sevenths of a degree. So the portion of each zodiac sign comprises two and a third mansions. Then, when the circuit was fixed by this division, they devised a way to fix the solar year by the manner in which the sun crosses these mansions. They found that it always covers three mansions in addition to the one it is in, by its rays, and what precedes it by the light of dawn, and what follows it by the light of the sun. They observed the appearance of what is hidden by the light of dawn, then by its rays, then by the light of twilight, and they found the time between each two appearances of two mansions to be approximately thirteen days. So the days of all the mansions amount to three hundred and sixty-four, but the sun crosses all of them in three hundred and sixty-five. So they added one day to the days of the mansion of Ghafr, and they added it here by their convention, or because of its nobility, as you will hear, God willing. It may need the addition of two days, so that the completion of the twenty-eight coincides with the completion of the year, and the matter returns to the first star.

Know that the Arabs made the signs of the twenty-eight divisions from the visible stars near the zodiacal belt (minTaqa) which approximate the path of the moon in its course or lie opposite it, so the moon is seen every night descending near one of them. The conditions of the stars of the mansions with respect to the mansions are like the conditions of the stars of the zodiacal signs with respect to the signs according to the people of astronomy (ahl al-hay'a): they are in line with the mansions while being in the sphere of the spheres. When the moon speeds up in its movement, it may leave a mansion in the middle; and if it slows down, it may remain two nights in one mansion, the first of the two nights in its beginning and the last of them in its end. It may be seen on some nights between two mansions. As for what is said about the months, that the visible mansions in each night are fourteen, and likewise the hidden ones, and that when one mansion rises, its "raqib" (watcher) sets, namely the fifteenth from the rising one, and it was named so as a comparison to a watcher who observes it so that it may fall in the west when it appears in the east, this is clearly invalid, because they are not on the zodiacal belt itself, nor are the distances between them equal. For this reason, the visible ones may be sixteen or seventeen, and the hidden ones may be thirteen. These stars called the mansions, which are in line with the true mansions, according to what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and others, are: first, al-Sharatan, with a fatha on the shin and the ra, the dual of "sharat," with two fathas, meaning sign. They are two bright stars of the third magnitude on the horns of Aries, lying across between north and south, with three spans between them. Near the southern one of them is a small star. The Arabs named all of them "ashrat," because by their setting they are signs of rain and wind. The moon is in line with them. Near the northern one of them is a bright star, which some say is the Sharatan itself, and the two Sharatan are also called "al-nathih" (the butter). Then al-Butayn, the diminutive of al-Batn (belly), which is three faint stars of the fifth magnitude in the shape of an acute-angled triangle on the thighs of Aries, between it and the two Sharatan lies the length of a spear. The moon passes by them at times. Then al-Thurayya, the diminutive of Thurwa, from al-tharâ' (abundance), which means multiplicity. It is also called al-Najm (the Star). According to the well-known view of the astrologers, it is six stars gathered together in the shape of a fan, its handle toward the east, with a curve on the northern side. It was said that it resembles a bunch of grapes, and to this is the verse of Uhayha ibn al-Jullah or Qays ibn al-Aslat:

"And al-Thurayya has appeared in the morning as you see, like a cluster of Mulla'iyya grapes when it blossomed."

Of them, the observed ones are four, all of the fifth magnitude, and their place is the hump of the bull. In al-Kashf it is the buttock of Aries. Sometimes the moon eclipses them. Then al-Dabaran, with two fathas. It was named so because it follows (dabura) al-Thurayya and is behind it. It is a red, bright star of the first magnitude on the edge of the figure of the Seven from the drawings of India, and it is called al-Mijdah. Its position is the eye of the Bull. The one at its other edge is of the third magnitude on its other eye, and the three remaining, which are also of the third magnitude, are on its face. The corner of this figure is on the muzzle of the Bull. Some call al-Dabaran "Qalb al-Thawr" (heart of the Bull). Sometimes the moon eclipses it. Then al-Haq'a, with a fatha on the ha, a sukun on the qaf, and a fatha on the 'ayn (unpointed). It is three faint stars gathered together, resembling the dots of the letter tha', as if they were a cloudy smear. It is likened to the circle that appears on the breadth of a horse's neck, or to where it strikes the rider's foot, or to a patch of white on the left side of a horse, and it is named after that. It is also called al-Athafiyy, and it is on the head of the giant called al-Jawza' (Orion). The moon is in line with it but does not come near it. Then al-Han'a, of the weight of al-Haq'a, and its second letter is a nun. It is two stars of the fourth and third magnitudes, likened to a mark in the depression of a horse's neck, and they are on the legs of the Twins on the northern side. In al-Kashf it is the left shoulder of al-Jawza'. The moon passes by them. Then al-Dhira' (the forearm), which are two bright stars of the second magnitude on the heads of the Twins. By them they mean the outstretched forearm of the Lion, since the contracted one is al-Shi'ra al-Shamiyya with its companion. The moon approaches the outstretched one. Then al-Nathra, which is the gap between the two moustaches opposite the bridge of the nose, which is the nose of the Lion. They are two faint stars of the fourth magnitude, with a forearm's length between them, and a cloudy smear. It lies at the middle of Cancer. Near it are two stars called "the two donkeys," and the smear that lies between them is called "the fodder," likening it to chaff, and "the Lion's hiding-place," meaning the place where it conceals itself. The moon eclipses each of them. Then al-Tarf, which are two small stars of the fourth magnitude: one is on the head of the Lion in front of its eyes, and the other in front of its forward paw. The moon is in line with the larger of them and eclipses the farther of them. By al-Tarf they mean the eye of the Lion. Then al-Jabha (the forehead), by which they mean the forehead of the Lion, which is four stars on a line that has a curve running from north to south. The largest of them, at the end of the line on the southern side, is called "Qalb al-Asad" (heart of the Lion) because it is at its position, and it is also called al-Malaki. It is of the first magnitude, and the moon passes by it and by the one next to it. Then al-Zubra, with a damma on the za' and a sukun on the ba', which are two bright stars on the trace of the forehead, between them a span greater than a forearm's length. They are on the mane of the Lion, that is, its shoulder according to the Arabs, while according to the astrologers they are at its rear. The mane of the Lion is the hair that bristles in its neck when angered. The farther of them is of the third magnitude and the larger of them is of the second, and they are called "the back of the Lion." The moon is in line with them from the south. Then al-Sarfa, which is a single star at the tip of the Lion's tail, and it is called "the tail of the Lion." The moon is in line with it from the south. It was named so because cold turns away (yansarif) when it sets. Then al-'Awwa', which is pronounced with or without the mad, and the shortened form is better. It is five stars of the third magnitude in the shape of the letter lam in Arabic script. Three of them extend from the left shoulder of Virgo to beneath her left breast, lying on a southern line from al-Sarfa. Then two of them bend onto a line which, together with the first, encloses an obtuse angle. The Arabs claimed that they are dogs barking (ta'wi) behind the Lion, and therefore it was named al-'Awwa'. It was also said: as if they bark on the track of the cold, and for this it was named "the chaser of the cold." It was also said that it is from 'awa al-shay' (to bend a thing), and because of the bending in it, it was named so.

In al-Kashf, al-'Awwa' is the lowest part of the human (sa-filat al-insan), and it is said that it is the Lion's hip. The moon passes through it. Then al-Simak al-A'zal, which is a bright star of the first magnitude on the left shoulder of Virgo, near the zodiacal belt. The moon passes by it and eclipses it. Opposite al-Simak al-A'zal is al-Simak al-Ramih, which is not one of the mansions. It was named "al-Ramih" (the lancer) because a star precedes it as if it were its spear, and it was named "al-Simak" because it "samaka," that is, rose high. Then al-Ghafr, which are three stars of the fourth magnitude on the tail of Virgo and her rear leg, on a crooked line whose curve is toward the north. It was said that they are two stars. The moon passes by the southern of them, and it may be in line with the northern one. It is the mansion of goodness, distant from two evils: the front of the Lion and the rear of Scorpio. It is said that it is the rising station of the prophets and the righteous. It was named Ghafr because it conceals and its light is diminished. Some have mentioned that they are among the stars of Libra. Then al-Zubana, with a damma and ending in an alif, which are two bright stars of the second magnitude, distant from each other in the north and the south, with a spear's length between them, on the two pans of the balance (al-mizan).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 39 (part 2 of 2):

Others said: They are the two horns of the Scorpion (al-'Aqrab). The Moon may eclipse their southern star. Then al-Iklil (the Crown), which is three faint stars extending from north to south in a curved line. Its shape resembles the shape of al-Ghafr. The middle one of them is ahead, and the other two follow. The Moon passes over all of them, and it is from the fourth (lunar mansion). It was said that they are four stars at the head of the Scorpion, and that is why it was named after it. Its original meaning is "the crown." Then al-Qalb (the Heart), which is the Heart of the Scorpion, a bright reddish star, the middle of the three that lie on the body of the Scorpion, in a straight line from west to east. It belongs to the second (mansion). The two stars before it and after it, which are called al-Niyatayn (the Two Sinews), belong to the third. The Moon passes by it and eclipses it, from the Zodiac belt. Then al-Shawla, with a fatha on the shin and the lam, which the people of the Hijaz call the Needle of the Scorpion. It is two stars from the second, bright and close to each other, at the edge of the Scorpion's tail at the place of the sting. The Moon is in line with them. Then al-Na'a'im (the Ostriches): four stars from the third, on a deviating path following al-Shawla. They are called al-Na'a'im al-Warida, that is, those coming toward the Milky Way. The Moon passes by two of them and is in line with the rest. Near them are four others from the third, on a deviating path, which are al-Na'a'im al-Sadira, that is, those departing from the Milky Way. All of them are from the constellation of the Archer (al-Rami). They were named al-Na'a'im by comparison with the wooden poles that are placed over a well. Then al-Balda (the Empty Expanse), which is a patch of the sky free of stars and round in shape. It is likened to the "balda" of the fox, which is what it sweeps with its tail. It is also called al-Mafaza and al-Furja. It was said that it was named so by comparison with the gap that lies between the two eyebrows. Its place is behind the stars called al-Qilada (the Necklace), which is the headband of the Archer. Then Sa'd al-Dhabih (the Fortune of the Slaughterer): two stars on the two horns of al-Jadi (the Kid), with a distance of one fathom (ba') between them. Its southern one is from the third. The Moon approaches it and does not eclipse it. Near the northern one is a small star that almost touches it. It is said that it is the goat which he intends to slaughter. It was also said that it is at its place of slaughter, and for this reason it is called the Slaughterer. Then Sa'd Bula' (the Fortune of Swallowing): two stars on the left palm of the water-pourer, above the back of al-Jadi, with a distance of one fathom between them. Its western one is from the third and its eastern one from the fourth. Near their forward one is a small star, as if it had swallowed it, and for this reason it was named after that. In the Qamus (the dictionary of al-Fayruzabadi): Sa'd Bula', on the pattern of Zufar, is a proper name. It is a lunar station that rose when Allah the Exalted said ﴿O earth, swallow up your water﴾. It is two stars of equal position in the path. One of them is faint and the other bright, and the bright one is called Bali' (swallower), as if it swallowed the other. It was also said that it is because it lacks what Sa'd al-Dhabih has, so it is as if it swallowed its goat. The Moon approaches its farther one and does not eclipse it. Then Sa'd al-Su'ud (the Fortune of Fortunes): two stars, and it was said three, on a curved line between north and south, its bulge toward the west. Its farther one, which the Moon approaches, is from the fifth, on the edge of the tail of al-Jadi. Its nearer one is from the third. In the other view it is, together with the other star, among the stars of al-Qaws (the Bow). The Moon approaches its farther one. It was named so because at the time of its rising it marks the beginning of what they live by and what their livestock lives by. Then Sa'd al-Akhbiya (the Fortune of the Tents): four stars from the third, and from the stars of the Archer, on the right hand of the water-pourer. Three of them are in the shape of a sharp-angled triangle, and the fourth is in its middle, and it is the Sa'd. The three are its tent, and for this reason it was named so. It was also said that it rises before the warmth, so the creeping things that had been hidden come out. The Moon is near them from the southern side. Then al-Far' al-Muqaddam (the Front Bucket Spout), also said to be al-A'la (the Upper). Two bright stars from the second, with a spear's length between them. The farther one is on the back of the Great Winged Horse (al-Faras), and the nearer one is on its shoulder. The Moon passes at a distance from them. Then al-Far' al-Mu'akhkhar (the Rear Bucket Spout): two bright stars from the second, also with a spear's length between them. The farther one is on the wing of the Horse, and the nearer one is shared between its navel and the head of al-Musalsala (the Chained Woman). The Arabs likened the four to the spouts of the bucket. Al-Far' (with a fatha on the fa, sukun on the ra, and a dotted ghayn) is the outlet of the water from them, because of the abundance of rains at that time. Then Batn al-Hut (the Belly of the Fish), which is also called al-Rishaa' (with a kasra on the ra), meaning the rope of the bucket. The Heart of the Fish is also a bright star from the third, on the side of the Chained Woman. The Moon is in line with it and does not approach it. It was named so because it lies in the belly of a great fish under the throat of the she-camel. The Arabs depict it with two lines, on which are faint stars, some from al-Musalsala and some from one of the two fishes of the Fish.

Know that the Arabs call the fourteen northern ones among these twenty-eight lunar mansions, from al-Sharatan at the beginning to al-Simak at the end, the Shami (Syrian) mansions. The remaining ones, from al-Ghafr at the beginning to Batn al-Hut at the end, they call the Yamani (Yemeni) mansions. They call the mansion's rising from the light of dawn its "tuloo'," and its setting, when its watcher falls at the time of morning, its "suqut." The mansions whose rising occurs in the seasons of rain are called al-Anwa' (the rain-star seasons), and their watchers, if they rise outside the seasons of rain, are called al-Bawaris (the baleful ones). This was said by al-Qutb. Al-Jawhari said: The nawʾ is the setting of one of the mansions in the west with the dawn, and the rising of its watcher from the east opposite it at the same hour, every night for thirteen days, except al-Jabha, for it has fourteen days. Abu 'Ubayd said: The word nawʾ has not been heard to mean "setting" except in this place. The Arabs attribute rains, winds, heat and cold to the one that sets from them. Al-Asma'i said: to the one that rises in its dominion. So they say, "We were rained upon by the nawʾ of al-Thurayya," for example. The plural is anwa' and nuwan, like 'abd and 'ubdan. Al-Tibi reported from al-Marzuqi that the nawʾ of al-Sharatayn lasts three days, the nawʾ of al-Butayn three nights, the nawʾ of al-Thurayya five nights, the nawʾ of al-Dabaran three nights, the nawʾ of al-Haq'a six nights. They only mention its nawʾ together with the nawʾ of al-Jawza'. The nawʾ of al-Han'a is also not mentioned, and it only occurs in the anwa' of al-Jawza' and al-Dhira', and it has no nawʾ. The nawʾ of al-Nathra lasts seven nights, the nawʾ of al-Tarf three nights, the nawʾ of al-Jabha seven, al-Zubra four, al-Sarfa three, al-'Awwa' one night, al-Simak four, al-Ghafr three, and it was said one night, al-Zubana three, al-Iklil four, al-Qalb three, and al-Shawla likewise, al-Na'a'im one night, al-Balda three, and it was said one night, Sa'd al-Dhabih one night, Bula', Sa'd al-Su'ud, and Sa'd al-Akhbiya and al-Far' al-Muqaddam three, and al-Mu'akhkhar four. In my copy, no nawʾ is mentioned for al-Rishaa'.

Then, if a person's saying "We were rained upon by the nawʾ of such and such" means that the nawʾ sent down the water, then it is kufr (disbelief), and the one who says it is a disbeliever whose blood is lawful to shed if he does not repent, as al-Shafi'i and others have explicitly stated. In al-Rawda: Whoever believes that the nawʾ literally causes rain has disbelieved and become an apostate. If he means that the nawʾ is a cause through which Allah the Exalted sends down water, according to what has been known and decreed, then it is not kufr but permissible. However, Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Even though it is permissible, it is kufr of the blessing of Allah the Exalted and ignorance of His subtle wisdom.

In the two Sahihs, from Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said, after a rain from the sky: 'Do you know what your Lord said?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'He said: In the morning, among My servants, there are believers in Me and disbelievers. As for the one who says, We were rained upon by the grace of Allah and His mercy, he is a believer in Me and a disbeliever in the star. As for the one who says, We were rained upon by the nawʾ of such and such, he is a disbeliever in Me and a believer in the star.'" Its apparent meaning is that kufr is the opposite of iman, so it is to be understood as the case where the speaker intends what you heard first. And Allah the Exalted is the Guardian from every evil; there is no lord besides Him, and none is hoped for except His good.

The Moon, in common usage, is the well-known heavenly body seen on all the nights of the month. According to the linguists, the well-known view is that after its conjunction with the sun and its separation from it, it is not called "qamar" except from the third night to the twenty-sixth night. Outside of that period it is called "hilal" (the crescent). Perhaps the more apparent meaning in the verse is to take it in the first sense, which is the common one when it is mentioned together with the sun. That is, We determined this known body with specific stations and distances, so it travelled through them and descended to them station by station, ﴿until it returned﴾, that is, it became at the end of its course and nearness to the sun, in appearance to the eye, ﴿like the old curved stalk﴾. Al-'Urjun is the return of a palm's cluster from between the stalk to its origin on the palm. This was reported from al-Hasan and Qatada. From Ibn 'Abbas it is said that it is the base of the cluster. It was also said it is the stalk, which is what the dates are on, the cluster's twigs and the spathe. The well-known view is the first. Its nun, according to what is reported from al-Zajjaj, is additional, so its form is fu'lun from al-in'iraj, which is bending and curving. Some people, and al-Raghib, al-Samin, and the author of al-Qamus, chose that it is original, so its form is fu'lul. Sulayman al-Taymi read "al-'irjawn," with a kasra on the 'ayn, a sukun on the ra, and a fatha on the jim, and it is a dialect for it, like al-buzyun and al-bizyawn, which is a Roman carpet or fine silk. ﴿The old﴾, that is, the ancient one which time has passed over and which has dried out. The aspect of resemblance is yellowing, thinness, and curvature. It was said that the minimum period of being "old" is a year. So if a man says, "Every slave of mine who is old is free," those among them who have passed a year or more are freed. It was also said six months, and some of the Imamiyya reported it from Abu al-Hasan al-Rida, may Allah be pleased with him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 40 (part 1 of 3):

﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾ That is, it is not made subservient or easy for it (yatasakhkharu wa-yatasahhalu), as in your saying: "Fire ought to burn the garment." Or it means it is not fitting or suitable (yahsunu wa-yalìq), i.e., by wisdom, as in your saying: "The king ought to honour the scholar." Many have chosen the first meaning. The root of yanbaghi is the reflexive form (mutawi') of baghā, meaning "to seek," and whatever is receptive to and accepts an action has become subservient and easy. In reality, the negation applies to yanbaghi, so it is as if it were said: it is not made easy for the sun, nor subservient, [to overtake the moon]. ﴿To overtake the moon﴾ means within its sphere of authority, by meeting it at the time God, exalted is He, has set for it and made a manifestation of His authority. For He, Mighty and Majestic, by the requirement of wisdom in governing this world, assigned to each of the two luminaries, the sun and the moon, a fixed limit and a specified time in which His authority is manifested, so that neither of them enters into the authority of the other, but they alternate until the command of God, Mighty and Majestic, comes. This clause negates that the sun should overtake the moon in what has been assigned to it. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor does the night outstrip the day﴾ negates that the moon should overtake the sun in what has been assigned to it, that is, the sign of the night does not precede the sign of the day, and its manifest authority is at the time of the manifestation of its authority. To this meaning the words of Qatada, al-Dahhak, Ikrimah and Abu Salih allude, and al-Zamakhshari chose it so as to be in harmony with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾, and because the discourse in the two verses is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the sun runs on to its resting place﴾, the two verses, and at the end ﴿each in an orbit they float﴾. He expressed "overtaking" first and "preceding" second, according to what is in the Kashshaf, for the correspondence
صفحة 21
with the state of the sun in slowness of its course and the state of the moon in its swiftness. He did not say "nor does the moon precede the sun," so as to indicate, as al-Tibi said, the alternation between night and day and the specificity of the governance upon succession, for this is derived from the daily motion on which the disposal of each of them depends. In al-Kashf, the verification is that the intended meaning is to explain the succession of each of the sun and the moon in the order of illumination and their independent authority; likewise the alternation of night and day. So it is said: "Nor does the night outstrip the day" is a metonymy for the sign of the one preceding the sign of the other, so the indication of alternation is also obtained by way of incidental inclusion (idmaj), for it does not contradict the intention of the literal meaning. This meaning also comes, from the necessity of antithesis, in respect of the day, from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾. Since overtaking, which indicates that it seeks to catch up, was mentioned with the sun, it was said "yanbaghi" (it is not fitting), observing the correspondence, and the verb which indicates renewal was used. When preceding was negated in the opposite case, this was emphasised by using a purely nominal sentence without yabtaghi, because it is what is sought to be overtaken. End.
He did not mention the secret in putting the negative particle before the sun rather than before the verb that indicates its attribute, and it is nearly more hidden than al-Suha. And this was so that it may be sensed from it, in the rhetorical context, that the sun, if left to itself, would be non-existent, as is the case with all contingent things; and what befalls it befalls it from its cause, which is a reference to the connection of His power, exalted is He, to it in accordance with His complete will, which nothing in the world of contingency refuses. This indicates in the utmost degree that it is subjected in the grip of His disposal, Mighty and Majestic; there is nothing above that subjection. It also contains an affirmation of what His saying, exalted is He, conveys: ﴿That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing﴾, and a decisive refutation of those to whom influence is attributed to it.
It is permitted that this is for conveying that it is subjected, so that nothing becomes easy for it except what is intended for it, in terms of placing the subject before the verb and putting it after the negative particle, as in: "It is not I who said this," and "No effort was made on your need," which conveys specification, i.e., it was not I who said this but another, and no effort was made on your need, but someone else, according to what the scholars of rhetoric have verified. The intended meaning of negating that the sun should find it easy to overtake the moon in its authority is negating that it should be easy for it to obliterate its light and remove its authority, and this returns to negating its power to obliterate and remove authority. So the meaning, according to the rule of fronting, is that the sun is not able to do that, but something else is able to, namely God, Mighty and Majestic. And this, after establishing the running for it by the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing, indicates that it is subjected, so that nothing becomes easy for it except what is intended for it. Some scholars wrote in the margin of the commentary of al-Baydawi, at his saying: "The placing of the negative particle before the sun is to indicate that it is subjected, so that nothing becomes easy for it except what is intended for it." The basis of the indication is that the said placing conveys specification, and yabtaghi in the sense of validity and facility, which are synonymous with capability, so the speech conveys that the sun has no power to overtake the moon or the swiftness of motion, which is the opposite of its own particular motion; rather, the power over both belongs to God, glorified is He. So He is the real doer of its motion, and it has merely the locus of motion. Thus the said indication is valid. Then he said: The detail of the matter is that God, glorified is He, first mentioned that the sun runs to its resting place, an indication of its particular motion; then He mentioned that He also determined the moon in the mansions of the sun until it returned like the old date-stalk, that is, it returned to the crescent shape, which happens only when it is near the sun and returns to it. And since the imagination has a way to suppose that the running of the sun and its course, and the determination of the moon's lights and its visible body, are attributable to their own will in the manner of our will, which relates at times to a thing and at other times to its opposite, so that both things would be possible and easy for the two luminaries as they are for us; and that the attribution of the matter of the sun and moon to the divine determination is like the attribution of our actions to Him, in that the empowering and enabling is from Him, and that He, glorified is He, is the origin and the end, and other such considerations, He, majestic is His affair, drew attention by the said specification, as a warning against this supposition, by way of alerting that the thing is subjected and compelled in its affair by the removal of its power over the opposite, although He did not mention all its opposites. So He indicated, glorified is He, that the swift motion leading to overtaking the moon, which is the opposite of the sun's particular motion, cannot validly be attributed to it, and the power over it belongs exclusively to another: ﴿And He is the Almighty, the All-Knowing﴾, so as to show that the existence of its particular motion is attributable to His determination and disposal, exalted is He, without any partnership of the sun with Him, glorified is He. Then he followed this with the ruling about the moon, saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor does the night outstrip the day﴾. The closer meaning is that the sign of the night does not have the power to precede the sign of the day in such a way as to escape it, nor to have any return to it or joining with it, alerting that the determination of the moon in the mansions in the observed manner, by which it returns to the crescent shape resembling the old date-stalk and leads to approaching the sun, is likewise attributable to His determination and disposal, glorified is He, without any partnership of the moon in it. Thus the two clauses are in the force of an emphasis upon the two preceding verses, and for this reason they were separated. End. In it there is a tickling not hidden from the intelligent, so reflect!
What he indicated, that the meaning of ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾ is that the sun has no power to overtake the moon in its course, because of the slowness of its own motion and the swiftness of its motion, has likewise been said by more than one. Al-Nahhas claimed that this is the clearest of what has been said about its meaning, and between it and the meaning previously mentioned there is some closeness. Indeed some of them said: the difference between the two aspects is one of consideration. Some of those who adopted this view regarding ﴿Nor does the night outstrip the day﴾ said that the intended meaning is that the moon does not precede the sun by the daily motion, which is what belongs to it and likewise to the other stars through the sphere of the spheres, for this motion does not produce any precedence or lag. It was also said: the intended meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon﴾ is that it is not fitting for it to overtake it in its effects and benefits, for He, glorified is He, assigned to each of them effects and benefits, such as colouring in relation to the moon and ripening in relation to the sun. Al-Hasan said that the intended meaning is that they do not meet in what is seen in the sky on the night of the crescent specifically, that is, the sun does not remain rising until the moon rises, but when it sets the moon rises. Yahya ibn Sallam said: the intended meaning is that it does not overtake it on the night of the full moon specifically, because it hastens to set before the sun rises. Both of these opinions are not relied upon, and one should not turn to them. It was also said regarding the meaning of the second clause: the night does not precede the day and come before its time, so that it enters before the day has passed.
In al-Durr al-Manthur, from one of the eminent scholars: that is, it is not fitting that when there is one night there should be another night until the day comes. Hold to what has preceded, for by my life it is the more upright. The verse has been cited as evidence that the day precedes the night in creation. Al-Ayyashi related in his tafsir with a chain of narration from al-Ash'ath ibn Hatim, who said: I was in Khurasan when al-Rida, may God be pleased with him, al-Ma'mun and al-Fadl ibn Sahl gathered in the hall at Marw. A table was set, and al-Rida said: A man from the Children of Israel asked me in Medina, saying: "Was the day created before the night, or the night? What do you have?" They wished to speak but had nothing. Al-Fadl said to al-Rida: "Inform us of it, may God set you right!" He said: "Yes. Is it from the Qur'an or from calculation?" Al-Fadl said to him: "From the side of calculation." So he, may God be pleased with him, said: "You know, O Fadl, that the rising sign of the world is Cancer, and the planets are in the places of their exaltation: Saturn in Libra, Jupiter in Cancer, Mars in Capricorn, the sun in Aries, Venus in Pisces, Mercury in Virgo, and the moon in Taurus. So the sun is in the tenth house, the midheaven. Thus the day is before the night. From the Qur'an is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor does the night outstrip the day﴾, i.e., the night has been outstripped by the day." End.
صفحة 23
As for the use of the verse as evidence, there is a manifest discussion; but as for calculation, it has some validity in general. The astrologers hold that the beginning of the cycle is the circle of midday, and it agrees with what was mentioned; but what prevails in opinion is that the report is not sound from its beginning. Al-Rida is too exalted to cite the verse as evidence for what you have heard him claim. The Imam understood from His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Nor does the night outstrip the day﴾ that the night is outstripped and not outstripping, and from His saying, glorified is He, ﴿He covers the night over the day, seeking it urgently﴾ that the night is outstripping, since the day seeks it. He answered the objection that follows from the night being both outstripping and outstripped, by saying that the night here means its sign, which is the moon, and it does not outstrip the sun in the daily motion, while the night there means the night itself, and each, since it is in the wake of the other, is seeking it. Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying that it involves making the subject pronoun in "yatlubuhu" refer to the day and the object pronoun to "al-layl," whereas the apparent reading is that the subject pronoun refers to what is the subject in meaning, namely the night, since before the insertion of the hamza of transfer it was "yughshi al-layl al-nahar," and the object pronoun refers to "al-nahar," since it is the object both before and after the transfer. In that case both verses convey that the day is outstripping, and there is no question. End. So reflect and do not be heedless.

Ammar ibn Aqil recited ﴿sabiqu al-nahara﴾ without tanwin and with the accusative on ﴿al-nahara﴾. Al-Mubarrad said: I heard him recite it, so I asked, "What is this?" He said: "I intended *sabiqun al-nahari* with tanwin, but I dropped it because it is lighter." In al-Bahr (*Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit*), the tanwin is dropped because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters. ﴿Wa-kullun﴾ means "each one of them," that is, each of the sun and the moon, since these two are the ones explicitly mentioned. The tanwin replaces the omitted genitive complement. Some scholars took it to be the pronoun for a plural of rational beings, to match what follows, meaning "all of them."
