Another took it to be a demonstrative, meaning "all that," that is, the sun and the moon mentioned. ﴿In an orbit﴾: as al-Raghib said, it is the path of the star, named so because of its roundness, like the *falakat al-mighzal* (the round wooden disc on the spindle) and the *falakat al-khaymah* (the round piece of wood placed on top of the tent pole so that the tent does not tear).

﴿Yasbahun﴾ means they move through it with freedom. Whoever spreads himself out in something swims in it, and from this comes swimming in water. This path is in the sky. There is nothing to prevent us from holding that a star moves on its own within the hollow of the sky, while the sky itself is at rest and does not rotate at all. This could be by there being within it a hollow filled with air or with another subtle body similar to it, through which the star moves as a fish moves through water or a pellet moves through a tube, for example. Or it could be a hollow empty of any other bodies that would occupy it, through which the star moves. Or the whole sky could be subtle, or only the part of it that is the star's path could be subtle, so that the star cleaves what lies beside it and moves as a fish moves in the sea, or in a channel within it, while the rest has solidified. The separation of the air-sphere from the fire-sphere adjacent to the concave surface of the moon's orbit, according to the philosophers, the confinement of subtle bodies to the three elements, the hardness of the body of the sky, the uniformity of its parts, the impossibility of rupture and rejoining in it, and the impossibility of a void: none of these has been proven by any demonstration. The strongest arguments offered for them are doubts weaker than the spider's web, and "indeed, by the Lord of the sky, the weakest of houses is surely the house of the spider."

It is also possible that *falak* means a round body, and that the star is in it, moving with its movement through the thickness of the sky, without the sky itself rotating. There is no objection to considering this *falak* for some of the stars to be the universal orbit, and in it there could be something like what the astronomers establish to account for the various motions of the particular orbits. But this is not necessary according to Islamic principles. As is not hidden, however, attributing swimming to the star has an outward character that resists this possibility. Among the words of the Imams from the Companions and others there are hints at some of what we have mentioned.

[Page 24]

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in *al-Azamah* transmitted from Ibn Abbas that he said concerning the verse ﴿Each in an orbit﴾: "A disc like the spindle's disc. ﴿They swim﴾ means they revolve in the gates of the sky, as the disc revolves on the spindle." The last two also transmitted from Mujahid that he said: "The spindle does not turn except by the disc, and the disc does not turn except by the spindle. The stars are in a disc like the spindle's disc, so they do not revolve except by it, and it does not revolve except by them."

In *al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya* of the Greatest Shaykh (may God sanctify his secret), it is said: God, exalted is He, made the heavens still and created stars in them, and for their course and swimming through these heavens He made measured movements that neither increase nor decrease, and He made them rational, hearing, and obedient, and He revealed in each heaven its command. Then, when He, mighty and majestic, made swimming for the stars in these heavens, paths came into being for their courses: for each star a path. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the sky having the tracks﴾. Those paths were named *aflak* (orbits). The orbits come into being with the coming into being of the stars' courses. They move swiftly through the body of the sky, which is its extent, and so they cleave the air adjacent to them, and sounds and melodies that delight the ear arise from their movement, because their movement follows a known measure. Those are the melodies of the orbits arising from the stars' crossing of celestial distances. They move along these paths in a constant habit whose quantities have been known through observation, and whose entering one upon another in movement is known. He made their movement appear to observers as alternating between slowness and speed. He made for them advance and retreat at known places in the sky, which the bodies of the stars determine by their light for those beneath them... to the end of what he said.

Al-Imam [al-Razi] said: God, exalted is He, is able to make the star such that it cleaves the sky and makes an imagined circle, as if a fish moved in the water in a circle. This is what is understood from His saying, exalted is He, ﴿in an orbit they swim﴾. The apparent meaning is that the star's movement is in this manner.

The astronomers denied this, because if the place of motion were cleft and rejoined there would be rupture and rejoining, or if it were cleft and did not rejoin there would be a void. Both are impossible in their view. For us, however, there is no impossibility in that. What is implied here is rupture and rejoining, because that is what is understood from ﴿they swim﴾. They have no proof of impossibility regarding anything other than the outermost sphere, and there they have a weak doubt, not a proof. The apparent meaning of the verse is that each of the two luminaries is in an orbit, that is, in a path peculiar to it. This is something sense perception bears witness to. The Islamic philosophers, like other philosophers, went in this direction, except that they hold that the orbit and the sky are one. When they heard from those before them that each of the seven wandering stars is in an orbit, and all the fixed stars are in an orbit, and above all this is an orbit that moves everything from east to west, called the *falak al-aflak* (orbit of orbits) because it moves them, the *falak al-a'zam* (greatest orbit) because it encircles them, and the *falak al-atlas* (the bare orbit) because, as its name implies, it has no stars, they wanted to reconcile the two matters. They said: the seven heavens in the Lawgiver's speech are the seven orbits in the speech of the philosophers. So each wandering star has a heaven among the heavens. The *kursi* (footstool) is the orbit of the fixed stars, and the *arsh* (throne) is the orbit that moves everything, called the orbit of orbits. But they erred in this and opposed the early community's scholars in it. The orbit is other than the heaven. His saying, exalted is He, along with what is here, ﴿Do you not see how God created seven heavens in layers﴾ and ﴿made the moon therein a light and made the sun a lamp﴾, does not indicate unity, for, as we have said, the star is in the orbit and the orbit is in the sky, so the star is in the sky without doubt, and the plural needs no assumption of identity. No proof has established that the throne is spherical. Rather, the apparent sense of what came in the reports, that it has legs, indicates that it is not spherical. Indeed, something has come that apparently indicates it is domed, and this is other than what they assert about it. Likewise, the *kursi* has not been shown by any proof to be spherical, as they claim. Yet they have no conclusive proof that all the fixed stars are in one orbit. So it is possible that they are in orbits, like models, all of them above Saturn, or some above it and some between the upper orbits. These orbits do not eclipse the fixed stars whose extent is greater than theirs, nor do they have a difference in appearance by which it could be known, in one of the two ways, that all are above the upper ones, or that they are epicycles. It does not follow that their distances from one another differ, since the bodies and movements of the epicycles could be equal. Nor does it follow that their movements differ in speed or slowness because of distance and nearness, or agreement and disagreement with the model; for we do not grant that their movements do not differ by that amount. Nor does it follow that their distances from the earth differ, since these are not verified. It is also possible that all of them are fixed in the convex surface of the model of Saturn, while Saturn moves slowly and the equant moves swiftly. Also, it is possible that in what they called the bare orbit there are stars that are not seen because they are very small, or are seen while moving swiftly. Not every star has been observed to verify the slowness of the movement of all of them. It is also possible that the wandering stars are more than seven, so that more than seven heavens would be needed. This is close to the discovery by the new observatories of a wandering star other than the seven, which they named after the one who discovered and identified it, namely Herschel. In sum, there is no decisive proof in what they have said. The Greatest Shaykh (may God sanctify his secret) has another statement on this subject, based on unveiling. It is that the throne upon which the Merciful, exalted is He, rose is a throne with four corners and four faces, which are its original legs. It rests upon the solid water. Within it is the *kursi*, which is in its shape in squareness but not in legs. Its place is also on the solid water, and between the concave surface of the throne and the *kursi* there is a wide expanse and a penetrating air. Within the *kursi* God, exalted is He, created the bare orbit, a transparent round body divided into twelve parts, which are the known zodiacal signs. Within it is the starred orbit, and between them are the gardens. After God, exalted is He, created the earths, and the air took on the form of smoke, God, exalted is He, created the seven heavens and placed in each of them a star. These are the *jawari* (the running ones).

Al-Khafaji claimed that the intended *falak* in the verse is the greatest orbit, because the sun, the moon, and likewise all the stars move by its movement. So swimming, for him, is a figure for forced movement. There is something troubling in this. Then, according to what is apparent, that each one has its own orbit, they held that the orbit of the sun is above the orbit of the moon, because the moon eclipses the sun, and the eclipsed is necessarily above the eclipsing. Most astronomers mention that the lowest orbit is the orbit of the moon, above it the orbit of Mercury, above it the orbit of Venus, above it the orbit of the sun, above it the orbit of Mars, above it the orbit of Jupiter, and above it the orbit of Saturn. They supported some of this by eclipse, and some of the rest by the fine order and excellent arrangement it contains. In my view there is no objection to saying this, but not in the way the astronomers have said it, namely that the heavens are the rotating orbits. Rather, it should be in a way that makes it possible to hold that the heavens are still and the stars revolve in their orbits and courses, some above others. You have already been given what benefits you in this matter, so return to it!

It has been permitted that the pronoun in ﴿they swim﴾ refers to the stars, which the mention of the sun, the moon, the night, and the day suggests. The first view is preferred because the use of the plural pronoun for it is evident and needs no strain, whereas for the first view one must say: the variation in the states of the sun and moon in their risings and other respects has been treated as equal to the multiplicity of their individuals, so the referent becomes suns and moons. My opinion is that this is not needed, on the basis that two may be considered a plural, or on the basis of what the Imam said: that the word *kull* may be made singular in view of its form, and plural in view of its meaning as *jami'* (all). But the dual is not indicated by the word or the meaning. He said: on this basis it is good to say "Zayd and Amr, each (*kull*) came," and "each came," but it is not good to say "each (*kull*) came" in the dual. The use of the plural pronoun for rational beings has been cited as evidence that the sun and the moon are rational. It has been answered that this is because the verb attributed to them is the verb of rational beings, as in His saying, exalted is He, regarding the idols, ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not speak?﴾, and His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿Will you not eat?﴾. The apparent meanings are other than what was mentioned by those who cited it.

Some of the philosophers of Islam who hold that the sky and the orbit are one used the verse as evidence for the sphericity of the sky, and they considered it one of the subtle points in it that ﴿each in an orbit﴾

[Page 25]

...does not stray into the impossible by reversal, as in: "Your speech is your perfection," and "Go, and the horse did not stumble with you." Some have said: This is not refuted by the fact that He, glorified is He, named it a roof (saqf) in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and by the raised roof﴾, because a vaulted roof does not cease to be a roof by being vaulted. You know that the heavens are other than the spheres (aflak). Nevertheless, I say that the heavens are spherical, as some of the early generations (al-salaf) held. Some apparent reports imply that they are halves of spheres, each heaven being a half-sphere like a dome over one of the seven earths. The Shaykh al-Akbar held this view and said that rotation belongs to the sphere of the mansions (falak al-manazil) alone, not to the seven heavens. He also claimed that beneath the seven earths, over each of which is a heaven, there is water, beneath it air, and beneath it darkness, and above it. Let one reflect on how the star moves after its setting until it rises.

Then, the philosophers who hold that the heaven is spherical relied on proofs, the closest of which, it is said, are two. The first: when we travel to several places along one line of latitude on the earth and observe the stars passing overhead at the zenith in each of them, then consider the distances between the paths of those stars in the meridian circle from one another, we find them in the same ratios as the earthly distances between those places. Likewise we find the elevation of the pole there varying by the same ratios. Thus the curvature of the heaven in latitude is similar to the curvature of the earth in it. But this similarity exists in every line of latitude and likewise in every line of longitude. So the entire surface of the heaven is parallel to the entire visible surface of the earth, and this surface is sensibly spherical, so the surface of the heaven parallel to it is likewise spherical.

The second: astronomers (ashab al-arsad) recorded in their books the sizes of the bodies of the stars and the distances between them at different places at one time, at midday. For example, those places are equal, and this indicates that the distances of the centers of the stars from the observers' vantage points are equal. This in turn requires that their distances from the center of the world are equal, because the earth is spherical, which requires that the body of the heaven be spherical.

This has been objected to on the ground that it holds only if the sphere is stationary and the star is moving. For if the sphere were moving, it could be square, and the equality of the distances of the centers of the stars from the observers' vantage points, and the equality of the sizes of the bodies of the stars, would still hold. And, as for the first proof, it holds only if the aforementioned consideration exists in every line of longitude and latitude. The application of each of the two objections to each of the two proofs is not hidden. They have other proofs besides these, stated with what supports them and what counts against them in their lengthy books.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 41:

﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring﴾, i.e., their children. Al-Raghib said: The *dhurriyyah* (offspring) originally refers to the young of children, but in common usage it applies to both the young and the adults together, and it is used for both the singular and the plural, though its original use is for the plural. There are three opinions about it. It has been said that it derives from *dhara'a Allahu al-khalq* (God created the creation), with its hamza dropped, like *bariyyah* and *rawiyyah*. It has also been said that its origin is *dhuruwiyyah*. And it has been said that it is *fu'liyyah* from *al-dharr*, like *qumriyyah*. Abu Hayyan preferred the interpretation that it refers to children in general. Others allowed that it may be understood as referring to adults, because they are the ones sent out for trade, meaning: We carried them when they were sent out for trade. ﴿in the ship﴾, i.e., the vessel, which was so named, according to what is in *Majma' al-Bayan*, because it turns (*tadur*) on the water. ﴿the laden﴾, i.e., the filled. It has been said that it is used in its original sense, and that they are the young children whom they take along with them. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the women, for the term is applied to them. In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) "forbade killing the *dharari* (non-combatants)," and it was interpreted as referring to women.

In *al-Fa'iq* [it is recorded]: "Hanzala al-Katib said: We were in a military campaign with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he saw a woman who had been killed, and he said: *Ha-ha, ma kanat hadhihi tuqatil*. Then he said to Khalid: *Qul la taqtulanna dhurriyyatan wa la 'asīfan* (Say: do not kill any *dhurriyyah* or any servant)." The *dhurriyyah* is a man's progeny, but the term has been applied to women, as they say *sama'* (sky) for rain. The intended meaning is the women whom they take along with them. The specific mention of the *dhurriyyah* on these two views is because their stability and steadiness in the ship is more remarkable. It has been said that *dhurriyyah* is applied both to fathers and to sons; this was said by Abu Uthman, and Ibn 'Atiyya criticized it, saying that it is a confusion that is not recognized in the language. It has also been said that *dhurriyyah* means the drops of semen, and that the laden ship refers to the wombs of women; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi and attributed to 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face. The apparent view is that this was not authentically transmitted from him, may Allah be pleased with him, and the verse contains what distances it from being his view. It is the most similar thing to the esoteric interpretations of the *Batiniyya* (the Esoteric sect). The word *al-fulk* is intended in its generic sense, and the description ﴿laden﴾ is stronger in emphasizing the favor of their safety in it. It has been said that this is because it is further from danger. The generic interpretation is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Suddi,

[p. 27]

It was explained that what is in His saying, ﴿And We created for them from the like of it that which they ride﴾, refers to camels, since they are "ships of the land" (safa'in al-barr) because of how much they carry and how little they tire on the journey. Applying the word "ships" (safa'in) to them is common, as in the saying:

*Ships of the land, with the mirage for their seas.*

This was related from al-Hasan and ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad. Mujahid explained it as livestock, namely camels and others. It was also reported from Abu Malik, Abu Salih and others, and this is also a report from Ibn ʿAbbas, that the intended meaning of "the ark" (al-Fulk) is the ship of Noah (peace be upon him), with the definite article indicating a known referent. Then "that which" (ma) refers to what you have also heard. According to some, and according to others, it refers to the ships and boats that came after that ship.

It was found problematic that their offspring were carried in Noah's ship (peace be upon him). It was answered that this means that their forefathers were carried, and these people and their offspring were in the loins of those forefathers. Singling out "offspring" (dhurriyyah), even though they are carried indirectly, is more eloquent in showing favour, because it implies the survival of their descendants. It is also more striking in wonder, because it implies carrying an uncountable multitude in a single ship, with brevity. For the apparent expression would have been "We carried them and those with them," so that their progeny might survive. Thus the mention of "offspring" indicates the survival of the lineage, and this entails the preservation of their origins. So with a few words a great meaning is conveyed.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: "In my view it is possible that the singling out is because those who existed were unbelievers, so there would be no benefit in their existence." That is, the carrying was not a carrying of them, but a carrying of what was in their loins of believers. It was also said that the speech involves the omission of a modifier (mudaf), meaning "We carried the offspring of their kind," but as you see, this is weak. It was also said that the pronoun in "for them" refers to the people of Mecca, and the pronoun in ﴿their offspring﴾ refers to the past generations who were of them. This was related from ʿAli ibn Sulayman, but it is nothing. Al-Imam allowed that both pronouns refer to "the servants" in His saying, ﴿Alas for the servants﴾ (36:30). The intended meaning in each case would not be specific individuals, but rather in the manner of: these people killed themselves, meaning some of them killed others. So the meaning is: a sign for each part of them, that We carried the offspring of each part of them, or the offspring of some part of them. There is in this what is in it of remoteness.

Taking "that which" to mean camels and similar livestock, rather than ships, was preferred on the ground that what is immediately understood from "creation" (al-khalq) is origination and invention, so it is far-fetched for it to relate to what is made by human servants. This was objected to: the actions of servants are created by God, Exalted, according to Ahl al-Haqq (the people of truth, i.e., orthodox Sunni scholars), and the immediate understanding of origination is disputed. On this view, there is in the verse a refutation of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school that held human acts to be created by humans), as was said regarding His saying, ﴿And God created you and what you do﴾ (37:96), on the reading that "what" (ma) is a relative pronoun. As for "from" (min) in "from the like of it," it may be explanatory, or partitive. Its being superfluous was also allowed, according to the view and opinion of al-Akhfash (a grammarian). The apparent reading is that the second pronoun in "for them" refers back to what the first pronoun referred to. It was also allowed that it refers to the offspring. It was further allowed that the pronoun in "its like" refers to an understood but unmentioned referent, the estimated meaning being: from the like of what We have mentioned of created things, in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs of what the earth grows﴾ (36:36), and this is further removed than al-ʿAyyuq (a star). In any case, the relevance of this verse to His saying, ﴿each in an orbit they swim﴾ (36:40), is not hidden. The reason it was not given in the pattern of its siblings, by saying, "And a sign for them is the ark, in which We carried their offspring," as He, glorified is He, said, ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth which We revived﴾, and ﴿And a sign for them is the night, from which We strip off the day﴾, is that the ark itself is not what is wondrous, but rather their being carried in it is the wonder.

Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir, al-Aʿmash, Zayd ibn ʿAli and Aban ibn ʿUthman read ﴿ذُرِّيّاتِهِمْ﴾ (dhurriyyatihim) in the plural. Zayd and Aban read the dhal with a kasra (ذُرِّيّاتِهِمْ, dhurriyyatihim, with the plural form read in the kasra vowel).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 43:

﴿And if We will, We drown them﴾ in the water, ﴿along with what We carry them in of the ships (fulk)﴾ and what they ride of the boats (sufun) and small craft (zawariq). So the speech is a continuation of what preceded. If what is meant there by "that" is the ships and small craft, the matter is clear. If what is meant by it is camels and the like, then the speech is a continuation of the beginning of the verse, meaning: We drown them along with what We carry them in of the ships (fulk), and the discussion of the creation of camels and the like comes in between as a digression (istitrad) for the sake of the parallelism (tamathul). Because of what this involves of a degree of remoteness, it has been said that His saying, glorified is He, ﴿And if We will﴾ ... etc., favours taking "ships" (fulk) in the generic sense, and what is on the ships and small craft existing among the children of Adam until the Day of Resurrection. In attaching the drowning to pure will there is an indication that what calls for their destruction on account of their sins has been fully completed, and nothing remains but the connection of His, exalted is He, will to it. It has also been said that in this there is an allusion to refuting the one who imagines that carrying the offspring in ships without their drowning is something demanded by nature and required by the impossibility of a vacuum (khala'). And al-Hasan read "nughharriqahum" with shaddah (intensive form).

﴿So there is no one to cry out (sarikh) for them﴾, i.e., there is no helper (mughith) for them who would protect them from drowning. The interpretation of sarikh as "helper" is reported from Mujahid and Qatadah. It may be in the sense of sarikh (the one crying out), which is the one seeking help, and that is not intended here. It may be a verbal noun like sURAKH (crying out), and it is used figuratively for rescue, because the one seeking help calls upon the one from whom he seeks help and cries out to him, saying: "The aid and the victory have come to you." Al-Mubarrad said at the beginning of al-Kamil: Salamah ibn Jandal said:

"We, when a terrified crier came to us, the crying out for him was the fear of the people of the valleys (al-mata'nib)."

He says: when a seeker of help came to us, his rescue was earnest in aiding him. It is permitted that it be intended here, i.e., there is no rescue for them. ﴿Nor are they rescued (yunqadhun)﴾, i.e., they are not saved from death by it after it has occurred.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 44:

﴿Except as a mercy from Us and a provision⦆ This is an exceptive (istithna' mufarragh, "exception from a general state of affairs") taken from the most general of causes, which encompasses both the antecedent motive (al-ba'ith) and the subsequent purpose (al-ghayah). The meaning is: they are not rescued or delivered for anything at all, except for a great mercy from Our side, which calls for their rescue and deliverance, and for enjoyment of life that follows from these two. It is also permissible that "mercy" be understood as that which accompanies the enjoyment of worldly life, so that both together become the purpose of the rescue and deliverance, i.e., for a kind of mercy and enjoyment. Al-Zajjaj and al-Kisa'i held that it is an exception from what would be the object of a purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi). The exception, according to what the apparent sense requires, is connected (muttasil). It has been said that the exception is disconnected (munqati') in the sense: "but rather, a mercy from Us and a provision, which would be the cause of their salvation." But this is not the case. It is also permissible that the accusative be by way of an implied preposition (taqdir al-ba'), i.e., "except with a mercy and a provision," with the prepositional phrase connected to "yunqadhun" (are delivered). Since it was deleted, its object took the accusative by removal of the preposition. It has also been said that it is in the verbal-noun sense (masdariyyah) for an implied verb, i.e., "except that We show them mercy and grant them enjoyment with enjoyment," and its status and that of what precedes it are not hidden.

﴿Until a time﴾ i.e., until a period in which, as wisdom requires, their terms (ajal) are determined. From this, Abu al-Tayyib took his saying:

"I did not survive in order to remain, but I was spared from one death only to reach another death."

The apparent reading is that the one spoken of is whoever God wills to drown. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The phrase ﴿So there is no one to cry out for them﴾ ... etc. is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) giving information about those traveling at sea, whether they are saved or drowned, i.e., there is no salvation for them except by the mercy of God Most High. It is not tied to the drowned, though it could be tied to them, and the first is better, so consider it." Yet we have considered it and found in it no goodness, let alone that it be better.

The fa' (then/so) clearly indicates the connection of what follows it to what precedes it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 45:

﴿And when it is said to them﴾ etc. is an explanation of their turning away from the revealed verses, following the explanation of their turning away from the cosmic signs which they were witnessing and their not reflecting upon them. That is: when it is said to the people of Makkah, by way of warning, regarding what has been sent down of the verses or otherwise, ﴿Beware of what is before you and what is behind you﴾. Qatadah and Muqatil said: that is, the punishment of the nations who came before you, and what is meant is:
Page 29
Beware of the like of their punishment. ﴿And what is behind you﴾ means the punishment of the Hereafter. Mujahid, in one report, said the opposite of this, and it was also reported from him in another report that "what is before them" is what of their sins has already passed, and "what is behind them" is what of them is yet to come. The same was reported from al-Hasan. It has also been said that "what is before them" is the calamities of the sky and "what is behind them" is the misfortunes of the earth. It has also been said that "what is before them" is the hardships from where they expect them, and "what is behind them" is the hardships from where they do not expect them. The sum of the matter, as has been said, is: beware of the punishment, or beware of that which punishment follows from. ﴿So that you may be shown mercy﴾ is either a circumstantial clause relating to the waw of "beware" or a purpose clause for it, meaning: hoping that you may be shown mercy, or in order that you may be shown mercy. Mercy has been interpreted as deliverance from punishment. The answer to "when" (idhā) is omitted, relying on its being understood from the words of the Exalted that follow.

(As is) clearly understood: if the warning is given by the noble verse itself, then it is by the explicit wording of the text ('ibarat al-nass). If it is given by something other than it, then it is by its implication (dalalatuhu), because when they turned away from the signs (ayat) of their Lord, they would turn away from other than them all the more. It is as if it were said: "And when it is said to them, 'Beware the punishment,' or 'Beware what necessitates it,' they turn away, because they have become accustomed to it and trained in it." The ma is negating, and the form of the present tense indicates continuous, renewed persistence. The first min is extra, for emphasizing generality, and the second min is partitive, attached to an omitted element that functions as an attribute of "ayah." The attribution of the signs to the name of the Lord, which is itself attached to their pronoun, serves to magnify their status, which entails the magnitude of what they dared to do against them. What is meant by them is either these verses that speak of the wondrous creation of God Most High and the abundant bounties of God Most High, which necessitate turning toward them and believing. Their being brought (itha') means the descent of revelation with them, that is, no sign from the signs that speak to this was revealed except that they turned away from it in the manner of denial and mockery. As for "ma," it encompasses them and the cosmic signs (al-ayat al-takwiniyyah), which include miracles and marvels of created things, of which the three signs mentioned just before are a part. Their being brought means their manifestation to them, that is, no sign from the signs of which what has been mentioned of His affairs is a part, bearing witness to His oneness, glorified be He, and His singular divinity, was manifest to them, except that they were turning away from it, abandoning correct reflection upon it, which leads to belief in Him, mighty and majestic.

In the statement there is an indication of their continued turning away in accordance with the continuing arrival of the signs. The phrase "'an" (from) is related to "mu'ridin" (turning away), and it was placed before it for the sake of a claimed restriction (al-hasr al-idda'i), as an exaggeration in denouncing their condition. It is also said it is a restriction of relation (al-hasr al-idafi), that is, turning away from them and not from what they are upon of disbelief. It is also said it is for the sake of observing the rhyme endings (al-fawasil). The sentence is in the accusative position, as a circumstantial clause (hal) either from the object of "ta'ti" or from its subject, specified by the attribute, because it contains a pronoun referring to each of them. The exception is an incomplete exception (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of states, that is: "No sign from the signs of their Lord comes to them in any of their states except in the state of their turning away from it," or "No sign from them comes to them in any of its states except in the state of their turning away from it."

The sentence "And there does not come to them" and so on, according to what al-Kashshaf's wording suggests, is a concluding statement (tadhyil) that confirms what preceded concerning the matter of turning away. To its being a concluding statement al-Khafaji went, then he said: "So it will be interjected (mu'taridah) or a circumstantial clause (hal) placed to confirm what precedes it, since it includes what it contains together with the additional benefit of the causal explanation indicating the omitted answer, which is what is given as the cause. So it does not need separation, because it is a new independent sentence (mustanifah), as it was imagined. So reflect."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 47:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Spend of what Allah has provided you"﴾. That is, what He, glory be to Him, has given you by way of bounty and favour, of various kinds of wealth. He expressed it this way to affirm the truth and to encourage spending, following the pattern of His saying ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you﴾, and to draw attention to the magnitude of their offence in failing to comply with the command. Likewise, the use of "min" (the partitive "some of") is for the same purpose. The speech, according to what has been said, is a rebuke for their failure to show compassion towards the creatures of Allah, Exalted is He, as a consequence of their rebuke for failing to magnify Him, Mighty and Majestic is He, by abandoning piety. This indicates that they had neglected all the obligations, because they all return to two matters: magnifying Allah, Exalted is He, and having compassion towards His creation, glory be to Him. It has also been said that it serves to indicate their indifference to the counsel of the adviser and his guidance to them towards what averts the calamity from them, akin to His saying ﴿And when it is said to them, "Fear Allah"﴾ etc. The meaning according to this is: when it is said to them, by way of advice and guidance towards what is beneficial for them, "Spend some of what Allah has given you of His bounty upon the needy", for that is among what turns away calamity and repels hardships. ﴿Those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "Shall we feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would feed?"﴾ The first (explanation) is more apparent. The apparent sense is that those who disbelieved are those to whom it was said, "Spend", and the speech turned away from their pronoun to the explicit noun, as an indication of the cause of the statement mentioned. As for the statement being addressed to those who believed, indicating that they were the ones who said it, it has been said: when the poor among the disbelievers' relatives and clients embraced Islam, the (disbelieving) people cut off from them what they used to give them in support, and this was in Mecca before the revelation of the verses on fighting. So the believers urged them to maintain relations with their (disbelieving) relatives, and they said, "Shall we feed" etc. It has also been said: Quraysh were stingy because of a famine affecting the poor, both believers and others, so the Prophet (ﷺ) urged them to spend on them, and they said this statement. It has also been said: the poor believers said, "Give us from your wealth which you claim belongs to Allah, Exalted is He", and they were denied and said that. This was related from Muqatil. Ibn Abbas said: there were zindiqs (heretics) in Mecca who, when commanded to give charity, would say, "No, by Allah! Shall Allah make him poor and we feed him?" They used to hear the believers attach actions to the will of Allah, Exalted is He, saying, "If Allah willed, He would have enriched so-and-so; if He willed, He would have honoured him; if He willed, glory be to Him, it would have been such-and-such." So they brought out this answer as a mockery of the believers and of what they used to say.

Al-Qushayri also said: the verse was revealed concerning a group of zindiqs who do not believe in the Creator and denied His existence, so their saying "If Allah willed" is by way of mockery of the Muslims. It is permissible that it be based on the belief of those addressed. It is understood from this that the zindiq is one who denies the Creator. Ibn al-Kamal has thoroughly investigated this matter in the most complete manner in a separate treatise, so refer to it if you wish to pursue that. From al-Hasan and Abu Khalid it is related that the verse was revealed concerning the Jews, who were commanded to spend on the poor, and they said that. The apparent sense of what preceded requires that it concerns the disbelievers of Mecca who were commanded to spend of what Allah has provided them, and this is general to feeding and other things. So they answered by denying feeding, which they had never ceased to boast of, as an indication of denying other things a fortiori. For this reason he did not say "Shall we spend?"

It has also been said that he did not say that because feeding is what is meant by spending, or because "nut'im" (we feed) means "nu'ti" (we give). But this is not the case. "Aṭ'amahu" is the answer to "law" (if), and the occurrence of the consequent as an answer without the lam is eloquent, and from it is ﴿That if We willed, We would have struck them﴾ and ﴿If We willed, We would have made it salty﴾. Indeed, the more common usage is with the lam.

The apparent sense is that His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿You are not but in manifest error﴾ is a continuation of the speech of those who disbelieved to those who believed, that is: "You are not but in clear error, in that you ask of us what opposes the will of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He." By my life, the vessel drips with what is in it, for their answer indicates the utmost of their error and the excess of their ignorance, in that they did not know that He, Exalted is He, feeds by means of causes, among them urging the rich to feed the poor, and His granting them success in that, glory be to Him. It is also permissible that it be an answer from Him, Exalted is He, by which He rebukes the disbelievers and their ignorance, or a narration of the believers' answer to them. In both cases it is an explanatory resumptive (istinaf bayani) answering what might be said: "What did Allah say?" or "What did the believers say in reply to them?"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say﴾ is a conjunction with the preceding conditional clause, indicating their denial of the Resurrection (al-ba'th), which is the source of every ugly deed. The Prophet (ﷺ) had never ceased promising them this. And among what is brought to mind for them are the commands that preceded, so they used the demonstrative for the near in their saying ﴿When is this promise﴾, meaning the promise of the Resurrection. It has also been allowed that this is by way of mockery, and that they meant: when will that occur and be realized in external reality? ﴿If you are truthful﴾ in what you say and promise, ﴿then inform us of it.﴾ The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, because they too were reciting to them the verses that point to it and that command belief in it. It seems that its being an evil for them was not taken into account, and therefore they expressed it as a "promise" rather than a "threat." It was also said that this is because they claimed that they would have the best reward (al-husna) with Allah, exalted is He, if the Resurrection were realized, based on the view that the verse concerns those other than the deniers of the divine attributes (al-mu'attilah).

Page 31

﴿They are not waiting for﴾ is a reply from Him, exalted is He, meaning: they are not awaiting ﴿anything but a single, great cry﴾, which is ﴿the first blast in the Trumpet (al-Sur), by which the people of the earth will die﴾. He expressed it as "waiting" in view of the outward sense of their words, ﴿When is this promise?﴾, or because the Cry must inevitably occur, so they were treated as if they were awaiting it. ﴿It will seize them﴾, meaning it will overpower them and take hold of them, so that they perish, ﴿while they are disputing﴾, meaning they are quarrelling and contending over their dealings and their trade, with no thought of its signs crossing their minds. This is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Or the Hour will come upon them suddenly while they are unaware﴾. So they should not be deceived by the absence of its signs in the way they wish, nor claim that it will not come.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Umar, who said: "The Trumpet will be blown while people are in their roads, their markets and their gatherings, to the extent that a garment will be between two men who are haggling over it, and neither of them will release it from his hand before the Trumpet is blown and they are struck dead by it." This is the blast of which Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿They are not waiting for anything but a single cry﴾, and so on.

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others transmitted from Abu Hurayra, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The Hour will certainly come while two men have spread their garment between them, and they will neither trade it nor fold it. The Hour will certainly come while a man is plastering his cistern, and he will not drink from it. The Hour will certainly come while a man has returned with the milk of his ewe, and he will not taste it. The Hour will certainly come while a man has raised his morsel to his mouth, and he will not eat it.'"

The original form of ﻳَﺨِﺼِّﻤُﻮنَ ("yakhissimun") is يَخْتَصِمُونَ ("yakhtasimun"), and Ubayy read it this way. The taʾ was then made sukun and assimilated into the ṣād after being converted into a ṣād; then the khāʾ was given a kasra because of the meeting of two sākins (unvocalised letters). It is also permissible that the kasra is for following the vowel of the second ṣād, and a sākin does not form an obstruction in this way.

The two Harameyn (the two readers of Mecca and Medina, namely Ibn Kathir and Nafi'), Abu 'Amr, al-A'raj, Shibl and Ibn Qustantin read with the assimilation of the taʾ into the ṣād and the transfer of its vowel, which is a fatha, to the khāʾ. Abu 'Amr also, and Qalun in one transmission, read with the brief pronunciation (ikhtilas) of the vowel of the khāʾ and the doubling of the ṣād. From both of them there is also the reading with a sukun on the khāʾ and a lightened ṣād, from khasamahu ("he contended with him") when he argued with him. The object of the verb in this case is omitted, meaning: some of them contend with others. It has also been said that ﻳَﺨِﺼِّﻤُﻮنَ ("yakhissimun") means that they argue on their own behalf. Some of them vocalise the yāʾ of the imperfect with a kasra, following the kasra of the khāʾ and the doubled ṣād. The kasra on the yāʾ of the imperfect is a dialect form which Sibawayh related from al-Khalil in several places. From Nafi' it is related that he read with a fatha on the yāʾ, a sukun on the khāʾ and a doubled ṣād with a kasra, and in this there is the joining of two sākins according to its well-known rule. It seems that joining the two sākins is permissible when the second letter is doubled, whether or not the first letter is a letter of prolongation (madd). This is what we have chosen in transmitting the readings, following some of the eminent scholars, while the transmitters differ regarding this.

**Ruh al-Ma'ani** (the commentary of al-Alusi) on surah 36, verse 50:

﴿So they will not be able to make any bequest﴾ concerning any of their affairs when they are among their families. The accusative of ﴿tawsiyah﴾ (bequest) is because it is the object of ﴿yastati'una﴾ (they will be able), and it has been permitted that it be an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of an implied verb.

﴿Nor will they return to their families﴾ when they are outside their homes. Rather, the Blast (al-Sayhah) will seize them, and they will die wherever they are, and they will return to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and to no other than Him, glorified is He. Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿yurja'una﴾ (they will be returned) in the passive voice, and the pronouns refer to those who said ﴿When will this promise be fulfilled?﴾, not from the standpoint of their individual persons, meaning the people of Makkah who were present at the time of the revelation, but rather to those who deny the Resurrection in general.

﴿And the Trumpet is blown﴾. It is the second blast, and between it and the first there are forty (years). That is, it is blown into. The past tense is used to indicate that the event will certainly occur.

Al-A'raj read "الصُّوَرِ" (as-Suwar) with a fatha on the waw. The discussion of this has already passed.

﴿Then, behold, they rush out of their graves (al-ajdath)﴾, that is, the graves. It is the plural of "جَدَثٍ" (jadath) with two fathas. It was also read with a fa' in place of the tha', and the meaning is the same. ﴿To their Lord﴾, the Master of their affair, ﴿they hasten (yansiluna)﴾, that is, they hurry, by way of compulsion (al-ijbar), in accordance with the words of God Most High, ﴿They will be brought before Us﴾. It has been said: the mention of "الرَّبِّ" (al-Rabb, the Lord) is to indicate their hastening after having done wrong toward the One who had been good to them, at the time they were compelled to it. There is no contradiction between this verse and the words of God Most High, ﴿Then, behold, they are standing and looking﴾, because standing, looking and walking can occur together, or because the time of standing and looking is close to the time of hastening in walking. Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu 'Amr, in one of the transmissions from him, read "يَنْسِلُونَ" with a damma on the sin.

[Page 32]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 52:**

﴿They say﴾, that is, at the beginning of their resurrection from the graves: ﴿Woe to us﴾, that is, our destruction, come, for this is your time. It was also said that it means: O our people, look at our woe and be amazed by it. On the view that the addressee is omitted, it was said that (wayy) is an exclamation of wonder and (lana) is an explanatory element (bayan). This is attributed to the Kufans, but it is worthless.

Ibn Abi Layla read ﴿يا ويْلَتَنا﴾ *yā waylatanā* with the feminine ending (tā' al-ta'nith). It is also narrated from him: ﴿يا ويْلَتى﴾ *yā waylatā*, with a tā' followed by an alif that replaces the ya' of possession. The meaning is that each of them says: O my woe! ﴿Who has raised us from our sleeping-place?﴾ That is, from our rest (ruqad). This is either a mimi verbal noun (masdar mimi, a noun of the form *mafʿal* from the verb) or the place of our rest (mahall ruqadina), taken as a noun of place (ism makan), with the singular meaning the plural, i.e., "our sleeping-places." In this there is a comparison of death to sleep, in that the action is not apparent and there is rest from voluntary acts. It is also possible that the sleeping-place is literal, and that the people, because their minds were confused, thought they had been asleep and had no awareness of the punishment of the grave; therefore they asked who had woken them. It was also said that they called it a sleeping-place while knowing the punishment they had suffered in it, because of the enormity of what they witnessed, so that it was like a sleeping-place in comparison. It is narrated that when they see Hell and the various kinds of punishment in it, they see what they were in as being like sleep beside it, and so they say this.

al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he said: "They will sleep a sleep before the resurrection." These (all) except Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid that he said: "The disbelievers have a dozing in which they find the taste of sleep before the Day of Resurrection. When the people of the graves are called, they say: O ﴿woe to us, who has raised us from our sleeping-place﴾." It is also narrated from Ibn Abbas that God, exalted is He, lifts the punishment from them between the two blasts, so they rest; then when they are raised by the second blast and witness the terrors, they say: "This is it."

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) it is stated that this chain of narration is not sound, and it chose that "sleeping-place" is a metaphor for the bed of death.

Amir al-Mu'minin Ali, Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak and Abu Nahik read ﴿من بعثنا﴾ *min baʿthinā* with the preposition min and a genitive verbal noun (masdar majrur). It is connected either to (woe) or to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial clause (hal) from it. A similar construction occurs in the report: "Woe to me because of you (wayli ʿalayka) and woe to me from you (wayli minka), O man." The second min is connected to (baʿth).

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he read ﴿من أهبنا﴾ *man ahabbanā* with the interrogative man, and *ahabba* with a hamza, from habba min nawmihi, meaning he woke up from his sleep, and ahbabtuhu, meaning I woke him, i.e., I roused him.

It is narrated from Ubayy that he read ﴿هبنا﴾ *habbanā* without a hamza. Ibn Jinni said: "The reading of Ibn Mas'ud is more analogically sound. As for habbanī meaning 'woke me,' I have not seen any basis for it, and in the language there has not come to us a *mahbub* meaning *muqaz* (roused). Unless the preposition is omitted, meaning habba bina, i.e., 'woke us,' then the preposition was dropped and the verb was connected directly; the meaning is not 'whoever arose, so we arose with him,' but rather 'whoever woke us.'" al-Baydawi said: "habbana without the hamza has the meaning of ahabbana with the hamza." It was also read ﴿من هبنا﴾ *min habbinā* with the preposition min, and the verbal noun from habba yahubbu.

﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised﴾: a sentence consisting of a subject and predicate. ﴿and the messengers spoke the truth﴾ is conjoined to what is in the position of (mā). Conjoining it to the nominal sentence, or making it a circumstantial clause without (qad), is contrary to the apparent sense. (Mā) is a relative pronoun whose returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: "This is what the Most Merciful promised and what the messengers made true," i.e., they spoke truly concerning it, from the expression "I told Zayd the truth of the matter" (ṣadaqtu Zaydan al-ḥadītha), meaning you spoke truly to him about it; and from this is the saying: "The age of his camel spoke the truth to me" (ṣadaqanī sinna bakrihi). Or (mā) is a verbal-noun particle, meaning: "This is the promise of the Most Merciful and the truth of the messengers," calling the promised thing and the thing spoken truly about by the name of the promise and the truth. This, it is said, is an answer from God, exalted and majestic. According to al-Farra', it is from the angels; according to Qatadah and Mujahid, it is from the believers. It would have been expected that they be answered with the agent, because he is the one they asked about, by saying: "The Most Merciful" or "God raised you," but He turned from that to what is mentioned, as a reproach for their disbelief and a rebuke to them for it, while it also contains an indication of the agent. Many have mentioned that this is from the wise style (al-uslub al-hakim), meaning: do not ask about the one who raised you, for this resurrection is not like the awakening of a sleeper, and that is not what concerns you now; what concerns you is to ask what this resurrection is, full of terrors and dread. This contains some of their reproach.

al-Tibi claimed that mentioning the agent is not sufficient in the answer, because their saying ﴿who has raised us from our sleeping-place﴾ is a report of what they said at the resurrection, after what preceded it of their saying "When is this promise, if you are truthful?" So the answer must contain a statement carrying two meanings. The apparent requirement was for it to be said: "The Most Merciful raised you, who promised you the resurrection and whom the messengers informed of it," but He turned to what indicates their denial, so that it would be more terrifying and more penetrating in reproach. This is of the wise style. There is room to dispute the claim that mentioning the agent is not sufficient in the answer. Regarding their choice of the name the Most Merciful, it was said to indicate an increase in reproach, since the promise of resurrection is among the effects of mercy, yet they paid it no heed, did not turn to it, denied it, and did not prepare for what it requires. It was also said that the responders among the believers chose it because mercy had overwhelmed them, so it was before their eyes. The restriction of the mercy of al-Rahman to what happens in this world and the mercy of al-Rahim to what happens in the Hereafter is disputed, since it is reported: "O Merciful of this world and the Hereafter, and its Merciful."

Ibn Zayd said: "This answer is from the disbelievers, in that they answered themselves when they recalled what they had heard from the messengers, peace be upon them; or some of them answered others. They chose the name the Most Merciful in hope that He would show them mercy. But far-fetched is it: there is no share of mercy from Him, exalted and majestic, for a disbeliever on that Day."

al-Zajjaj permitted that ﴿this﴾ (hadha) be an adjective of ﴿our sleeping-place﴾ (marqadina), by interpreting it as a derived noun, so that stopping on it is correct. It is narrated from Hafs that he stopped on it and paused briefly; therefore the claimed consensus of the readers on stopping at ﴿marqadina﴾ is not complete. (Mā) is a subject whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "It is true"; or it is a predicate whose subject is omitted, meaning: "It is" or "This is what was promised." In this there is from the rhetorical art (badi') the device of interlocking (tajadhub), namely that a word may belong either to what precedes it or to what follows it. A similar example, as the great Shaykh (Ibn Arabi), may God sanctify his secret, said in his tafsir called *Ijaz al-Bayan fi Tarjamat al-Qur'an*, and which I copied from his noble hand, is the verse ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize it as they recognize their sons﴾ after His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, then indeed you would be among the wrongdoers﴾; and His saying: ﴿In it is guidance﴾ after ﴿there is no doubt﴾. So let it be memorized!

[Page 33]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 53:

﴿Not⁠ it was⁠﴾ i.e., whatever the deed or the blast that was related just now was, ﴿but a single cry﴾ produced from the blast of Israfil (upon him peace) into the Trumpet. It has also been said: it is the words of Israfil (upon him peace): "O decayed bones, severed joints and torn hairs! Indeed Allah commands you to gather for the judgment of the decision." It has also been read with the nominative "ṣayḥatun" (a cry), and its explanation has already passed. ﴿Then behold, they are all⁠ brought together⁠﴾ gathered, ﴿present before Us⁠﴾ with Us, in the place of Our judgment and where the apparent authority of others besides Us has ceased, ﴿to be brought up⁠﴾ for the settling of the reckoning without tarrying even for the twinkling of an eye. In this there is, from the lessening of the matter of resurrection and gathering, and the indication that they do not depend on causes, what is not hidden.

Note on terms: *Tafsir* (exegesis); *Israfil* is the angel charged with the Trumpet (ṣūr).

﴿So today﴾ refers to the present day or the known day, which is the Day of Resurrection, indicated by the blowing of the Trumpet on it. It is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarf*, a noun of time or place functioning adverbially). Its governing element (*ʿāmil*) is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿no soul will be wronged﴾ of souls, whether pious or wicked, ﴿in anything﴾ of wrongdoing. It is then in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*, al-maṣdariyya), or "anything" (*shayʾan*) means "of things," as a direct object (*mafʿūl bihi*) by way of *ḥadhf wa-īṣāl* (elision of a preposition so that the verb reaches its object directly).

[Page 34]

﴿And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾, i.e., except the recompense of what you used to do in the world, continuously, of disbelief and sins. So the speech involves *ḥadhf al-muḍāf* (elision of the first term of a construct phrase) with the second term standing in its place, to draw attention to the strength of the connection and association between the two, as if they were one thing. Or it means: except by what you used to do, i.e., in exchange for it or because of it. It was said: you will not be recompensed except the very essence of what you used to do, by its appearing in the form of punishment. This is a report of what is said to the disbelievers when they see the punishment prepared for them, as confirmation of the truth and rebuke for them. Abu Hayyan preferred that the address encompasses the believers, so that the statement is information from God, exalted, about the people of the gathering (*al-maḥshar*) in general, as indicated by the indefiniteness of *nafs*; al-Sakkaki chose this view. It was said: the restriction (*ḥaṣr*) contradicts this, because He, exalted, fulfils the believers' rewards and increases them from His bounty manifold. It was refuted: the meaning is that the righteous one's reward is not diminished and the wicked one's punishment is not increased, because wisdom rejects what is in the form of injustice; as for increasing reward and reducing punishment, it is not like that. Or the meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾ is: indeed you are only recompensed from the kind of your deeds: if good, then good; if evil, then evil.

Al-Alusi's commentary on Surah 36, verse 55:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in enjoyment, reclining﴾ — on the assumption that the preceding address was specific to the disbelievers, as part of what will be said to them on that Day, to increase their regret and remorse, for conveying the good condition of their enemies after describing their own bad condition adds grief upon grief; and in relating this there is a deterrent for these disbelievers from what they are upon, and an incitement to imitate the conduct of the believers. And on the assumption that it is general, it is a fresh statement and an information for us about what will happen on the Day of Resurrection when each goes to what has been prepared for them of reward and punishment.

Ash-shughl (business, occupation; here: preoccupation) is the affair that distracts a person and occupies him away from his other concerns, because it is more important to him than all of them, either because it entails complete joy or complete distress. The intended meaning here is the first. Its being indefinite (nakira) is for magnification, as if it were a preoccupation whose true nature cannot be grasped. What is meant by it is the bliss they are in, which occupies them away from everything that comes to mind. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud and Qatadah that it is the deflowering of virgins; this is also related from Jaʿfar al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him. In another narration from Ibn ʿAbbas, it is the striking of lutes; it was also said to be listening (to music). It is related from Waki' and from Ibn Kaysan that it is mutual visiting. It was also said that it is the hospitality of Allah, may He be exalted, which takes place on Friday in al-Firdaws al-A'la, at the mound of musk, where He, glory be to Him, manifests Himself to them and they all see Him, exalted is His majesty. It is related from al-Hasan that it is a bliss that preoccupies them from what the people of the Fire are suffering of punishment. It is related from al-Kalbi that it preoccupies them from their families among the people of the Fire, so that they do not remember them, lest their enjoyment be disturbed. Perhaps generalization is preferable.

The intention of the proponents of these sayings is not to restrict their preoccupation to what they have mentioned alone, but rather to clarify that it is among their preoccupations; the specifying of each of them with mention is taken to be due to what the context of explanation requires. The word shughl is in the singular in view of it being a single bliss from this perspective. The preposition with its object is related to a omitted predicate which occurred as the predicate of inna; "wa-fakihun" is a second predicate of it. It is permitted that the predicate be "fakihun", with "fi shughl" related to it, or as a circumstantial clause (hal) from its pronoun.

As for "fakihun", according to what Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, it means "joyful" (farihun); and they transmitted from Mujahid that the meaning is that they marvel at what they are in.

Abu Zayd said: al-fakih is one of good disposition, cheerful; no verbal form of it from the triliteral has been heard. Abu Muslim said: it is derived from al-fukahah, with a damma, which is speaking of what gladdens. It was said: it means enjoyment and delight. It was also said: fakihun means "possessors of fruit," like laabin and tamir.

The apparent practice of Abu Hayyan is to prefer this, and the expression of their state by the nominal sentence before its realization is to make the awaited, anticipated event stand in the place of the actual event, to signal the extreme speed of its realization and occurrence. And in it, on the assumption of the specificity of the address, there is an increase in the distress of those addressed.

The two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') and Abu ʿAmr read "shughlun" with a damma on the shin and sukun on the ghayn; this is a dialect of "shughulun" with two dammas, for the Hijazis, as al-Farra' said.

Mujahid, Abu al-Simal, and Ibn Hubayrah, as transmitted from him by Ibn Khalawayh, read it with two fathas; Yazid al-Nahwi and Ibn Hubayrah also, as transmitted from him by Abu al-Fadl al-Razi, read it with a fatha on the shin and sukun on the ghayn; these are also two dialects of it.

Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Qatadah, Abu Haywah, Mujahid, Shaybah, Abu Raja', Yahya ibn Subayh, and Nafi' in one narration read "fakihun", the plural of fakih, like hadhir and hadhirun; it is an adjective of the form of intensity indicating emphasis and permanence. Talhah and al-A'mash read "fakihina" with alif and ya' in the accusative as a circumstantial clause, with "fi shughl" being the predicate. It was also read "fakihina" without alif and with ya' similarly. It was read "fakuhun" with a fatha on the fa' and damma on the kaf; fa'ul with a damma on the ayn is among the patterns of the intensive adjective, like nattus, which means the shrewd one, keen of sight, true in physiognomy.

[Page 36]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They and their spouses, in shade, reclining on couches﴾. This is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a sentence that begins a new clause), brought to explain the manner of their occupation and enjoyment, and to complete it with what increases their delight and joy through the company of their spouses. ﴿Hum﴾ ("they") is the subject (*mubtada'*), ﴿wa-azwajuhum﴾ ("and their spouses") is a conjunction (*'atf*) on it, ﴿muttaki'un﴾ ("reclining") is the predicate (*khabar*), and the two prepositional phrases are a complement (*sila*) to it. It has been said: they were placed before it to observe the rhyme endings (*fawasil*, the rhyming pause-endings of the verses), or ﴿hum﴾ together with the two prepositional phrases, along with what they attach to of the sense of being settled, are successive predicates. It is also permissible that the predicate is the first adverbial phrase, and the second adverbial phrase is connected to ﴿muttaki'un﴾, which is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are reclining on the couches; or the adverbial phrase is connected to an omitted predicate placed first, and ﴿muttaki'un﴾ is a delayed subject. On both possibilities the sentence is an explanatory resumptive sentence (*isti'naf bayani*). It has also been said that ﴿hum﴾ is an emphasis of the pronoun concealed in the predicate of *inna*, namely ﴿fakihun﴾ ("enjoying") or ﴿fi shughul﴾ ("occupied").

Some scholars prohibited this, on the claim that it involves separating the emphasized from the emphasizer by an alien element, and that ﴿muttaki'un﴾ is another predicate for them, with ﴿'ala al-ara'ik﴾ ("on the couches") connected to it, and likewise ﴿fi zilal﴾ ("in shade"). Or it is connected to an omitted element which is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of both the conjoined and the conjoined-to. Whoever permits a circumstantial clause to come from the subject also permits this possibility, on the assumption that ﴿hum﴾ is also a subject.

The word ﴿zilal﴾ is the plural of ﴿zill﴾, and the pattern of *fi'al* pluralized as *fi'al* is common, like *sha'b* and *sha'ab*, *dhi'b* and *dhi'ab*. It is also possible that it is the plural of *zullah* (with a *damma*), like *qubbah* and *qibab*, and *burmah* and *biram*. This is supported by the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), al-Sulami, Talha, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i: ﴿fi zulal﴾ with a *damma* then a *fatha*, for it is the plural of *zullah* and not of *zill*, and the basic principle is the agreement of readings. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: it is the plural of *zillah* with a *kasra*, which is a dialectal variant of *zullah* with a *damma*, so it is like *liqhah* and *liqah*, and this is rare.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) interpreted the shade as protection from the places of harm. For the people of Paradise there is, from the shade of Allah the Exalted, what protects them from evils. The plural is with regard to what each one of them has of that, or it is multiple for a single person with regard to the multiplicity of what provides protection. It is possible that it is pluralized in regard to its being of great importance and sublime rank, like the plural of *yad* (hand) in the sense of power, according to one opinion, in His saying the Exalted: ﴿And the heaven We built with hands (*bi-aydin*)﴾.

Abu Hayyan interpreted ﴿al-zilal﴾ as the plural of *zullah* as clothing and similar things that provide shade, like curtains. I say: Ibn al-Athir said: *al-zill* is the shade resulting from a barrier between you and the sun, whatever it may be. It has been said that it is specific to what is before the sun's decline, and what is after that is *fay'* (the shade cast after noon). You know that the shade in the sense in which the sun is considered cannot be conceived in Paradise, since there is no sun there. From here al-Raghib said: *al-zill* is the opposite of *al-DIhh* (direct sunlight), and it is more general than *fay'*, for it is said *zall al-layl* (the shade of night) and *zill al-jannah* (the shade of Paradise).

What has come concerning its shade indicates that it is like the shade that exists in this world before sunrise. Ibn al-Qayyim in *Hadi al-Arwah* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked: "What is the earth of Paradise?" He said: "A white marble of silver, as if it were a mirror." It was said: "What is its light?" He said: "You have not seen the hour before the sunrise; that is its light, except that there is in it no sun and no zamharir (intense cold)." Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned something similar, but did not attribute it. Abu Hayyan criticized him, saying: this requires a sound transmission, and how could that be when there is a hadith indicating that a *hawra'* (maiden) of the maidens of Paradise, if she appeared, the world would be illuminated by her, or something similar to this? The answer can be that the intent is to bring the matter closer to the understanding of the questioner and to clarify the situation with what he understands, or the explanation of its light in itself, not in the general sense that includes what occurs in it from the lights of its inhabitants, the *hur al-'in* (maidens with lovely eyes) and others.

Indeed, its light in itself is more complete than the light of this world before sunrise, as is indicated by what Ibn Majah narrated from Usamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Is there anyone who strives for Paradise? For Paradise has no *khatar* (equal), that is, it has no equal and no like, and by the Lord of the Ka'bah, it is a light that shines (*nur yatalalla'*)..." The hadith. It is permissible to interpret ﴿zilal﴾, the plural of *zill*, here in this sense, and its plurality is for multiplicity in regard to consideration. It is also permissible to interpret *zill* as might and protection, for it is sometimes expressed by it, and by this al-Raghib interpreted His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed the righteous are in shades (*zilal*) and springs﴾. This is other than the meaning of protection from places of harm which al-Imam mentioned. It is also permissible to interpret it as the plural of *zullah*, as coverings that are above the head, of roof, tree, and the like. The existence of that in Paradise is beyond doubt, for it has come in the Book and is authentically established in the Sunnah that in it are *ghuraf* (upper chambers), which are clearly roofed structures; indeed some reports explicitly mention a roof. And there has also come in it what is clear that there is in it a tall tree which shades whoever is beneath it. It is authentically narrated in the report of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) that he (ﷺ) said: "In Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a rider could travel for a hundred years without crossing it. Recite, if you wish: ﴿And extended shade﴾." Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The extended shade is a tree in Paradise on a trunk, such that a diligent rider would travel in its shade for a hundred years in all its directions. The people of Paradise, the people of the upper chambers and others, come out to it and converse in its shade..." the report. Ibn al-Athir says: the meaning of ﴿fi zilalaha﴾ ("in its shade") is in its branches and its direction. This was to avert the notion that it shades from the sun or the like.

*Al-aradik* is the plural of *arikah*, which according to one opinion is a couch (*sarir*). It was said it is a cushion, narrated by al-Tabrisi. Al-Zuhri said: whatever one reclines upon is an *arikah*. Ibn 'Abbas said: an *arikah* is not so until the couch is within a canopy (*hajlah*); if there is a couch without a canopy it is not an *arikah*, and if there is a canopy without a couch it is not an *arikah*; the couch and canopy together are an *arikah*. In *Hadi al-Arwah*: it is not an *arikah* unless the couch is within a canopy and there is a mattress upon the couch. In *al-Sihah* (of al-Jawhari): the *arikah* is a cushioned, adorned couch in a dome or a house. Al-Raghib said: the *arikah* is a canopy upon a couch, and its plural is *arai'ik*. Its being named so is either because it is in the land made of *arak* (a well-known tree), or because it is a place of residence, from their saying *araka bi-al-makan uruka* (he stayed in the place), and the original meaning of *uruk* is staying to graze the *arak* tree, then it was extended to other kinds of staying.

In summary: the speech of most scholars indicates that the couch alone is not called an *arikah*. Yes, one who reclines upon an *arikah* may be said to be reclining upon a couch, so there is no contradiction between what is here and His saying the Exalted: ﴿Reclining upon couches arranged in rows﴾, since it is permissible that the couches are within canopies, and thus they are *arai'ik*. It is also permissible to say that the people of Paradise at times recline upon *arai'ik*, and at other times upon the couches that are not *arai'ik*. What has been reported concerning the description of their couches will come, God willing. May Allah the Exalted grant us and you to sit upon those couches and to recline with spouses upon the *arai'ik*.

The apparent meaning is that by ﴿azwaj﴾ ("spouses") is meant their believing spouses whom they had in this world. It has been said: their spouses whom Allah the Exalted married to them from the *hur al-'in*. It is permissible, as appears, that what is intended is the more general of the two categories, and of the believing women who died without marrying in this world, whom Allah the Exalted married in Paradise to whomever of His servants He wills. Indeed, the more general of all that and of the believing women who married in this world to husbands who died as disbelievers and were admitted to the Fire, abiding therein forever, and they were admitted to Paradise like the wife of Pharaoh; for it has come in reports that she will be the wife of our Prophet (ﷺ). It is also permissible that what is meant by ﴿azwajihim﴾ ("their spouses") is their counterparts in goodness and their peers in faith, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And others of similar kind (*min shaklihi azwaj*)﴾. Close to this is what has been said

[Page 37]

that what is meant by it is their companions (*akhilla'*), as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their spouses﴾. It has also been said: it is permissible that what is meant by it is what encompasses the counterparts, the companions, and the ones you heard of first. You know that after the intention of all that, and likewise the intention of the counterparts or the companions specifically...

﴿لَهم فِيها فاكِهَةٌ﴾ (For them therein is fruit) is an explanation of what they enjoy in Paradise, of foods and drinks, and of the pleasures they delight in, both bodily and spiritual, after the explanation of the gatherings of intimacy and assemblies of holiness they have there. This serves to complete the explanation of the manner of their occupation and joy, so it is said. It is also permissible that it be a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani) that came as an answer to a question arising from what the preceding speech indicates: that they are occupied with intimacy and reclining on couches, and do not pursue the means of eating and drinking. It is as if it were said: "If their condition is what has been mentioned, how do they deal with the matter of their food?" So it was answered by His words, glorified is He: ﴿لَهم فِيها فاكِهَةٌ﴾. It indicates that they have of food what they have in the most perfect form. It is also conveyed that there is an indication in it that there is no hunger there, and eating is not for the removal of the pain of hunger; their food is fruit, even if it were meat. The tanwin (nunation) is for magnification, meaning a fruit of exalted rank. In His words, glorified is He, ﴿لَهم فِيها فاكِهَةٌ﴾ rather than "they eat therein fruit," there is an indication that the reins of choice are in their hands, and that they are possessors and capable: if they wish, they eat, and if they wish, they refrain.

﴿ولَهم ما يَدَّعُونَ﴾ (And for them is whatever they ask for). That is, whatever they call for for themselves. That is, for them is everything anyone asks for for himself, not that they must request it; it is available just as when someone asks you and you say, "For you is that," meaning, "Why do you ask?" Or, for them is what they actually request, with the understanding that there is request and response, for the joy of being answered produces the pleasure of asking, since it is a lofty station, especially as the one asked and the one who answers is God, the exalted King, may His majesty be glorified and His bounty be general. So "yadda'una" (they ask) is from du'a' (supplication) in the sense of request. Its original form is yadtani'una on the pattern of yaftani'una. The vowel of the ya' was transferred to what preceded it, and it was elided because of its being sukun and the sukun of the waw after it. It is also said: rather, the 'ayn was given a damma because of the waw of the plural, and the vowel of the ya' was not transferred onto it; it was elided out of heaviness, then the ya' was elided because of the meeting of two sukun letters, so it became yadtu'una; then the ta' was changed into dal and assimilated. The use of ifta'ala in the sense of fa'ala (the basic triliteral form) is common, and from it comes ishtawa in the sense of shawa (he roasted), and ijtamala in the sense of jamala, that is, he melted the fat.

Labid said:

"So he roasted (it) on a windy night and melted (the fat)."

(Lahum) is a predicate placed first, and (ma) is a postponed subject. It is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and the clause after it is its relative clause (sila), and the returning pronoun is elided; it is either a genitive pronoun or an accusative pronoun elided with transfer of the verb. It is also permitted that (ma) be an indefinite descriptive noun (nakirah mawsufah), and that it be a verbal-infinitive (masdariyyah); the verbal noun then becomes the subject, and this is contrary to what is apparent. The clause is coordinated with the clause before it. Not being content with coordinating (ma) upon (fakihah) is so that it is not wrongly thought that it refers to accompaniments and complements of fruit.

It is also permitted that (yadda'una) be from the ifti'al form in the sense of tafa'ul (mutual action), like irtamawhu in the sense of tarama-wahu (they threw at one another), meaning: for them is what they call one another to, and the meaning is: everything that it is correct for one person to ask of his companion is available to them, or what some of them actually ask of others out of mutual affection. It is also permitted that it be from ifti'al as previously heard, except that du'a' here means tamanni (wishing).

Abu 'Ubayda said: The Arabs say "ud'u 'alayya ma shi'ta" (ask of me whatever you wish), meaning "tamanna 'alayya" (wish of me).
