And they say, "Fulan fi khayri ma idda'a," that is, "tamanna" (he is in the best of what he wished for). That is, for them is what they wish for. Al-Zajjaj said: It is derived from du'a' (supplication), that is, whatever the people of Paradise call for will come to them. It was said: ifta'ala is in the sense of fa'ala, so yadda'una means yad'una from du'a' in its well-known meaning, that is, for them is what they used to call upon God, exalted is He, for in the world, of Paradise and its ranks.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 58:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Peace﴾ may be taken as a substitute (badal) for "ma" (what), a substitution of part for whole (badal ba'd min kull), but the necessity of a pronoun (in the substitute) is not accepted. And His saying, Exalted is He: (qawlan) is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of a deleted verb, and the sentence is an attributive (sifah) of "salaman". And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from a Lord Most Merciful﴾ is an attribute of (qawlan), meaning: peace is said to them as a word from a Lord Most Merciful, that is, He greets them on His own behalf, without intermediary, as an honouring of them. For Ibn Majah and a group (of narrators) related from Jabir, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said: While the people of Paradise are in their bliss, a light shines upon them, so they raise their heads, and behold, the Lord has looked down upon them from above and said: 'Peace be upon you, O people of Paradise.' That is the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord Most Merciful.﴾ He said: So He looks at them and they look at Him, and they turn to nothing of the bliss so long as they are looking at Him, until He veils Himself from them, and His light and blessing remain upon them in their abodes."

It is also said that (the greeting is) through the intermediary of the angels (upon them be peace), for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the angels enter upon them from every gate﴾ ﴿Peace be upon you﴾. This is related from Ibn Abbas. The majority hold the first view. As for what has been said, that this is the greeting of the angels to the believers at death, it is "nothing" (i.e., baseless). The stated substitution is based on the premise that "ma" is general.

It is also permissible that it be a substitution of whole for whole (badal kull min kull), on the assumption that the term is intended in a specific sense, or on the claim of unity (ittihad) for the sake of honouring. There is no objection to substituting this indefinite noun from it, on the assumption that it is a relative (mawsulah), because it is an indefinite noun qualified by the sentence after it. Moreover, it is permissible to hold that substituting an indefinite noun for a definite one is allowed in all cases without ugliness. It is also permissible that ﴿peace﴾ be the predicate of a deleted subject, with the sentence after it being its attribute, meaning: that is, or it is peace, said as a word from a Lord Most Merciful. The pronoun refers to "ma", and likewise the demonstrative. It is also permissible that it be an attribute of "ma", meaning: for them is what they claim, safe, or possessing safety from what is disliked. "Qawlan" is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid) for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and for them is what they claim﴾, peace, that is, a promise from a Lord Most Merciful. This attributive relation holds on the assumption that "ma" is an indefinite qualified noun, and it is not valid on the assumption that it is a relative, because of the difference in definiteness and indefiniteness; and (it may be) that it is the predicate of "ma", with (lahum) attached to it to specify the direction, as one says: "For Zayd is abundant honour", meaning: what they claim is safe, pure for them, without any admixture. The accusative of (qawlan) is as you have just heard.

In the Kashshaf: The most suitable view is that it is in the accusative by way of specification (ikhtisas), which is one of its figures of speech, so the sentence becomes a separate clause unconnected to what preceded it, and there is no harm in the accusative of the indefinite noun in that case. It is also permissible that it be a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is deleted, meaning: and for them is peace, said as a word from a Lord Most Merciful. The predicate is placed first so that the sentence follows the pattern of its sisters, not in order to permit beginning with an indefinite noun, since the indefinite noun is qualified by the sentence after it. Their statement apparently implies the implicit conjunction (al-'atif) too, though it is possible that it is not implied. The separation of the clause, according to what has been said, is because it works like a reason (ta'lil) for what the preceding verses contain, for the peace of the Lord Most Merciful is the source of every honour and dignity. It is also permissible, on the assumption that it is a subject, to take the deleted predicate as "upon them". The Imam said: Then this would be an announcement from Allah, Exalted, in this world, as if He, glorified is He, related to us and said, Exalted is His majesty: ﴿Indeed, the companions of Paradise today are busy in joy﴾, then, when the description of their condition was complete, He said: ﴿Peace﴾ upon them. This is like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Peace upon Noah﴾, and ﴿Peace upon the messengers﴾. Thus He, Exalted, has done good to His believing servants just as He did good to His messenger servants. Then he said:

This is an original and excellent view that what it indicates is evident. Or we say its estimate is "Peace be upon you", and this would be a kind of iltifat (shift of address), in that He, Exalted, said to them such-and-such, then He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾. End quote.

The justification for beginning with "salam" in such a construction, whether qualified or not, is well known among junior students. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi read "silm" with a kasra on the sin and a sukun on the lam, meaning the same as salam. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: "musalim lahum", meaning: that is peaceful for them. But this is not the case.

Ubayy, Abdullah, Isa and al-Ghanawi read "salaman" with a fatha, as an accusative of the verbal noun (masdar), meaning: He greets them with a greeting (yusallimu 'alayhim salaman); or as a state (hal) from the pronoun of "ma" in the predicate; or from it, on the view that a state may come from the subject, meaning: and for them is their desire, pure.

Page 39

﴿And separate yourselves today, O criminals﴾. That is, withdraw from the believers toward your destination in the Fire. ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and others narrated from Qatadah: that is, "Withdraw from every good." And from al-Ḍaḥḥāk: "For every disbeliever there is a house of Fire in which he will be, neither seeing nor being seen." That is, contrary to what the believers have of gathering with those they love. Perhaps this is after a period from their first entry, and so it does not contradict the mutual reproach among them that appears in other verses, such as His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And when they dispute in the Fire﴾. It is also possible that he meant each category of disbelievers, such as the Jews and the Christians. Al-Imam (al-Razi) permitted that the command is a command of creation (takwin), as in "Be, and it is," meaning that God, Exalted is He, says this to them, and there appears upon them a mark by which they are recognized, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿The criminals will be known by their marks﴾. Its remoteness is not hidden.

The clause is either conjoined to the preceding clause, which is set forth to explain the conditions of the people of Paradise, as a conjunction of narrative to narrative, so the difference between the nominal (insha'i, imperative) and the declarative (khabari) does no harm. The change of construction seems intended to depict the complete contrast between the two groups and their two states. Or it is conjoined to an implied element to which the narration of the state of the people of Paradise leads, as if it were said after explaining that they are in a matter of great importance and their success in lasting bliss, which explanation falls short of describing it: "Let them therefore rejoice with their eyes, and separate yourselves from them, O criminals."

Abu al-Suʿud said, and al-Khafaji said: It is permissible that it be by supposing "and it is said: separate yourselves," conjoined to the supposed "it is said" which governs qawlan (speech). This is closer and less forced, because the omission of the verb "say" with its object standing in its place is common, to the extent that it was said of it: "It is the sea; speak of it and there is no blame." In this there is a point which becomes evident on slight reflection. It was also said: what is mentioned from His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the companions of Paradise﴾ up to here is an elaboration of the preceding general statement, namely His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾. Based on this, the conjoined element includes the meaning of a demand, in the sense: "Let the believers separate from you, O people of the gathering, toward Paradise, and separate from them toward the Fire." Its author (al-Kashshaf) objected to this, saying that it is not evident, since with either of the two matters there is sufficiency from the other. Then he said: "The correct view is that the intended purpose is to conjoin the account of the people of the Fire to the account of the people of Paradise, and the demand was chosen here to add intensity of dread and rebuke. Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Burn therein today﴾? Even if there must be an implied element, the conjoined element is more fitting to be taken in the sense of a declarative statement, meaning that the criminals are separated and set apart."

The benefit of the shift lies in the subtle point contained in address and demand.

Yet Abu al-Suʿud also said concerning this: the consideration and supposition of "let the believers separate" is far from correct, since what is reported about them is not their destiny toward what was mentioned of the pleasing state, such that the mentioned command could be arranged upon it. Rather, what is meant is their actual settling in it. The fact that this is a treatment of the awaited as if it were the realized does not benefit, because the basis for consideration and supposition is the mind's being led to it and the flow of the speech's arrangement converging upon it. After the mentioned treatment, and removing expectation from the level of consideration, it becomes an attempt to suppose something to which the command relates, which entirely removes the noble composition from its eloquence. Apparently there is no difference in this between the implied element and the included element. What most strongly suggests itself is that what is mentioned gives no more than the preference of supposing "let them rejoice with their eyes" over supposing "let them separate." So let this be understood.

Some of the clever ones said: it is permissible that "imtazu" be a past-tense verb, with the pronoun referring to the believers, meaning: the believers have separated from you, O criminals, in attaining Paradise and its bliss. In that case it carries humiliation for them, and the conjunction is then a conjunction of a declarative verbal sentence upon a declarative nominal sentence, and there is no prohibition against it. It was objected that, together with what it contains of departure from the well-known style, namely the occurrence of the vocative with a command, such as ﴿Joseph, turn away from this﴾, this is of little value; and what it mentions of humiliation is sufficiently provided by what came before concerning what they were in of
Page 40
luxury. Also, the transmitted report (al-ma'thur) strongly rejects it, and it is almost explicit that "imtazu" is an imperative verb, and this would hardly occur to any reader.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 60:

﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan﴾ Among the things said to them, in a manner of rebuke, reproach and confounding, between the command to separate themselves (from the guilty) and the command to endure the heat of Hell. The ʿahd (covenant, charge) is a commandment and a forward instruction containing good and benefit. What is meant here is what came from Him, exalted is He, through the tongues of the Messengers, peace be upon them, of commands and prohibitions, among which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan seduce you as he removed your parents from the Garden﴾ to the end of the verse, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not follow the footsteps of Satan; indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾, and other verses coming in this sense. It has also been said: it is the covenant taken from them in the world of atoms (ʿalam al-dharr), when He, glorified is He, said to them: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ It has also been said: it is what was set up for them of rational and revealed proofs, commanding the worship of God, exalted is He, and forbidding the worship of other than Him, mighty and majestic is He. So it is, as it were, a metaphor for the establishing of proofs. What is meant by worshipping Satan is obeying him in what he whispers to them and makes attractive to them; it is expressed as worship to intensify the warning and aversion from it, and because it stands in opposition to the worship of Him, mighty and majestic is He. It is also permissible that it means worship of other than God, exalted is He, among the false gods, and its attribution to Satan is because he is the one who commands it and makes it attractive; so the figurative usage lies in the attribution.

Ṭalḥa and al-Hudhayl ibn Sharaḥbīl al-Kūfī read ﴿iʿhad﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, as mentioned by the author of al-Lawāmiḥ, who said it is the dialect of Tamīm, and this kasra on the nūn and the tāʾ is more common among the letters of the present tense. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: al-Hudhayl and Ibn Wathhāb read ﴿alam iʿhad﴾ with a kasra on the mīm and the hamza and a fatḥa on the hāʾ, and this is from the kasra of the letter of the present tense other than the yāʾ. It is narrated from Ibn Wathhāb ﴿alam ʾaʿhid﴾ with a kasra on the hāʾ. It is said ʿahada and ʿahida.

Perhaps he meant that the kasra on the mīm indicates the kasra on the hamza, because the vowel of the mīm is the vowel that was transferred to it from the hamza, and the hamza was dropped after its vowel was transferred, not that the mīm is kasra and the hamza after it is also kasra so that it is pronounced. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it was read ﴿iʿhad﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, and all verbs of the pattern faʿila permit a kasra on the letters of their present tense except the yāʾ; and ﴿aʿhid﴾ with a kasra on the hāʾ. Al-Zajjāj permitted that it be from the pattern naʿima yanʿamu and ḍaraba yaḍribu. And ﴿aḥhad﴾ with the ʿayn alone replaced by an unpointed ḥāʾ, and ﴿aḥḥad﴾ with its replacement together with the replacement of the hāʾ and its assimilation, and this is the dialect of Tamīm; and from it is their saying dahhā maḥḥā, meaning leave it with it. What he mentioned, about his saying "except in the yāʾ," is based on some dialects. It is narrated from some of Kalb that they also put a kasra on the yāʾ, saying yiʿlamu for example. His saying regarding aḥhad and aḥḥad, that it is the dialect of Banū Tamīm, is the well-known view; and it has been said: aḥhad is the dialect of Hudhayl and aḥḥad is the dialect of Banū Tamīm. And their saying dahhā maḥḥā either means "leave this waterskin with this woman" or "leave this woman with this waterskin."

﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾, that is, of manifest enmity; and this is the reason for the obligation to refrain. It has been said that it is the reason for the prohibition. The enmity of the accursed one came before his enmity toward Adam, peace be upon him. The address with the attribute of prophethood to Adam serves as a preparation for this reason and an emphasis on their failure to act according to the requirement of knowledge; so they and the deniers are alike.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 61:

﴿And that you worship Me﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with ﴿that you do not worship Satan﴾, on the basis that the ﴿that﴾ (an) here is either explanatory (mufassirah) of the covenant (ʿahd), which contains the meaning of speech but not its letters, or a verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah) particle from which the preposition has been dropped, meaning: Did I not enjoin upon you the abandonment of worshipping Satan and [the act of] worshipping Me? The placing of the prohibition before the command is because the right of clearing (takhliyah, removal of what is bad) is to precede adornment (taḥliyah, the adding of what is good). It was said: and so that the statement of the Exalted, ﴿This is a straight path﴾, may be connected to it, based on the view that the reference is to worshipping Him, the Exalted, since that is what is known as the straight path.

Some have made the reference to be to what was covenanted to them, namely abandoning the worship of Satan and performing the worship of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

It has been preferred that His worship, if it is not distinguished from the worship of other than Him, glorified be He, is not called a straight path. So reflect!

The sentence is resumptive (istiʾnafiyyah), brought to explain what necessitates the covenant of worshipping Him, the Exalted, or the covenant in both its parts. The indefinite form (tankir) is for emphasis and magnification, meaning: this is a path that is eloquent
Page 41
in its straightness, comprehensive of everything it must have, reaching a rank that description and definition fall short of. For this reason He did not say ﴿this the straight path﴾ or ﴿this is the straight path﴾, although the latter would indicate restriction (ḥaṣr). It is also permitted that the indefiniteness is for partiality (tabʿiḍ), meaning: this is part of the straight paths, and this is a diminishment of its due in an equitable statement. Within it is the inclusion (idmaj) of reproach, in the sense that if it were only part of the paths described as straight, that would suffice for following it; how much more so when it is the origin and the reliable one, as it has been said:

And I say: some of the people [are] for you a metaphor, out of fear of informers, but you are all of the people.

In it [is the point] that what is sought is straightness, the matter revolves around it, and its little is much.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 62:

﴿And he had certainly led astray from among you a great multitude.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnaf) brought to intensify the rebuke and reinforce the reproach, by showing that they did not take warning from others, following the explanation of their breaking of the covenant. The address is to their later generations, among whom are disbelievers, who are singled out for added rebuke and reproach so that their offences may be multiplied. The attribution of misguidance to the pronoun of Satan is because he is the one who directly carries out the seduction.

Al-Jibill, according to al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani), means a great company. It was applied to them as a metaphor for a mountain in its greatness. Al-Dahhak reported that the least of al-Jibill, which is a great nation, is ten thousand. Some commentators explained it as a company, and others as a nation without the qualifier. It has also been said that it is the innate nature created upon which a person is, which does not change, as if it were a mountain. Here, however, this meaning goes against the apparent sense.

Al-ʿArabiyyan and al-Hudhayl read ﴿جُبْلًا﴾ (jubulan) with a damma on the jim and a sukun on the ba. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisai read it with two dammas and a light lam. Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Zuhri, Ibn Hurmuz, ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and Hafs ibn Humayd read it with two dammas and a doubled lam. Al-Ashhab al-ʿUqayli, al-Yamani and Hammad ibn Salamah, from ʿAsim, read it with a kasra on the jim and a sukun on the ba. Al-Aʿmash read it with two kasras and a light lam, as the plural of jibla, like fitrah and fitar. The Commander of the Faithful ʿAli, may God honour his face, and some of the Khurasanis read ﴿جِيلًا﴾ (jilan) with a kasra on the jim followed by the letter ya, the singular of ajyal, which is a category of people, such as the Arabs and the Romans.

﴿Did you not then understand?﴾ This is coordinated (ʿatf) with an implied clause required by the context, meaning: Were you witnessing the traces of their punishments, and yet you did not understand that these were due to their misguidance? Or: you did not understand anything at all, so that you would desist from what they were upon, lest the painful punishment befall you.

Talha, ʿIsa and ʿAsim, in the narration of ʿAbd ibn Humayd from him, read it with the ya of the third person, so the pronoun refers to al-Jibill.

This is the commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 63:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿This is Hell, which you were promised﴾ is a resumed statement (isti'naf), which they are addressed with after the completion of the rebuke, reproach, censure and confounding when they stand at the brink of Hell. That is: this which you see is Hell, with which you were continually being threatened, by the tongues of the Messengers (upon them be peace) and those who conveyed on their behalf, [warning] that you would enter it in return for worshipping Satan.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 64:

﴿Burn in it today﴾ is a command of humiliation and disgrace, like His saying, ﴿Taste, indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ etc. That is: experience its heat on this day for which you did not prepare yourselves. Abu Muslim said: that is, become its fuel (ṣilā) or its firewood (wuqūdahā).

al-Ṭabrisī said: Cling to the punishment through it. The root of ṣilā (ṣalā) is "lizūm" (adherence, clinging), and from it comes "al-muṣlā," the one who follows closely behind the forerunner, because he clings to his trace.

﴿because you used to disbelieve﴾: your persistent disbelief in the world. The bāʾ (ba) is causal (sababiyyah), and "mā" is verbal-masdarial (maṣdariyyah). The possibility that it is relative (mawṣūlah) is remote.

[Page 42]

﴿Today We shall seal their mouths﴾ is a metaphor (kinaya) for preventing them from speaking. There is no barrier to there being an actual seal on their mouths.

It is also permissible that the seal is used figuratively (isti'ara) for the meaning of prevention, by likening the creation of a state in their mouths that prevents speech to a real seal. Then the word "seal" is borrowed for it, and "We shall seal" is derived from it. The metaphor is then a metaphor of the dependent kind (isti'ara tab'iyya), meaning: today We shall prevent their mouths from speech with a prevention resembling sealing. The first interpretation, however, is preferable in my view.

﴿And their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness to what they used to earn﴾: that is, to what they persisted in earning in the world. The prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa'l-majrur) appears to be governed by two verbs, "yukallimu" and "tashhadu" (the verbs "speak" and "bear witness"). Perhaps the meaning, and God Most High knows best, is: their hands will speak to Us about what they persisted in doing and did not repent of, and will inform Us of it, and will say: they did such-and-such to us and through us; and their feet will bear witness against them of that.

The attribution of speech to the hands, rather than testimony, is for the greater specificity of their connection with the performance of deeds, to the extent that the deed is frequently attributed to them in the sense of agency, as in His saying: ﴿On the Day when a man will look at what his hands have sent forward﴾, and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and what their hands had done﴾, and His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿by what the hands of people have earned﴾, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾, and so on. This is not so with the feet. Therefore testimony is more appropriate for them, since deeds are not attributed to them; they are like outsiders. Speech is more appropriate for the hands because of their frequent direct involvement in deeds and the attribution of deeds to them, so that they seem to be the ones doing them. Along with this, there is the beauty of combining speech with the sealing of the mouths, whose meaning is prevention from speech.

It seems that God, glorified is He, when He introduced the verse of light (the Verse of Light, 24:24), which is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will bear witness against them﴾, with testimony, and mentioned the limbs from the highest to the lowest, attributed it to all of them. He did not single out the hands for speech, because they lie between the witnesses, even though what proceeds from them is also testimony in reality. Their being agents is not literal; rather they are instruments, and the true agent is the human being. In that context, considering testimony as coming from the source (i.e., the speaker) was more fitting to the situation, because of the preceding story of the slander (al-ifk) and what relates to it. For this reason, the tongues were explicitly mentioned there, but are not explicitly mentioned here. Rather, the verse is silent about whether they testify or not. Sealing the mouths is not the absence of their testimony, since what is meant by it is preventing those spoken of from speaking with their tongues. This is a matter beyond the speech of the tongues themselves and their testimony, which is by making knowledge, will and the ability to speak present in them, so that they speak, testify to what they testify to, while their owners are sealed in their mouths and do not speak.

From this it is known that there is nothing in the Verse of Light that is explicit about the absence of sealing on the mouths. Yes, the apparent meaning there is that there is no sealing, and here the apparent meaning is that there is no testimony from the tongues. According to this apparent meaning, it is permissible that the one spoken of in both verses is one and the same: that their mouths are sealed and their hands and feet are made to speak first, then the seal is lifted and their tongues bear witness, either together with a renewal of what comes from the hands and feet, or without it, relying on what was previously said by them. This may be in one station of the stations of the Day of Resurrection or in two stations. Neither verse contains anything indicating restriction, or denying the testimony of limbs other than those mentioned. So there is no contradiction between them and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until, when they reach it, their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them about what they used to do﴾. It is possible that there is testimony there of the hearing, the sight, the tongues, the hands, the feet and the rest of the limbs, as the apparent wording of His saying, Exalted is He, "and the skins" (al-julud), in the verse of prostration (the verse of prostration, 41:20), suggests. However, some of this is not mentioned in some verses, being content with its mention in other verses, or because it is indicated in some respect.

It is also possible that the one spoken of is in each group of people. Some have made the one spoken of in the verse of prostration the people of Thamud. The enemies of God are to be understood as referred to in His saying after it: ﴿the word has come true against them, along with communities that passed away before them, of jinn and humans﴾. It is not far-fetched that the one spoken of in the Verse of Light is the people of the slander (ahl al-ifk) among the hypocrites and those who accuse chaste women.

Then, the verse of prostration makes clear that the testimony is at the time of arrival at the Fire. The Verse of Light contains nothing that indicates this. As for this verse, the words of some suggest that the sealing and the testimony in it come after the address to those spoken of with His saying: ﴿This is Hell which you were promised﴾, ﴿burn in it today for what you used to disbelieve﴾, so that this also takes place at the arrival at the Fire. In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim (the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud), it is said: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Today We shall seal﴾ ... and so on, is a shift to the third person (iltifat ila al-ghayba), to signal that mention of their vile states called for turning away from them and relating their dreadful states to others, together with what this implies, that this is among the requirements of the sealing, because the address is for receiving an answer, and this has completely ceased. But he said in another place:

The testimony is realized at the place of reckoning, not after the completion of the questioning and answering and driving them to the Fire, and the reports are clear on this.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, from a hadith: "The disbeliever and the hypocrite are called to the reckoning, and his Lord presents his deed to him, and he denies it and says: O Lord, by Your might, this angel has written down for me what I did not do. So the angel says to him: Did you not do such-and-such on such-and-such a day in such-and-such a place? He says: No, by Your might, O Lord, I did not do it. When he does that, He seals his mouth. I think that the first thing that speaks of him is his right thigh." Then he recited: ﴿Today We shall seal their mouths﴾, the verse.

And in a hadith that Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurayra, raised (marfu'), "the servant meets his Lord, and God, Exalted is He, says to him: O so-and-so, did I not honour you?" [...] (ﷺ) said: "He says: I believed in You, Your Book and Your Messenger, and I prayed, fasted and gave charity, and he praises himself with the best that he can. So He says: Shall We not send forth our witness against you? He reflects within himself about who would testify against him. Then his mouth is sealed, and it is said to his thigh: Speak! So his thigh, his flesh and his bones speak of his deeds."

Some reports indicate that the servant asks for a witness from himself, and then his mouth is sealed. Ahmad, Muslim and Ibn Abi al-Dunya related, and the wording is his, from Anas, concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Today We shall seal their mouths﴾, that he said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he laughed until his molars showed. He said: Do you know what I laughed at? We said: No, O Messenger of God. He said: At the servant's address to his Lord. He says: O Lord, did You not protect me from injustice? He says: Yes. He says: I do not accept against me except a witness from myself! He says: Your own self is sufficient as a witness against you, and the honourable scribes as witnesses. Then his mouth is sealed, and it is said to his limbs: Speak! So they speak of his deeds. Then he is left free between himself and speech, and he says: Away with you, and destruction! It was for you that I was contending." Combining these reports requires holding to plurality: sometimes this takes place at the reckoning, and at other times at the Fire, and the view that the states of people differ with regard to what is mentioned.

What preceded in the hadith of Abu Musa, that the right thigh is the first to speak, according to what he thinks, was affirmed by al-Hasan. Ahmad and a group related from Uqba ibn Amir that he heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "The first bone of a human being to speak on the Day when the mouths are sealed is his thigh from the left leg."

Then the apparent meaning is that speech and testimony are with actual utterance, and that happens after God, Exalted is He, has given the limbs life, knowledge and ability. Thereby this refutes the one who claims that a specific evidence (al-bayyina al-makhsusa) is a condition for what is mentioned. The attribution of the sealing to Him, Exalted is He, rather than what comes after, has been said to be so that the compulsion (al-jabr) regarding testimony and speech is not understood. He indicated this by choosing the mentioned limbs after God Most High had enabled them, for this is more revealing of the disgrace of those spoken of.

Does each limb testify only to what was done to it, or does it testify to that and to what was done to others? There is a difference of opinion on this, and the second is more effective in disgracing. Knowledge of what is testified to may be attained by God Most High creating it in them at that time, and it does not exist in the world. It may also be that this knowledge was attained in the world, in that God Most High has created perception in the limbs, so that they perceive the actions as the doer does. When the Day of Resurrection comes, God Most High restores to them what they were, makes them recall what they did at first, and makes them speak with a speech that the one testified against understands. This is like what they said about the glorification of all things with the tongue of speech (bi-lisan al-qal). God Most High is powerful over all things, and reason does not rule this out. It is not more remote than God Most High creating in them knowledge, will and ability, so that they speak on the Day of Resurrection. Whoever believes in this, let him believe in that. Clinging to the tail of improbability (al-istib'ad) leads to denying resurrection altogether, God forbid, or interpreting it in the way the Batiniyya (esoteric sect) interpreted it. The killing of one of them, said Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali, is better than killing a hundred disbelievers. In light of this, the verse is among the supports of the view that inanimate things and the like glorify with speech. On the first possibility, the view is supported that the witness may testify when he has acquired knowledge by which he is certain, by whatever means he acquired it, even if he did not witness it or was not present.

Al-Shaykh al-Akbar (Ibn Arabi), may his secret be sanctified, in his tafsir called Ijaz al-Bayan fi Tarjamat al-Qur'an (Concise Clarification in Translating the Qur'an), stated that His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾ indicates the permissibility of this. He mentioned in it that the witness is sinful if he does not testify from his knowledge. You know well what the jurists have said on the issue.

It seems that on the second possibility the testimony comes after being asked, by saying to the limbs: "Did he not do such-and-such?" and they say: "Yes, he did."

It is also possible that it comes after the limbs are commanded to testify, by saying to them: "Testify to what they did." Then they testify, enumerating their deeds. This may be either by mentioning all their deeds, sins and other things, without distinguishing sin from other things, and this being testimony against them in terms of reality, since it includes harming them by mentioning what is in fact sinful; or by mentioning only the sins. The latter requires holding that the limbs, in this world, distinguish which deeds are sins and which are not. I do not think you would say this, and I have not heard that anyone claims it.

Some have gone to the view that the speech and testimony of the limbs is their indication of their deeds, and the appearance of the traces of sins upon them, in that God Most High changes their forms into other forms, from which the people of the gathering understand and infer what proceeded from them. Thus the indicative state is treated as the verbal one, figuratively. But this is objected to: one does not resort to figurative meaning when literal meaning is possible, especially since what comes in the chapter of prostration, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will say: God, who made everything speak, has made us speak﴾, is very clearly in verbal speech, and reporting is even clearer. Yes, on this view the matter of improbability becomes easier, and the great scholars would hardly abandon the apparent meanings for its sake.

This, and the verse, appear to indicate that unbelievers are addressed with the subsidiary (furu') rulings, since if they were not obligated by them, there would be no benefit in the limbs testifying to what they earned, nor would the proof be established against them by it. And restricting what they earned to disbelief is something that one would hardly consider. I do not think anyone says this, and it may even be claimed that it is restricted to what is other than disbelief, on the basis that it is among the acts of the heart rather than of the limbs, which testify. But what appears to me to be preponderant is generality.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 65 (part 2 of 2):

Their (the limbs') testimony to it (the deeds) is either by their testifying to what indicates it of bodily actions and verbal utterances, or by the necessary knowledge (al-'ilm al-daruri) which Allah Most High creates for them on that Day, or by knowledge acquired by them through a creation of Allah Most High in this world, so they know it by means of the actions and utterances that indicate it, or by another way that Allah Most High knows. And it is apparent that the gathering (al-hashr) occurs with the original parts of the body, not with another body in which are not the original parts of the body that existed in this world; for the constituent parts of that body (the one of this world) were not the ones upon which the evil deeds were performed, so it is not fitting for them to testify to them. So let this be noted.

And it was read "yukhtamu" (is sealed) in the passive voice, and "wa-tatakallamu aydihim" (and their hands speak) with two tas', and it was read "wa-liyukallimuna aydihim wa-liyashhad arjuluhum" (and let their hands speak to us and let their feet testify) with the imperative lam, on the basis that Allah Most High commands the limbs to speak and to testify. And 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad ibn Talhah narrated from his father, from his grandfather Talhah, that he recited "wa-liyukallimana aydihim wa-liyashhada" with the lam of purpose (lam kay) and the accusative, meaning: "for the hands to speak to us, and for the feet to testify." "We seal upon their mouths."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 66:

﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes﴾ This explains that they are today within the grip of power and deserving of punishment, except that He, Mighty and Majestic, did not will that, due to His dazzling wisdom, Exalted is He. Al-tams (obliteration) is the removal of a trace by erasing, and the meaning is: if We willed the obliteration of their eyes and the complete removal of their light and their form, so that they would return wiped smooth, We would have obliterated them and eliminated their trace.

It is also permitted that by al-tams is meant the removal of sight without the removal of the organ and its trace; that is, "if We willed, We would have blinded them." The choice of the future form, although the meaning is past, serves to convey that the non-obliteration of their eyes is due to the continuing absence of the will; for the negated present tense used in the position of the past is not explicit in indicating the cessation of the continuation of the act, but may indicate the continuation of its cessation.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so they raced to the path﴾, it is coordinated with ﴿We would have obliterated﴾ on the supposition, and "al-sirat" (the path) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, meaning: they intended to race towards the clear path familiar to them.

﴿how then could they see﴾, meaning: how could they see that path
Page 45
and the direction of travel? The intended purpose is the denial of their seeing. Its summary: if We willed, We would have removed their pupils and their sights, so if they intended to race and to travel the road they were accustomed to travelling, they would be unable to do so and would not see it. Interpreting "istabaqu" (they raced) as "aradu al-istibaq" (they intended to race) is among what some have held; but it was said that there is no need to interpret it, for a blind person may begin a race. "Al-sirat" is put in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, and it was not put in the accusative as an adverb of place, because the path, like "al-tariq" (the road), is a specific place, and such a word is not put in the accusative as an adverb. It was also permitted that it be an object, by implying the meaning of "ibtadaru" (they hastened to) in "istabaqu." Al-Zamakhshari's Asas (in the section on literal usage) reports: "fastabaqu al-sirat" means they hastened to it. Al-Kashshaf says: on this basis there is no implication. Some have claimed that it is a mistaken assumption that this is a literal meaning, and the author of al-Asas mentioned it only at the end of the figurative section. The meaning: if We willed, We would have done to their eyes what We did; so if they intended to race, hastening along the path, they would not see. It was also said that it may be an object with "istabaqu" meaning "sabaqu" (preceded), and the path is made the thing preceded by way of metonymy in the attribution, or by implicit metaphor; or that it means "jawazu" (passed beyond). Al-Qamus says: "istabaqa al-sirat" means he passed beyond it, and its apparent sense is that this is literal in that. Many others said: it is figurative, and the relation is causality. The meaning: if We willed, We would have done what We did to their eyes; so if they sought to be made to leave the path they were accustomed to walking in, they would be unable and would not know any road. That is, they cannot manage except to follow the familiar road, not the other roads and paths beyond it, just as you see the blind guided in what they are used to and what they have set out to reach, but not in other things.

Ibn al-Tarawah held that "al-sirat," "al-tariq" and similar spatial nouns are not specific, so their accusative as adverbs of place is permissible. This is contrary to what Sibawayh explicitly stated, and he regarded their accusative as adverbs of place as an anomaly, and he recited:

*A lance that, when the hand shakes it, its shaft glides, as the fox glides along the road.*

The meaning in the verse, if it were in the accusative as an adverb: if We willed, We would have done what We did to their eyes; so if they wanted to walk racing along the familiar road, as was their custom, they would not be able to. Taking "the eyes" in their apparent sense, namely the known organs, and "the path" as the sensible road, is what is related from al-Hasan and Qatadah. From Ibn Abbas: taking "the eyes" as insights and "the path" as the intelligible road.

Ibn Jarir and a group reported from him that he said: "And if We willed, We would have obliterated their eyes" — We would have blinded them and led them astray from guidance; "how then could they see" — how then could they be guided. This is contrary to the apparent sense. Isa read "fastabiqu" in the imperative, and it is on the supposition of an implied saying, meaning: it will be said to them, "Race!" This is an imperative of incapacitation, since racing is impossible for them while their eyes are obliterated.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 67:

﴿And if We willed, We would surely have transformed them⁠﴾ — that is, We would have changed their forms into other, hideous forms. From Ibn Abbas: that is, We would have transformed them into apes and swine. And it has been said: We would have transformed them into stones, and this is narrated from Abu Salih. It is known from this disagreement that in the transformation (maskh) of a specific animal, it is not required that the animal form remain. Some scholars called the turning of an animal into an inanimate object "raskh" (solidifying), and turning it into a plant "fask" (dissolving), and maskh was specific to turning it into another animal. The object of the will, by analogy with the preceding, is: And if We willed to transform them in their place, We would have transformed them. ﴿In their place⁠﴾ — that is, in their location, like "al-maqamah" and "al-maqam" (standing place).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said regarding the meaning of the verse: "If We willed, We would have destroyed them in their dwellings."

Al-Hasan, Qatadah and a group said the meaning is: If We willed, We would have made them sit, paralysed them, and made them crippled, unable to stand. Al-Hasan and Abu Bakr read "makanatihim" in the plural, because there are many of them. ﴿So they were not able⁠﴾ for that ﴿to proceed⁠﴾ — that is, to go on to their destinations ﴿nor to return⁠﴾.

It has been said that "and not return" is coordinated with "to proceed," the direct object of "were able," and this is of the type of "Hear of Mu'idi, it is better than seeing him." So the sense is: they were not able to proceed or to return. Otherwise, the object of "were able" cannot be a clause. The expression with a verb rather than the explicit noun is said to be for the sake of the verse-endings (fawasil), together with an indication of the difference between return and proceeding, based on what al-Imam (al-Razi) said: that return is easier than proceeding, because it implies having previously traversed the path, while proceeding does not imply this. It has also been said that it is for the sake of the verse-endings together with an indication of the continuity of the negation, looking to the apparent wording; and there would be progression from two aspects if what al-Imam pointed to is considered. It has also been said that it is with an indication that the negated return is that which occurs by will and choice, for considering these two in a verb ascribed to its agent is closer to being understood than considering them in the verbal noun.

Some scholars limited the explanation to the verse-endings, but al-Imam regards limiting the reason for departing from the apparent sense to the verse-endings as a shortcoming. It has been said: it is coordinated with the clause "they were not able," and the meaning is: "nor return" from their denial, because a seal has been set upon their hearts. It has been said: it is coordinated with what was mentioned, except that the meaning is: "nor return" to what they were upon before the transformation; and this is not far-fetched.

On both views, "proceeding" means departing from the place, and the negation of their ability to it suffices for the negation of ability to return. Whichever is the case, the apparent meaning is that this, and likewise what precedes it, if it occurs, occurs in this world. Ibn Salam said: this whole threat is on the Day of Resurrection, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning and hardly sound on some of the views.

The original form of ﴿mudiyyan⁠﴾ is *mudwiyun*; the waw came together with a yā' while silent, so it was changed to yā' as is the rule, and the yā' was assimilated into the yā', and the ḍamma of the ḍād was changed to a kasra so as to be lighter and to harmonize with the yā'. Abu Haywa and Ahmad ibn Jubayr al-Antaki, from al-Kisa'i, read "midiyyan" with a kasra on the mīm, following the vowel of the ḍād, like *al-'utiyy* with a ḍamma on the 'ayn and *al-'itiyy* with a kasra. It was also read "madiyyan" with a fatha on the mīm, in which case it is among the verbal nouns that came on the pattern *fa'il*, like *al-rasim* and *al-wajif*, and *al-ṣa'iyy* (with a fatha on the unpointed ṣād, followed by a hamza with a kasra, then a shaddahed yā'), the verbal noun of "ṣa'a al-dik" or "al-farkh" when it cried out.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 68:

﴿And whomever We grant long life﴾, i.e., We prolong his lifespan, ﴿We reverse him in creation﴾, i.e., We turn him around within it, so that his weakness and the diminishing of his build and his strength keep increasing, the reverse of what he was at the beginning of his affair. In this there is a comparison of the figurative reversal (*tankis ma'nawi*) with the physical reversal (*tankis hissi*), and the use of the physical term as a metaphor (*isti'arah*) for it. It is reported from Sufyan that the reversal occurs at the age of eighty years. The truth is that the time at which weakness begins and the build diminishes differs according to the differing temperaments and accidents, as is not hidden.

The statement is conjoined (*'ataf*) to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And if We willed, We would have obliterated...﴾ etc., by way of *'atf al-'illah 'ala al-ma'lul* (conjoining the cause to the effect), because it serves as evidence for that.

A group of the Seven [readers] read ﴿nunkisuhu﴾ as "nunkisuhu" (*nunkisuhu*), lightened, from *al-inkas*. ﴿Will they not then understand?﴾ i.e., do they see that and not understand that the One who is able to do that is able to do what was mentioned of obliteration and transformation, and that the non-occurrence of those two is due to the non-attachment of His will, exalted is He, to them?

Nafi', Ibn Dhakwan, and Abu 'Amr, in the narration of Ayyash, read ﴿ta'qilun﴾ with the *ta'* of address, because the address preceding it continues.

[p. 47]

**"And We did not teach him"** poetry, by teaching him this Book, which contains this clarification and summary regarding the origin and the return. **"Poetry."** It is not hidden from anyone with even a little understanding that this wise Book, which includes all religious and worldly benefits in a style that silenced every logician, is distinct from poetry, and is no more like it than the Pleiades is like the dust. As for wording, poetry lacks metre and rhyme. As for meaning, poetry consists of imaginings that either encourage or deter, or the like, and it is the home of falsehoods. For this reason it has been said, "The sweetest of it is the most false." The Qur'an, however, contains wisdom, beliefs and laws.

The purpose of negating that the Prophet (ﷺ) was taught poetry by teaching him the Book is to negate that the Qur'an is poetry by way of **kinaya** (allusion, implicit meaning). This is because what God Most High taught him is the Qur'an, and if what was taught is not poetry, then the Qur'an is absolutely not poetry. In this there is also the implication that he (peace and blessings be upon him) is not a poet, by way of **idmaj** (incorporation, a secondary point embedded within the argument). There is no allusive kinaya here, as some have said. This is a rebuttal of what they used to say, that the Qur'an is poetry and the Prophet (ﷺ) is a poet. Their aim in this was that what he (peace and blessings be upon him) brought of the Qur'an was fabrication and imagination, and far be it from him, and then far be it from him.

**"And it is not fitting for him."** This is an interjection to confirm what was incorporated, meaning that poetry is neither suitable nor proper for him (ﷺ). This is because it leads to altering meaning for the sake of wording and metre, and because its finest form is exaggeration, extravagance and excessive description, while most of it beautifies what is not beautiful and ugly-izes what is not ugly. All of this requires falsehood or resembles falsehood, and the Lawgiver is far exalted above that. Thus it is said.

Ibn al-Hajib said: That is, it is not rationally consistent for him (ﷺ) to say poetry, because if he were one who composed it, suspicion would arise among many people that what he brought came from himself and was of that poetic power. For this reason He followed this with His words, Most High, **"and the word will be fulfilled against the disbelievers,"** because when doubt is removed, nothing remains but obstinacy, and so the word will be fulfilled against them.

This was objected to, on the grounds that concision removes suspicion. Otherwise, his (peace and blessings be upon him) being at the highest level of eloquence and rhetoric in prose is no less conducive to suspicion than composing poetry. Indeed, it may be imagined that it is even greater than composing poetry in this respect. So if the reason for preventing him (peace and blessings be upon him) from poetry were what was mentioned, it would follow that he should be prevented from eloquent and eminent speech too, to close the door of doubt, refute misgivings and magnify the proof. Since that was not the case, it shows that this is sufficient through the inimitability (of the Qur'an), and that suspicion and doubt in his case are things that should not proceed from a sensible person. For this reason doubt was negated. Yet it is known that the reason why it is not fitting for him (peace and blessings be upon him) to have poetry is something else. Ibn 'Atiyya chose this view and made the reason the imagination and embellishment of speech that are in the composition of poetry. This is close to what you heard at first, and it is what should be relied upon. In the verse there is an indication of the blameworthiness of poetry, and it is clear that he (peace and blessings be upon him) was not given a poetic nature, as a mark of care for his station, elevation of his rank, and distancing him (ﷺ) from having within him any source of what would harm his dignity in general.

He (peace and blessings be upon him) was not given the capacity for poetry, although he was preserved from composing it, because that would have removed the capacity for him to keep far from what would harm his exalted position (ﷺ). The analogy to what we have mentioned is infallibility and protection. From the words of al-Mawahib al-Ladunniyya it is understood that some people held that he (peace and blessings be upon him) had the capacity for poetry, but that it was forbidden for him to versify. This is not correct. Yes, the claim that composing poetry is forbidden is acceptable, and its meaning, according to the previous view, as it has been said, is the forbiddance of seeking to attain it. It may also be said that there is no need for interpretation, and that the prohibition of a thing is compatible with lacking the capacity for it.

Is the absence of poetry specific to him (peace and blessings be upon him), or general to the category of prophets? Some said it is general to this verse, since no point of specificity appears. It was said that it may be specific, and the point is the increase of honour, since his station (ﷺ) is above the stations of the prophets (peace be upon them). What is established for them is protection from composing, together with their having the capacity for it. Even if the report that Adam (peace be upon him) composed poetry when his son was killed is sound:

*The lands have changed, and whoever is upon them,
and the face of the earth is dusty and ugly.
Every one of taste and colour has changed,
and the bright cheerfulness of the fair face has diminished.*

The matter of specificity is now clear, and it is known that there is no protection from composing either. Perhaps protection in that case concerns what contains that which disgraces and harms the dignity of prophethood absolutely. The point of specificity is clear according to what is reported from Ibn al-Hajib, because his greatest miracle (peace and blessings be upon him) is the Qur'an, so suspicion might arise regarding it if he (ﷺ) said poetry. Likewise are the miracles of the prophets (peace be upon them). So reflect.

Be that as it may, the following is not an objection: that he (peace and blessings be upon him) "said on the day of Hunayn, while he was on his white mule, with Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith holding its bridle, and only a few people remained with him (peace and blessings be upon him):

*I am the Prophet, there is no lie;
I am the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib.*"

This is not an objection because we do not accept that it is poetry. They defined poetry as speech that is rhymed and metred intentionally. This was something that happened to him (peace and blessings be upon him) without intending its metre. Such things occur often in prose and are not called poetry, nor is the speaker called a poet. Nor is it imagined from his (ﷺ) attributing himself in it to his grandfather rather than his father that there is evidence of intention, because attribution to the grandfather is common. Also, it is he who raised him, since his father died (peace and blessings be upon him) while he was in the womb, and so when he was born, he (the grandfather) took charge of his affairs beyond what a father does for a son. Also, he was well known among them for truthfulness, nobility and honour. For this reason he mentioned him specifically, to serve as evidence for what came before, or as another barrier against defeat. Also, many people used to call him (peace and blessings be upon him) "the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib." From this is the hadith of Dimam ibn Tha'laba: "Which of you is the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib?"

Moreover, some did not count rajaz (a metre) as poetry at all. Its origin was what was in the pattern *mustaf'ilun* repeated six times, which is why its composer is called a *rajiz* (rajaz-poet) and not a poet. From al-Khalil, the *mashtur* (halved) form, which is what has half of it removed so that its metre remains *mustaf'ilun* three times, and the *manhuk* (reduced to a third), which is what has two-thirds removed so that its metre remains *mustaf'ilun* twice, are not poetry. In another report from him, the *majzu'* (truncated), which is what has one foot removed from each hemistich, so that its metre remains *mustaf'ilun* four times, is likewise not poetry. Thus, his (ﷺ) saying "I am the Prophet, there is no lie," if it is half a line, is *majzu'* and is not poetry according to this report. And if it is supposed that he intended it, and it is a complete line, it is also not poetry according to the first report. That it is not poetry according to the view of those who do not consider rajaz poetry at all is evident.

It has come in some reports that he (peace and blessings be upon him) moved the *ba'* in *kadhib* and *al-Muttalib*, so that it would not be metred. Thus its not being poetry is even more evident. As for the claim that the pronoun in "to him" refers to the Qur'an, which is known from the context, meaning that it is not appropriate for the Qur'an to be poetry, so that the Prophet (ﷺ) could be said to have uttered poetry, and no need for justification arises, this is worthless. Indeed, it is sufficient to negate poetry from him (peace and blessings be upon him) by His words, glorified be He, **"And We did not teach him poetry,"** even though the apparent reference of the pronoun is to him (peace and blessings be upon him). The best of the justifications is to exclude this from poetry by the absence of intention, and by this, what occurs in the Qur'an of its like is also excluded. We have mentioned to you much of it earlier.

There is nothing in the verse indicating that the Prophet (ﷺ) should not speak a line of poetry composed by some poet, or quote one. In the reports there is what indicates that he occasionally spoke a line that happened to be metred, as it is narrated that he (peace and blessings be upon him) recited the line of Ibn Rawaha:

*He spends the night with his side turned away from his bed,
when the couches grow heavy with the idolaters.*

His recitation of it in this form is mentioned in al-Bahr. It is also narrated that a stone struck his blessed finger in one of his campaigns and it bled, so he quoted the words of al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, according to what Ibn Hisham mentioned in the Sira, or the words of Ibn Rawaha, according to what Ibn al-Jawzi confirmed:

*You are but a finger that bled,
and what you suffered was in the way of God.*

It has been said that it is his (peace and blessings be upon him), and the discussion of it is like the discussion of his saying "I am the Prophet," etc., except that this may be considered a halved line if each of its two halves is a line. Regarding the occurrence of speech in a line that is not metred, while preserving the meaning, many instances are reported, such as that he (peace and blessings be upon him) recited:

*The days will show you what you were unaware of,
and there will come to you one who has not been supplied with news.*

Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, said: "It is not like this, O Messenger of God." He (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "By God, I am not a poet, nor is it fitting for me."

In a report that Ahmad and Ibn Abi Shayba recorded from Aisha, she said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was seeking news, he would quote the line of Tarafa:

*And there will come to you one who has not been supplied with news.*"

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from al-Hasan that he (ﷺ) used to quote this line:

*Islam and grey hair are sufficient to restrain a man.*

Abu Bakr said: "I bear witness that you are the Messenger of God. He did not teach you poetry, nor is it fitting for you."

Ibn Sa'id recorded from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi al-Zinad that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas: "What do you think of your saying:

*Shall my plunder and the plunder of the slaves be divided between al-Aqra' and 'Uyayna?*"

Abu Bakr said to him, may God be pleased with him: "May my father and mother be ransomed for you, O Messenger of God. You are neither a poet, nor a transmitter of poetry, nor is it fitting for you. He only said: between 'Uyayna and al-Aqra'."

It is reported that he (peace and blessings be upon him) was asked: "Who is the best poet among the people?" He said: "The one who says:

*Do you not see me, whenever I come to a campsite,
I find in it something of fragrance, even if it is not perfumed with perfume.*"

Al-Bayhaqi recorded in his Sunan, with a chain that includes an unknown narrator, from Aisha, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) never combined a line of poetry except one line:

*Hope for what you desire, for rarely is it said of anything that happened, but it came true.*"

Aisha said: "He did not say *tahaqqqa* (it came true), lest he inflect it and it become poetry." Then, despite this, he (peace and blessings be upon him) did not love poetry. In the Musnad of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, from Aisha, she said: "The most hateful speech to him (ﷺ) was poetry." In the Sahihayn and others, from Abu Hurayra, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "For one of you to have his belly filled with pus is better for him than to have it filled with poetry." This is clear in condemning excess of it. As for what is reported from al-Khalil, that he said: "Poetry was more beloved to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) than much of speech," it contradicts what you heard from the Musnad. Perhaps the reconciliation is by detail, distinguishing one kind of poetry from another. The discussion of poetry has already been detailed in the surah of the Poets, so recall it.

**"It is only"**, that is, the Qur'an is nothing but **"a reminder,"** that is, an admonition from God, Mighty and Majestic, and guidance for the two weighty things (humans and jinn), as He, glorified be He, said: **"It is only a reminder to the worlds."** **"And a clear Qur'an,"** that is, a heavenly Book, evidently not the speech of humans, because of the inimitability it contains, which made silent anyone who undertook to oppose it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 70:**

﴿So that he may warn﴾: that is, the Qur'an or the Messenger, peace be upon him. This is supported by the reading of Nafi' and Ibn Amir, *"li-tundhira"* (so that you may warn), with the second-person *ta'* (تاء الخطاب). Al-Yamani read *"li-yundhara"* in the passive voice (مبنيًّا للمفعول). Ibn Khalawayh (ابن خالويه) transmitted it from al-Jahdari (الجحدري) and said: "From Abu al-Simmal and al-Yamani, that they both read *"li-yandhara"* with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and the *dhal*, the imperfect of *nadhira bi-l-shay'* (نَذِرَ بِالشَّيْءِ) with a *kasra* on the *dhal*, when one knows of something."

﴿whoever is alive﴾: that is, sensible (عاقلًا), as Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* transmitted from al-Dahhak. In this there is a *isti'arah* (metaphor, استعارة) that is explicitly stated (مصرِّحة), comparing intellect to life. Or it means believing (مؤمنًا), by the indication of its being contrasted with "the disbelievers." Also in this there is an explicitly stated *isti'arah* comparing faith to life. It is permissible for it to be a *majaz mursal* (unrestricted figurative usage, مجازًا مرسلًا), since faith is the cause of the true, eternal life. The past tense in *kana* (كان) is according to what is in the knowledge of Him, Mighty and Majestic, since its occurrence is certain. It was said that *kana* means *yakun* (will be), and it was said that the statement contains *majaz al-mushara'ah* (figure of imminence, مجاز المشارفة), and it was placed in the position of the past tense; but this, as you see, is weak. The restriction of the warning to him is because he is the one who benefits from it.

﴿and the word may be due﴾: that is, the word of punishment becomes binding (تجب كلمة العذاب) ﴿upon the disbelievers﴾, those marked with this mark, who persist in disbelief. In their being mentioned in contrast with "whoever is alive" there is an indication that they, by being devoid of the effects and rulings of life, such as knowledge, are in reality dead. It has also been permitted that there is in the statement an implicit *isti'arah* (استعارة مكنية), whose indicator is another *isti'arah*. It seems that the words of Him, glorified be He, *"so that he may warn"* etc. were brought as a return to what the surah began with, His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿so that you may warn a people whose fathers were not warned﴾. Were you to consider this transition from the discourse of the Hereafter to the discourse of the Qur'an and warning, you would marvel at the excellence of its placement.

﴿Have they not seen﴾. The hamza is for rebuke and wonder, and the waw conjoins with an implied negative sentence that the conjoined clause follows. The meaning is: "Have they not reflected, or not taken notice, or not known with a certainty close to direct observation?" Some have said that this is conjoined to His saying, exalted is He, ”Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed…“, and that the first (the earlier verse) urges monotheism by warning against chastisements, while this one reminds of the blessings indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That We have created for them﴾, meaning for their sake and their benefit, ﴿from what Our hands have done﴾, meaning from what We Ourselves undertook to bring into being directly, with no share in it for anyone else, neither creating nor acquiring.

The statement is a metaphorical image (isti'ara tamthiliyya, an extended metaphor, lit. "figurative borrowing") regarding what has been mentioned. It has also been permitted that it is a kinaya (allusion, lit. "metonymy by implication") for bringing into existence by the action of hands in the case of one who has hands, and then, after this became common, it was used for what is meant by way of majaz (figurative usage), derived from the kinaya. Some said: the intended meaning of "action" is bringing into being, and "hands" means power, by way of majaz. The plural form of magnitude was chosen, and "hands" is in the plural, to glorify the matter of the effect, and that it is a wondrous affair and a strange making. But this is not the case. It has also been said that "hands" is a majaz for the angels charged with carrying out the works that He, exalted and glorified is He, wills in the world of generation and corruption, such as the angels of shaping (the angels of the forms of the fetus) and the angels who breathe spirits into bodies after their shaping is completed, and others like them. But what is in this is not hidden.

Similar to this is what has been said: "hands" is a majaz for the Names, for every effect in the world occurs through a specific one of His Names.

You know that this verse is among the mutashabih (ambiguous verses, lit. "those resembling one another") according to the salaf (the early pious predecessors), and they do not take the hand when attributed to Him, exalted is He, to mean power, whether it is singular, as in ﴿The hand of Allah is above their hands﴾, or dual, as in ﴿I created with My two hands﴾, or plural, as here. Rather, they affirm the hand for Him, exalted and glorified is He, as He affirmed it for Himself, together with the declaration of His transcendence (tanzih) in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾. This is what many of those whom Allah has granted success among creation have chosen, and I see those who criticize them as none but ignorant.

﴿Cattle﴾ is the object of ﴿created﴾, and it is placed after the two prepositional phrases attached to it, out of concern for what is placed first, and to create anticipation for what comes later, and to join it with what is attached to it of its rulings that branch from it. By "cattle" is meant the eight pairs (az-zawaj al-thamaniya), and He singled them out for mention because of the marvels of their natural design and the abundance of their benefits. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not look at the camels, how they were created?﴾

﴿So they are owners of them﴾, meaning they are those who possess them by Our giving them ownership of them. The fa' (so) has been said to indicate a result of an implied premise: "We created cattle for them and made them possessors of them, so they, by reason of that, are owners of them." It has been said that it indicates a result of their being created for them, but there is obscurity in this. It has been permitted that "milk" (al-mulk) means power and dominance, from the expression "I mulked the dough" (malaktu al-'ajin) when you kneaded it well. From this is the saying of al-Rabi' ibn Mani' al-Fazari, when he was asked about his condition after he grew old:

"I have become one who no longer carries a weapon, nor controls the head of a camel when it bolts."

(Page 51)

The first meaning is more apparent, so that what follows constitutes a new information rather than an emphasis. In any case, ﴿for them﴾ is connected to ﴿owners﴾, and the lam (la) strengthens the governing word. It was placed first to observe the rhyme (fawasil) together with emphasis. The choice of the nominal sentence indicates the stability of their ownership of them and its continuity.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 72:

﴿And We made them subservient to them﴾, i.e., We made them easy, not resisting them in anything they wish to do with them, even slaughtering, as is indicated by His - exalted is He - saying: ﴿So some of them they ride﴾. The fa' (so) here is for the sequential arrangement of the rulings of subjugation and their details upon it; i.e., some of them are their mounts. So rukub (ridden one) is fu'ul in the sense of maf'ul (passive), like hasur (one who is prevented from intercourse), halub (milch animal) and qazu' (one who is weaned), and this is of what is not analogically applied (la yantaqis).

Ubayy and A'isha read ﴿rakubatuhum﴾ with a ta' (rakubatuhum), which is fa'ula in the sense of maf'ula, like halubah (milch animal); it was also said to be the plural of rakub, but this was objected to on the grounds that fa'ula with an initial fatha is not heard in plurals or their names.

Al-Hasan, al-A'mash and Abu al-Barahsam read ﴿rukubuhum﴾ with a damma on the ra' and without a ta', and it is a masdar (verbal noun) like quud (sitting) and dukhul (entering). Either it is interpreted in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ul), or a mudaf (an elided genitive-governed noun) is supposed in the sentence, either on the side of the predicated subject, i.e., "the one who is their riding" (dhu rukubihim), or on the side of the predicate, i.e., "so from its benefits is their riding" (fa-min manafi'iha rukubuhum).

﴿And from them they eat﴾, i.e., and some of them they eat the flesh of. The partitive here is considered with respect to parts, and according to what was said, with respect to individual units. The clause is conjoined to what precedes it, and the style was changed because eating is general over all livestock and frequent and continuous, unlike riding; so it is said. It was also said: the verb is placed in the position of the masdar, and it has the meaning of the passive participle for the sake of the fasila (verse-end rhyme).

﴿And for them therein﴾, that is, in the cattle, both kinds of them, ﴿are benefits﴾ other than riding and eating, such as hides, wool, and fleece, and so on, and plowing with bulls. ﴿And drinks﴾: the plural of *mashrab*, which is a verbal noun used in the sense of the object (*maf'ul*). What is meant is milk. It was singled out, although it falls under the benefits, because of its nobility and the Arabs' concern with it. It was put in the plural with regard to its varieties, and there is no doubt about their multiplicity. Extending *mashārib* (drinks) to include butter, ghee, cheese, and *aqit* (dried curd) is valid only through *taghlīb* (a rhetorical device in which one term is used to encompass what is not literally included) or *tajawwuz* (metaphorical usage), since these are not drunk. There is no need for this, given that they are included among the benefits. It is also permissible for *mashārib* to be the plural of *mashrab* in the sense of a place of drinking.

The Imam said: It means the vessels, for drinking vessels are made from hides, such as water-skins and similar things. Al-Khafaji said: If it refers to a place, then *mashārib* are themselves the place, because of His saying, ﴿in it﴾, for they are its location. Perhaps this is more evident than the Imam's view.

﴿Will they not then be grateful?﴾, that is, they witness these blessings, yet they do not thank the Bestower of them, and they do not devote worship exclusively to Him, glorified is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 74:

﴿And they took besides Allah⁠ ⁠﴾ i.e., transgressing Allah, exalted is He, who they saw had that overpowering power and manifest blessings, and they knew that He, glorified is He, is the sole One who possesses them, ﴿gods﴾ from among the idols, and they associated them with Him, mighty and majestic is He, in worship. ﴿Perhaps they would be helped﴾, hoping that they would be helped, or for the purpose that they would be helped by them against what befell them and what calamities struck them, or that they would intercede for them in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 75:

God's words, ﴿They are not able to help them﴾ ... etc., are a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to explain the falsehood of their opinion, the frustration of their hope, and the reversal of their scheme; that is, their gods are not able to help them. As for the statement of Ibn 'Atiyya, "It is possible that the pronoun in ﴿they are able﴾ refers to the polytheists and the pronoun in ﴿their help﴾ refers to the idols," it is nothing at all. ﴿And they﴾, that is, those polytheists who took them, ﴿for them﴾, that is, for their gods, ﴿are a host brought forth﴾, that is, prepared to guard them and defend them in the world.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated this from al-Hasan and Qatada. It has also been said that the meaning is: the polytheists are a host for their gods in the world, brought forth to the Fire in the Hereafter. This was reported in a narration that Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Hasan. Some of the eminent scholars chose the meaning: "and the polytheists are for their gods a host brought forth on the Day of Resurrection, following them into the Fire." Making them a host is by way of mockery and derision, and likewise the lam in ﴿for them﴾ which indicates benefit. It has also been said that "they" refers to the gods, and the pronoun in ﴿for them﴾ refers to the polytheists; that is: the gods are prepared and brought forth to the punishment of those polytheists on the Day of Resurrection, because they will be made fuel for the Fire; or they are brought forth at the reckoning of the disbelievers, to demonstrate their impotence and to make the polytheists despair of their intercession. Making them a host, and the expression with lam in both aspects, are as mentioned just above. The variation in the referents of the pronouns in the verse is not the forbidden kind of disjointedness (tafkik). The waw in His words, glorified is He, ﴿and they﴾ etc., according to all the aspects mentioned, is either conjunctive or circumstantial; except that the circumstantial sense is merely presumed (muqaddara) in some of the aspects, as is not hidden.

The fa' in His words ﴿So let not their saying grieve you﴾ is the fa' of elliptical connection (al-fa' al-fasiha), meaning: if this is their condition before their Lord, Exalted and Majestic, then do not grieve because of their saying about you, "He is a poet," or if their condition on the Day of Resurrection is what you have heard, then do not grieve because of their saying about God, Glorified be He, "He has partners!" Exalted is God far above that, with great exaltation. Or the meaning is: "About you, he is a poet," or "About God and about you, what is unbecoming of His majesty, Exalted and Majestic, and of your station." Limiting the statement of their saying about him (ﷺ) to his being a poet, and far be it from him, is because it best fits what precedes it in His words ﴿We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him﴾. It may be generalized to include all sayings unbecoming of his station, peace and blessings be upon him. Explaining the condition that the fa' makes explicit by what we mentioned first is what fits what was reported from al-Hasan and Qatadah regarding His words ﴿and they are an assembled host for them﴾. What we mentioned second fits what is mentioned afterward regarding its meaning. It has been said that the estimate, according to the first reading, is: "If they are in this degree of feebleness of intellect, in that they took the hope of victory as gods besides God, Exalted and Majestic, who cannot give them victory or defend them, but rather they themselves defend those gods, then do not grieve because of their saying about you what they said." But the first is probably preferable. In any case, the prohibition, although apparently directed at their saying, is in reality, as we have indicated, directed at the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and what is intended is forbidding him, peace be upon him, from being affected by grief, by way of kinaya (metonymy) in its most emphatic and forceful form, as is not hidden.

Nafi' read ﴿فَلا يُحْزِنْكَ﴾ (so let it not grieve you) with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the zay, from aḥzana, the causative of ḥazina (intransitive), as in "ḥazanahu" and "aḥzanahu."

﴿Indeed, We know what they conceal and what they reveal﴾ is an explicit justification for the prohibition, given by way of resumption (isti'naf), after its justification by way of implication, according to the second estimate of the condition. The knowledge of what is mentioned is a metaphor (majaz) for requiting them for it, or a metonymy (kinaya) for it, because it entails it: for the knowledge of the Sovereign, the Mighty, the Wise, regarding what His enemy has done, to which wisdom calls for retribution, necessitates requiting and avenging him.
