According to the first estimate, it has been said to be an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), occurring as an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "O Lord, if their condition with You and with Your Prophet is that, what will You do with them?" Then it is said: ﴿Indeed We know﴾ and so on, meaning: We will requite them for all their crimes. It has been said also that it is a justification for the ordering of the prohibition upon the condition, so reflect. The ma here is relative (mawsula), and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: We know what they keep secret of corrupt beliefs and enmity towards you and the like, and what they make public of words of association and denial and the like. It is also permitted that it be verbal (maṣdariyya), meaning: We know their concealing and their declaring. The object is omitted, or the two verbs are treated as intransitive. The more immediate is the first, and it is the better.

The mention of the secret before the public is to show the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, Glorified be He, such that knowledge of the secret with Him, Exalted is He, is, as it were, prior to knowledge of the public. It has been said: because the level of the secret precedes the level of the public, for there is nothing that is made public except that it, or its beginnings, was previously hidden in the heart. Thus the attachment of His knowledge, Exalted is He, to its first state precedes its attachment to its second state in reality. It has also been said: it is to indicate concern with rectifying the inner, for it is the foundation of the matter, and because it is the locus of ambiguity that needs clarification. It is well known that pausing at ﴿their saying﴾ is obligatory. It has been said: it is not so, because it is permitted regarding ﴿Indeed We know﴾ and so on that it be a object of the saying, and that this is by way of stirring and allusion, like His words ﴿and do not be among the polytheists﴾. Or that the intended meaning is: "So let not their saying grieve you, by way of mockery and derision: Indeed We know" and so on. From this it is known that if a reciter reads ﴿أنّا نَعْلَمُ﴾ with a fatha and makes it a substitute (badal) for ﴿their saying﴾, his prayer is not invalidated, and he is not declared a disbeliever if he holds the meaning that it gives, just as if he made it a justification with the omission of the particle of justification. The truth is that there is no harm in accepting such an interpretation for the purpose of averting disbelief. As for the matter of the pause, what should be said about it is that, according to their saying, it is nearly obligatory.

Page 53

Ruh al-Ma'ani (al-Alusi) commentary on surah 36, verse 77:

﴿Have they not seen that We created man from a drop of semen?﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (*kalam mustaʾnaf*) brought to explain the falsehood of their denial of resurrection, after they had witnessed within themselves what necessitates belief in it. Just as what preceded was brought to explain the falsehood of their associating partners with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, after they had observed in what lies in their own hands what necessitates monotheism and Islam. It was also said that it is a consolation for him (ﷺ), like His saying ﴿So let not their saying grieve you﴾, by minimizing what they say in comparison with their denial of the Gathering. But this is of no account.

The hamza is for denial and wonder, and the waw is for conjunction upon an implied sentence which is required by the conjoined sentence, as mentioned in His saying ﴿Have they not seen﴾ etc. That is: Has man not reflected and not known that We created him from a drop of semen? Or it is the very same sentence repeated as emphasis of the earlier denial and as a preparation for denying what is more deserving of denial. This is because what is denied is precisely their knowledge of what concerns the creation of themselves. There is no doubt that a person's knowledge of his own state is more important, and his comprehension of it is easier and more complete. So the denial and wonder at the neglect of that is as if it were said: Did they not know His creation of the means of their livelihood, and did they not know His creation of themselves as well, even though knowledge of this is at the utmost clarity and the highest importance? The remarks of some eminent scholars indicate that the conjunction is upon the earlier ﴿Have they not seen﴾, and the common factor is that each of them is built on inversion. For He created for man what He created so that he would be grateful, but he disbelieved and denied the Benefactor and the blessings! And He, glorified be He, created him from a vile drop so that he would be submissive and humble, but he transgressed, became arrogant and disputed. The mention of "man" in place of a pronoun is because the basis of the denial relates to his states insofar as he is a human being.

As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Then he is an open adversary﴾: that is, exceedingly active in dispute and false argumentation, ﴿clear﴾, manifest, openly so in that. It is conjoined to the negated sentence and falls within the scope of denial and wonder, as if it were said: Has he not seen that We created him from the basest and most contemptible of things, and then he suddenly disputes with Us about a matter to which the origin of his own nature testifies with clear testimony? The use of nominal sentences indicates his firm persistence in the dispute and his continuance upon it. In the glosses of al-Khafaji, the sequence of the denial with *fa'* and *idha al-fuja'iyya* (the sudden "then"), upon what calls for the opposite, strengthens the wonder. The intended meaning of "man" is the species, and the adversary is only the disbeliever who denies resurrection absolutely. Yes, the verse was revealed concerning a specific disbeliever. Al-Diya in *al-Mukhtara* and a group of others reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Al-As ibn Wa'il came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with a decayed bone, crumbled it with his hand, and said: O Muhammad, will Allah bring this back to life after it has decayed? He said: Yes. Allah will resurrect this, then He will cause you to die, then bring you back to life, then admit you into the Fire of Jahannam." So the verses ﴿Has man not seen﴾ to the end of the surah were revealed. In a narration of Ibn Mardawayh from him, the one who said this was Ubayy ibn Khalaf, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) killed with a spear on the Day of Uhud. This has been reported from Abu Malik, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Ikrimah and others, as in *al-Durr al-Manthur*. In another narration from al-Habr (Ibn Abbas), he was Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. In another narration from him as well, he was Abdullah ibn Ubayy. Abu Hayyan criticized the attribution of this to Ibn Abbas, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them both, as a mistake, because the surah and the verse are Meccan by consensus, and because Abdullah ibn Ubayy never openly displayed this kind of open defiance. It is reported from Mujahid and Qatadah that he was Umayya ibn Khalaf. What he chose, and claimed to be the soundest of the views, is that he was Ubayy ibn Khalaf. Then he said: It is possible that each of these disbelievers did this.

It was also said that the meaning of His saying ﴿then he is an open adversary﴾ is: then he, after having been a despised water, is a discerning, articulate man, capable of disputation, clearly expressing what is in his mind, eloquent. In that case it is conjoined to "We created him", and the sequence and the suddenness look to his creation. "Mubin" is transitive. The speech is among the supplements of the evidences for the soundness of resurrection.

[Page 54]

Therefore His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he sets forth for Us a parable﴾ is then coordinated with the negated sentence and falls within the scope of denial. As for the first reading, it is coordinated with the sentence of sudden surprise (al-jumla al-fujā'iyya), and the meaning is: "he was suddenly confronted with our dispute and set forth for Us a parable," i.e., he produced concerning us a strange story which, in reality, is in its strangeness like a parable, namely the denial of Our reviving the bones; or a story he deemed strange in his own assumption, found improbable and regarded as being of the category of parables, and denied most vehemently, namely Our reviving them; or he made for Us a parable and a likeness from creation and compared Our power to their power, and negated all of it in general. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And forgets his creation﴾, i.e., Our creation of him in the aforementioned manner, which indicates the falsity of what he set forth, is either coordinated with "set forth" and falls within the scope of denial and wonder, or is a circumstantial clause (hal) from its subject, with "qad" implied or not implied. His forgetting his creation means that he did not remember it, according to what has been said, and there is some feebleness in this. Or it means that he left off remembering it out of his disbelief and obstinacy. Or he is like one who forgets, since he did not act in accordance with what remembrance requires. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He says﴾ is a resumptive sentence which came as an answer to a question arising from the narration of his setting forth the parable, as if it were said: "What parable did he set forth?" or "What did he say?" So it was said: ﴿He says: "Who will give life to the bones when they are decayed?"﴾, denying that and rejecting, among the states of bones, what makes life extremely improbable for them, which is their being decayed (ramīm), i.e., utterly worn away. The apparent view is that "ramīm" is an adjective, not a fixed noun. If it derives from ramma, the intransitive meaning "to decay," then it is a fa'īl in the sense of fā'il, and it was not feminized because its usage became predominantly non-attributive, so it was attached to fixed nouns; or it is taken as fa'īl in the sense of maf'ūl, which is the same for masculine and feminine. Muhyi al-Sunna said: he did not say "ramīma" because it is a deviation from fā'ila, and whatever deviates from its form and pattern is turned away from its counterparts. Similar to it is "baghiyyan" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your mother was not unchaste﴾, where the ta' was dropped because it was turned away from bāghiya. Al-Azhari said: since 'izām, being of the pattern of the singular like kitāb and qirāb, was treated as such, it was said "ramīm" rather than "ramīma," and evidence was cited for it, though this is strange. If it derives from transitive ramma, meaning "to wear away," one says "ramma-hu," i.e., "abla-hu," and its original meaning is eating, as al-Azhari mentioned from "ramma-t al-ibil al-hashīsh" (the camels grazed the herbage), so what has decayed has been eaten by the earth, and it is a fa'īl in the sense of maf'ūl. Its masculine form on this basis is evident, since there is consensus that fa'īl in the sense of maf'ūl is the same for masculine and feminine. In al-Mut li': "al-ramīm is a noun, not an adjective, like al-rumma and al-rufāt, not a fa'īl in the sense of fā'il or maf'ūl; and because it is a noun and not an adjective, one does not ask why it was not feminized when it is predicated of a feminine subject." It is not hidden that it has a verb, which is ramma, as the lexicographers mention, and it is one of the patterns of the adjective, so its being a fixed noun is not apparent.

﴿Say﴾, as a rebuke to him, by reminding him of what he had forgotten of his own innate nature, which points to the reality of the matter, and guiding him to the method of using it as evidence: ﴿He who brought them into being will give them life﴾, meaning He who originated them and nurtured them, ﴿the first time﴾, meaning at the first time, since there was no previous origination of them. There is no doubt that giving life after death is easier than bringing into being before, so whoever is able to originate is even more able to restore life, again and again. There is no possibility of incapacity befalling Him, for His power, glory be to Him and exalted is He, is essential, eternal, and does not accept cessation or change in any respect.

In the Khafajiyya glosses it is stated: al-Farabi used to say, "I wish that Aristotle had come upon the clear analogy (al-qiyas al-jali) in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Say: He will give them life﴾, etc." That is: God, exalted is He, created the bones and gave them life the first time, and whoever creates a thing first is able to create it and give it life a second time. It follows that God, glory be to Him and exalted is He, is able to create them and give them life with their powers a second time. The verse is clearly in support of the view held by Imam al-Shafi'i, and it is said by Malik and Ahmad, that life inheres in the bone, so death affects it as it affects the other limbs, and on this basis they ruled that the bone of carrion is impure. The question of whether life inheres in bone or not is one on which the jurists and philosophers differ. Those who hold that life does not inhere in it argue that life entails sensation, and bone has no sensation, for it does not feel pain when cut, as is observed in the horn. Whatever pain may arise from cutting bone is only due to what is adjacent to it. Ibn Zuhr said in the book al-Taysir: "The words of Galen concerning bones are confused: is there sensation in them or not? What appears to me is that they have a slow sensation. I wish I knew what prevents them from decay and crumbling during life, other than the inhering of the animal spirit (al-ruh al-hayawani) in them!" End of quotation.

Some jurists who held that bones have no life built on this the ruling that they are pure of carrion, since death is the cessation of life; where life does not inhere, death does not inhere either, so they are not impure. They were confronted with this verse, and it was said that the word "bones" in it means its owner, by implication or figurative usage, or that "giving life to them" means returning them to what they were, fresh and moist, in a living, sensitive body. This was preferred over the meaning of the owner of the bones, because the occasion of revelation must be included, and under that meaning it would not be included, whereas it is included under the interpretation of "giving life to them" as "restoring them to what they were." It is not hidden that taking the verse in this way goes against the apparent meaning. The apparent meaning is with the Shafi'is and with those jurists who hold that the bones of carrion are not impure, one of whom saw the strength of the argument from the verse that bones are receptive to life, and so he gave a different reason for their purity, saying: "The impurity of carrion is not due to its essence but to the moisture in it and the flowing blood, and the bone has none of that; therefore it is not impure." The Shafi'is rejected that impurity is due to moisture. The full discussion belongs to the branches of jurisprudence.

﴿And He﴾, glory be to Him and exalted is He, ﴿is knowing of every creation﴾, meaning every created thing, ﴿Knower﴾, emphatically so in knowledge. He, exalted and high is He, knows all the scattered and dispersed parts of each individual person, their roots and branches, and the arrangements of some of them in relation to others, by connection and separation, by joining and parting. So He will restore each of these in the earlier pattern with the powers that had been there before. The sentence is either a concluding parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ tadhyili) confirming the content of what preceded, or it is conjoined to the relative clause. The shift to the nominal form serves to draw attention to the fact that His knowledge, exalted is He, of what has been mentioned is a continuous matter, unlike His bringing into being of the created things.

[p. 55]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 80:**

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Who has made for you fire from the green tree﴾, is a *badal* (substitute, in apposition) for the first relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*). Its *sila* (relative clause) is not simply conjoined to the previous *sila* for emphasis and because the two differ in the manner in which they indicate meaning. The two adverbial phrases are connected to *ja'ala* (made), and they were placed before *naran* (fire), its direct object, to give attention to what is placed first and to create anticipation for what comes later. *Al-akhdar* (the green) is an adjective of *al-shajar* (the tree). It has also been read as *al-khadra'* (feminine).

The people of the Hijaz treat collective nouns whose singular is marked by a *ta'* (feminine ending) as feminine, like *al-shajar*, since its singular is said to be *shajara*. The people of Najd treat them as masculine, except for certain words excluded in the grammar books. Some scholars said that the masculine form observes the word (*lafz*) and the feminine observes the meaning (*ma'na*), since it carries the sense of *al-ashjar* (trees), and a plural's adjective is made feminine. It was also said that it carries the sense of *shajara* (a single tree), and just as its adjective is made feminine, its pronoun is made feminine, as in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿from a tree of zaqqum﴾ and ﴿then you will fill your bellies from it﴾.

The well-known view is that what is meant by this tree is *al-markh* and *al-'affar*. Fire is made from *al-markh*, which is the male of the upper firestick (*zand*), and from *al-'affar* (with a fatha on the ʿayn), which is the female of the lower firestick. The first is rubbed against the second, and both are green. Water is extracted from them, and fire is struck by God's leave. That *al-markh* is like the male and *al-'affar* like the female is what al-Zamakhshari and others mention, and the wording seems to support it. al-Jawhari reversed this.

From Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi: in every tree there is fire, except *al-unnab* (jujube). It was said that for this reason a pestle for launderers is made from it. al-Khafaji recited, of his own composition:

*O tree of the jujube, your fire has kindled in my heart, yet the jujube is not of the trees of fire.*

The generality (that fire is in every tree) and the absence of an exception became well known. Thus the proverb says: "In every tree is fire, and *al-markh* and *al-'affar* have been made to abound (in fire)." That is, the two have made a great deal of fire abundant, from *majadat al-ibil*, when camels fall into a wide and abundant pasture. From this comes *rajul majid*, meaning a generous man.

Some scholars chose to take "the green tree" as a genus, and what is mentioned about *al-markh* and *al-'affar* as an example. The two were specified because they are quicker to produce fire and yield more of it, as the proverb indicates. And from the sayings used as proverbs: "*al-markh* and *al-'affar* do not give birth to anything but fire."

﴿Then, from it, you kindle⁠﴾ serves as an emphasis for what precedes and a confirmation of it. That is: from that green tree you kindle fire, and you do not doubt that it is real fire coming out of it, not like the fire of the *hubahib* (a glowworm-like light, a deceptive spark).

By His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Who⁠﴾ and so on, He indicates that whoever is able to produce fire from the green tree, despite the watery nature in it which is opposed to fire in its quality (since water is cold and moist, and fire is hot and dry), is more capable, may He be exalted, of restoring freshness to what was fresh and then dried and decayed. Then, this fire is created by God, may He be exalted, when one of the two trees is rubbed against the other, and it is not that there is a hidden fire which comes out by the rubbing. The evidence of "from the tree" does not support that. And "in every tree there is fire" is one of the Arabs' permissive usages, so do not be heedless, and beware of believing in *kumun* (fire being latent within things).

[Page 56]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 81:

The statement of Him, exalted is He: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth...﴾ etc., is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) brought forward by Him, exalted is He, to establish the content of the answer which the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to address to them, and to impose the proof upon them. The hamza (interrogative particle) is for denial and negation, and the waw is for coordination (ataf) upon an implied element which the context requires, meaning: "Is not He who originated them the first time, and is not He who made for you fire from the green tree, and is not He who created the heavens and the earth, despite their great bulk and the magnitude of their station, ﴿able to create the like of them﴾ in smallness and insignificance in comparison to them?" This is so that the meaning of "their like" is them and their likes, or so that the meaning of it is themselves by way of metonymy (kinayah), as in the expression "one like you does such-and-such." Some have said: "Their like" means like them in the fundamentals of essence and its attributes, namely the resurrection (ma'ad). God willing, the detailed discussion of this matter will come later. A group of exegetes claimed that the pronoun in ﴿their like﴾ returns to the heavens and the earth, because they include the rational beings within them; therefore the pronoun of rational beings is used by way of predominance (taghlib), and the purpose of the statement is to repel the supposition of the eternity of the world, which would entail the impossibility of its return. But this is forced and contrary to the apparent meaning, and the polytheists, as far as is apparent, do not hold to the eternity of the world. It has also been objected that even if the eternity of the world were assumed, together with the eternity of the human species and the non-finitude of its individuals on the side of the beginning, it would not preclude bodily resurrection, since that concerns the responsible persons, who are finite. And the claim that what is proven to be eternal cannot be non-existent is not conclusive, as has been established in its proper place, so do not be heedless! Al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-A'raj, Salam and Ya'qub in one narration read ﴿yaqdir﴾ with a fatha on the ya and a sukun on the qaf, as an imperfect verb.

﴿Yes [bala]﴾ is an answer from Him, exalted is He, and a declaration of what the interrogative of denial conveyed, namely the affirmation of what follows the negation, that is, the capacity to create; and it is an indication of determining it as the answer. They either spoke it or stammered over it, out of fear of being bound by it. The statement of Him, exalted is He: ﴿And He is the Creator, the All-Knowing﴾ is a conjunction upon what the affirmative (yes) implies, meaning: "Yes, He, glory be to Him, is capable of that, and He, exalted and majestic, is the one who excels in creation and knowledge, in quality and quantity."

Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Zayd ibn Ali and Malik ibn Dinar read ﴿al-Khallaq﴾ (the Creator) in the form of the active participle pattern (fa'al).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 82:

﴿Indeed, His command﴾ means His affair, exalted is He, in bringing things into existence. It is also permissible that what is meant is the verbal command, so that it accords with His saying ﴿Indeed, Our word to a thing﴾, and by it is meant the effective word.

﴿When He intends a thing﴾ means the bringing into existence of any of things, ﴿that He says to it: "Be!"﴾ means: bring into being, ﴿and it is﴾ means: so it comes to be and is brought into existence. The apparent meaning is that there is a verbal utterance, which is the word "Be!" (kun), and this is the view of the majority of the early scholars (al-Salaf). The affairs of God, exalted is He, lie beyond what human understandings can reach, so set aside speech and dispute. It has also been said that there is no verbal utterance at all, lest an infinite regress (tasalsul) follow. It is also possible that there is an inner speech (qawl nafsi), and His saying to the thing is its being related to it; but this contains what the early scholars utterly reject. Another group of scholars held that there is no speech at all, and that what is meant is an illustration of the effect of His power on His will, by analogy with the command of a obeyed commander to an obedient subordinate, regarding the swift attainment of what is commanded without refusal or hesitation or dependence on anything.

Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read ﴿fa-yakuna﴾ with the accusative (fatha), as a conjunction following ﴿yaqula﴾. It is also permissible that it is in the accusative as a response to the imperative, but some have rejected this on the grounds that it is not a true imperative; and there is discussion on this point.

﴿So glory be to Him in whose hand is the dominion of everything﴾: a declaration of His transcendence, exalted is He, above what they ascribe to Him, and an expression of amazement at what they say about Him, may His dignity be exalted. The *fa'* (فاء) is either *jaza'iyyah* (the conditional *fa'*, "then"), meaning: when this is known, then glory be to Him; or *sababiyyah* (the causal *fa'*, "therefore"), because what precedes is the reason for His glorification, glory be to Him. *Malakut* (ملكوت), meaning the dominion, is an intensive form of *mulk* (ملك, sovereignty), like *rahamut* and *rahabut*, so it means complete sovereignty. Attaching "glory be to Him" (*subhan*, سبحان) to what follows it implies that His being the complete owner of all sovereignty and being capable of everything requires glorifying Him. *Malakut* has also been explained as the world of command and the unseen, and it is said that singling it out for mention is because the disposal of it belongs to Him alone, without intermediary, unlike the world of witnessing.

Talhah and al-A'mash read *malakah* (ملكة) on the pattern of *shajarah*, meaning: in His hand is the controlling of everything. It was also read *mamlakah* (مملكة) on the pattern of *maf'alah*, and it was read *mulk* (ملك).

﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾: not to anyone other than Him, exalted is He. This is a promise to those who affirm and a threat to those who deny. The address is general, to believers and polytheists alike. It has also been said that it is solely a threat, with the address directed only to the polytheists, as a rebuke to them. For this reason the verse departs from what the apparent wording would require, which would be "and to Him the affair all returns," and this indicates that they deserved a great anger. Zayd ibn 'Ali read *turji'un* (ترجعون) in the active voice.

This is what has been summarized from their words on these noble verses. They contain clear evidence for bodily resurrection (*al-ma'ad al-jismani*, the resurrection of the body) and an allusion to repelling some doubts about it. This question is one of the most important matters of religion. Since this noble surah contains of its matters what made it, according to the great scholars, "the heart of the Qur'an," there is no harm in mentioning, to complete the discussion of it, what the scholars have said in investigating this matter. So I say, asking Allah, exalted is He, for success in reaching the acceptable statement: know first that the Muslims differed over what the human being is. It was said: it is this perceptible frame together with subtle parts pervading it, pervading it as rose water pervades the rose and fire pervades coal. These are a subtle, luminous body, different in reality and quiddity from the bodies of which this frame is composed, even though its pervasion in it gives it a likeness of form. We do not know the reality of this body, which is the spirit (*al-ruh*), referred to by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: The spirit is of my Lord's command﴾, according to the majority of the righteous early generation (*al-salaf al-salih*, the pious predecessors). Between it and the body there is a connection expressed as the animal spirit (*al-ruh al-hayawani*), which is a subtle vapor. When it decays and leaves its suitability to be a connection, the spirit leaves the body involuntarily and life ceases. As long as it remains in the state in which it is suitable to be a connection, the spirit and life remain. This body, which is expressed by the term spirit, is, according to Imam al-Qurtubi in *al-Tadhkirah*, something that has a beginning but no end, meaning that it does not perish even if it separates from the perceptible body. In the same work he mentioned that whoever says it perishes is a heretic (*mulhid*). It was also said: it is this perceptible frame together with the rational soul (*al-nafs al-natiqah*), which is a simple, immaterial substance. Indeed, the human being in reality is this, as some have explicitly stated. Those who affirmed the existence of this substance include al-Halimi, al-Ghazali, al-Raghib, Abu Zayd al-Dabbusi, Ma'mar from the early Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites, a rationalist school), the majority of the later Imamiyyah (the Twelver Shi'is), and many of the Sufis. It is the spirit of command (*al-ruh al-amriyyah*), and it is neither inside the body nor outside it, so its relation to it is the relation of Allah, glory be to Him, exalted is He, to the world. In their view, after its temporal origination it also does not perish.

Ibn al-Qayyim refuted this position in his book *al-Ruh* with what leaves nothing more to be added. Just as they differed on this, they differed on whether the body, after death, only disintegrates, or disintegrates and its essence ceases to exist. Some held each view. Perhaps whoever held the second view excepted the coccyx (*'ajb al-dhanab*), because of the authentic report of its being excepted from decay. All these differing scholars agreed on affirming bodily resurrection, except that some of them said that there is bodily resurrection only, meaning that nothing is resurrected except a body, since in their view there is beyond the body no immaterial substance called the rational soul. Others said there is both bodily resurrection and spiritual resurrection together, meaning that the body is resurrected with something not a body attached to it, which is the rational soul. Each of these two positions includes those who say that when the body has disintegrated, its parts will be gathered together on the Day of Resurrection for the resurrection, and the spirit will stand in it or become attached to it as in this world. Indeed, its standing or attachment there is more complete, since there is no severance from it at all after it has been realized. So resurrection for these people means the gathering of the scattered parts and the return of the spirit's standing in them or its attachment to them. By "the parts" is meant the original parts, which are the parts of the body at the moment the spirit was breathed into it in this world, not the atom upon which the covenant was taken on the Day of ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾, as has been said. Allah, exalted is He, is capable of preserving them from dissolution and change, and likewise of preserving them from becoming parts of another body, even if they have been scattered throughout the earth's regions and mixed with the elements. It has also been said: it is possible that the original parts are seized by the angel by Allah's leave at the presence of death, so that eating does not affect them, they do not mix with the dust, and no growth of plant or animal comes from them. But this is merely a possibility with no evidence for it, indeed it contradicts His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿He says: Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ ﴿Say: He will give them life who produced them the first time﴾. This clearly indicates that what is resurrected is decayed parts mixed with dust. It is also possible that the original parts are the earthly parts which the angel scatters into the womb upon the sperm, as reported in the authentic hadith, and he does not scatter the same dust twice. The body, after being gathered, will be resurrected in its most complete state, as indicated by the Prophet's saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "People will be resurrected barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised." Then the bodies of the people of Paradise will be increased, so that each of them will be like Adam, peace be upon him, in height and breadth. Likewise the bodies of the people of Hell will be increased, contrary to the Mu'tazilah, so much so that one of their molars will be like Mount Uhud. Both increases are reported in hadith. So the one who has an amputated limb or a deformed limb, for example, will be resurrected only complete, as he was before the amputation or the deformity. And whoever was created in this world with four arms, for example, will be resurrected in the usual, well-known form of his kind, and likewise whoever was created without a hand or foot, for example. The claim that this would require punishing a body that did not disobey while not punishing a body that did disobey arises from a great heedlessness, since the one punished is only the spirit, and it is the one that disobeyed. Disobedience and punishment cannot be conceived of for the body itself. Burning it with fire is not a punishment to it in itself, otherwise burning wood would be a punishment to it. Rather, it is a means to punishing the spirit. This is like a person placed in an iron box, for example, and put into fire, or wrapped in cloth and beaten with whips until the cloth tears. The spirit is in the position of this person, and the body is in the position of the box or the cloth. On the view that everything has a life suited to it, punishment also does not arise, since not every living thing is hurt by fire. This is illustrated by the salamander and the ostrich, and likewise by the guardians of Hell, its snakes and its scorpions, and we seek refuge in Allah, exalted is He.

Among the people is one who says that the body is annihilated, not merely that its parts are scattered, and then it is restored for the resurrection exactly as it was. Among them is one who says it is annihilated and then a likeness of it is created on the Day of Resurrection, and the spirit stands in it or becomes attached to it. The first view has been supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He says: Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ ﴿Say: He will give them life who produced them the first time﴾. This clearly indicates that the bones are not annihilated in their essence in external existence, and "decayed" cannot be understood as meaning more than the scattering of the parts. It seems the deniers found its gathering improbable, so attention is drawn to dispelling their improbability by the fact that the original creation is more improbable, and that has already occurred. Then what might be imagined is dispelled, namely that the mixing of the parts after their scattering and their return to their elements makes them indistinguishable, so their gathering would not be easy, by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿He has knowledge of every creation﴾. Then attention is drawn to dispelling what might be imagined, namely that the original creation was gradual, with the parts transferred from one state to another until they became prepared for life and suited to the spirit. But this is not so on the Day of Resurrection, so there is no suitability between the parts being gathered and the spirit and life. Therefore the validity of the original creation does not necessitate the validity of resurrection. This is supported by His saying: ﴿He who made for you fire from the green tree﴾. Since this was well known among them, seen by young and old alike, He, glory be to Him, drew attention to the answer through it. Otherwise, His creation of what comes into being by spontaneous generation from animals, such as mice and flies, is itself a refutation of that objection.

Some people claimed that what occurs before the Hour, such as earthquakes and the sending down of rain like the semen of men and the like, is meant to prepare a suitability for the spirit in those parts. But this is not something that needs to be committed to. Likewise, this view has been supported by what Abraham, peace be upon him, was guided to when he said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾, and by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones? Yes, We are able to put together even his fingertips﴾, and by other verses. Some reports also indicate this. The claim that the body is annihilated in its essence, in the second view, has been supported by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Everything will perish except His face﴾, and by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Everyone upon it is perishing﴾. It was answered that it is possible for dispersion to be perishing. Indeed, some verifying scholars said: the meaning of the verse is that everything is not existent at present in itself except the Essence of the Necessary Existent, exalted is He, on the basis that the existence of the contingent is derived from another, so there is no existence in it when its dependence on another is set aside. This is unlike the existence of the Necessary Existent, exalted is He, since it is from His own essence, glory be to Him, indeed it is identical with His essence. The same can be said of the second verse, if it is granted that the body is included in the generality of "whoever" (*man*). The claim that a likeness of it will be created on the Day of Resurrection, in the third view, has been supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them? Yes﴾. It was answered that what is meant is the likeness of them in smallness and in the state of being mere dust, as you have heard in what preceded. It is not meant that He, exalted is He, is able to create on the Day of Resurrection the likeness of their bodies that existed in this world and then return their spirits to them, since this is hardly understood from the verse. There is no need to commit to the view that resurrection is by the creation of a body like the former one, even if it is said that the former body has been annihilated in external existence. Some people imagined that it is obligatory to commit to this if that view is held, because it is impossible to restore what has been annihilated.

The impossibility is argued thus: if it were restored, it would entail the intervention of nonexistence between a thing and itself, and that is impossible.

Page 60

This is rebutted on the basis that time is not among the particularising attributes that are required for existence. We do not concede that the interposition (*takhallul*) is impossible here. Its meaning is that the thing existed for a period, then ceased to exist in another period, and then came to exist in a third period. In reality this is the interposition of non-existence and the severing of continuity between the two periods of existence. There is no impossibility in this, since the two extremes are different in essence. What is impossible is the interposition of non-existence between a thing's essence and itself, in the sense of severing the connection between a thing and itself, such that the thing exists while its very self does not exist, and then it brings its very self into existence. That is not the case here. The thing existed together with itself in the first period, then it became characterised together with itself by non-existence in the other period, and then it became characterised together with itself by existence in the third period. So the severing of the connection between a thing and itself has not occurred at any moment of time. Is this not like a person who puts on a particular garment, then takes it off, then puts it on again?

It is also argued that if the re-creation of the non-existent in its very same individuality were permissible, then its re-creation along with its like in every respect would be permissible. The consequence is false, because two like things are either such that one of them is re-created and not the other, which is false and entails arbitrariness (*tahakkum*) and preponderance without a preponderant cause (*tarjih bila murajjih*). Or both are re-created, which is also false and entails the unity of the two. Or neither of them is re-created, which is also false and entails the opposite of what was supposed, since it was supposed that one of them is re-created.

Against this: it is only complete if the loss of the essence and the annulment of identity between the prior and the subsequent existence are established, since this is the basis of the entailment of arbitrariness. It may be said that when a thing is annihilated in external reality, it remains in *nafs al-amr* (the actual state of affairs) in accordance with its mental existence, and so it preserves its individual unity in accordance with that existence, just as if it were distinct and fixed in non-existence, with a fixity separate from external existence, as the Mu'tazilah and those who agree with them held. It is claimed that its individual unity is not preserved in the mind, since there is no unity without existence, and no existence without individuation, whether it is external or mental. The mental identity exists in the mind only with its mental individuating features, and with those features it is not an external identity; otherwise it would follow that the external identity is characterised by the accidents specific to mental existence, which is absolutely false. Rather, it is on condition of abstracting it from these features. Their statement that it is united with them, in the sense that after abstraction it is their very self, so it is not them absolutely in actuality, is countered by saying that the abstraction of identity from its individuating features does not mean making it empty of them in reality, but rather means setting them aside and not taking them into consideration. Not taking them into account does not entail taking their non-existence into account, let alone their non-existence in reality. Setting aside does not prevent unity in reality. As for the claim that our statement "this is re-created" and "this is the beginning" is an external individual proposition, whose truth depends on the subject's existence in external reality, and not a mental one, which is sufficient for its truth merely by the subject's existence in the mind, so the unity must be preserved in external reality and it is not sufficient that it be preserved in the mind, it is countered that the truth of a mental judgement suffices to dispel arbitrariness. So reflect!

It has been said: just as the non-existent exists in the mind, so too the supposed beginning exists in the mind. Therefore the relation of the second existent to the prior non-existent is no more appropriate than its relation to the supposed beginning. It has been objected that there is a problem in this. As for the doctrine of the philosophers, the form of the prior non-existent is imprinted in the powers inscribed in the celestial spheres, according to their view that the forms of all bodily events are inscribed in them. So it has a particular imaginal form, preserving its individual unity after its non-existence. This is unlike the newly originated thing, which does not have that form before it exists in its particular form. So when it exists with that particular form, it is a re-creation, and when it exists with the universal form, it is a new beginning. As for the doctrine of the Ash'ariyyah among the theologians, the non-existent also has a particular form, obtained through the connection of the attribute of sight (*sifat al-basar*) to it from the Originator, exalted is His majesty. That form does not belong to the new beginning's existence, since although it is particular, it is also real, but it was not established by the connection of the attribute of sight. There is no doubt that what is established by the connection of the attribute of sight is more perfect than what is not established by it, so there is clear distinction between the two forms. If the unity of the external existent is preserved by the particular imaginal form for us, then its preservation by the particular form that exists for Him, glorified be He, through the connection of sight is more fitting. As for the claim that the relation of the imaginal form and what is in its position to each of the re-created and the new beginning is equal, so that the preserved unity is specific in kind and not individual, it entails that the imaginal form is not particular but universal, which contradicts what they have declared.

It is also argued that if the re-creation of the non-existent in its very same form were permissible, then the non-existence of a thing could not be known with certainty to have been newly originated, since it would be possible that for everything we believe to be newly originated there is a prior existence which is sometimes annihilated and sometimes re-created. The consequence is false, by the agreement of rational people. It has been objected that rational possibility cannot be denied, but the default is the absence of a prior existence, and by this a kind of knowledge is obtained. Perhaps this is of the same kind as our knowledge that Mount Uhud will not turn into gold, even though reason allows for its transformation. In summary, the arguments for the impossibility of the re-creation of the non-existent are not free from flaws, as will not be hidden from one who consults the extended works of theology. Already in the preceding verses, the removal of the doubt concerning the non-preservation of individual unity has been indicated by His saying ﴿And He is Knowing of every creation﴾. The most preponderant of these doctrines is that the gathering (*hashr*) is by the reassembly of the original parts that remained from the beginning of life to its end. These are either elemental parts, most of which return to dust and mix with it just as the rest of the parts mix with its elements, or earthly parts only, according to what you have heard earlier, which is not far-fetched. This is what should be relied upon, since the account of the four elements and the body's composition from them, particularly the account of the element of fire, is not authentically reported from the Lawgiver ﷺ and is not mentioned in the books of the early scholars. Rather it is something the philosophers were enamoured with. Moreover, the adherents of the new philosophy are heard denying the sphere of fire that the earlier thinkers spoke of. So the original parts, after they disperse and become dust, are gathered by God, the Exalted, wherever they are, and He, glorified be He, has knowledge of them: ﴿Does not He who created know, and He is the Subtle, the All-Aware?﴾ If this is combined with the doctrine of re-creating the form, which is an essential component of the body according to those who hold that it is composed of it and of matter, or of the accidents specific to the species which are a component of the individuals of the species, such as the essential specific form, as is the view of those among the theologians who deny that the body is composed of matter and form, then this doctrine depends on the permissibility of re-creating the non-existent. But if this is not combined with it, and one is content with the claim that the original elemental parts are gathered and shaped into a form like the first form, and adorned with accidents similar to the prior accidents, then the doctrine does not depend on that at all. Difference in form and the non-identity of the accidents in essence are not harmful to the gathered being being the one originated, both by religious law and by custom. It does not entail the technical *tanasukh* (metempsychosis), as will not be hidden.

In *Abkar al-Afkar* of al-Amidi, after a thorough detailing that cites the verses and hadiths indicating the occurrence of the bodily resurrection, he says: "The scriptural proofs on this cannot be contained in one book, nor can any discourse enumerate them. All of them are clear in indicating the gathering of bodies and their raising, and it is possible in itself, so it is not permissible to abandon them without evidence. But is the re-creation of bodies by bringing them into existence after their non-existence, or by composing their parts after their dispersal? This has been disputed. The truth is that each of the two is possible, and revelation requires one of them without specifying which. If the re-creation of bodies is by composing their parts after their dispersal, is it obligatory to re-create the very same compositions that passed in this world, or may God, the Exalted, compose them with another composition? Abu Hashim held that it is prohibited to re-create them with another composition, on the ground that the essences of individuals are alike, and each part is distinguished only by its specific determination and composition. When that specific composition does not return to it, that individual is not the one who returns but another. This contradicts what revelation has reported about the gathering of human bodies in their forms. The doctrine of all others among the People of Truth is that each of the two is rationally permissible, and there is no evidence specifying one of them from revelation or otherwise. What is said, that the determination of each individual is specifically by its composition, is not granted. Rather it may be by its colour or some other feature together with the composition. Abu Hashim's doctrine is that it is not obligatory to re-create accidents other than composition. Whatever is his answer regarding other than composition is our answer regarding composition. What has come about the gathering of people in their forms does not indicate the re-creation of the very same composition that has passed, and there is no obstacle to the re-creation being by the like of that composition and not its very same." End of quotation.

The Imam claimed the consensus (*ijma'*) of the Muslims on the resurrection by the reassembly of parts after their dispersal, but this is not so, given the disagreement you have heard about its manner, which is mentioned in *al-Mawaqif* and elsewhere. The question of re-creating accidents is more disputed than that of re-creating substances. Most of the People of Truth held that their re-creation is permissible absolutely, to the extent that some of them permitted their re-creation outside their substrates. The Mu'tazilah agreed that the re-creation is permissible for those accidents which, according to their principles, remain and are not generated. They differed concerning the permissibility of re-creating what does not persist, such as heat, sounds, and volitions. Most of them held that their re-creation is prohibited, while a minority, such as al-Balkhi and others, permitted it. Among the Muslims, Abu al-Hasan al-Basri and some of the Karramiyyah held that the re-creation of the non-existent is absolutely impermissible. Some people restricted the prohibition to what has ceased to exist both in essence and in existence, and permitted it for what has ceased to exist only in its existence. The doctrine of the bodily resurrection was held by the Jews and the Christians, as al-Dawani explicitly states. However, the Imam mentioned in *al-Muhassal* that all the prophets other than our Prophet ﷺ spoke only of the spiritual resurrection (*ma'ad ruhani*).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 36, verse 83 (part 3 of 3):

Al-Muhaqqiq al-Tusi said in his *Talkhis*: As for the prophets who came before our Prophet (ﷺ), the apparent meaning of the words of their communities is that Musa (peace be upon him) did not mention the bodily resurrection (al-ma'ad al-badani), nor was it revealed to him in the Torah. However, it appears in the books of the prophets who came after him, such as Ezekiel (Hizqil) and Isaiah (Sha'ya), peace be upon them both. For this reason, the Jews acknowledged it. As for the Gospel, the more evident view is that what it mentions is the spiritual resurrection (al-ma'ad al-ruhani). This contradicts what you have heard from the Imam, and it also contradicts what Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali said in his book *al-Madnun bihi 'ala ghayr ahlihi* (*The Precious Knowledge Withheld from Those Not Worthy of It*): that the Torah states that the people of Paradise will remain in bliss for fifteen thousand years and then become angels, and that the people of Hell will remain in it for such and such a period, or longer, and then become devils. For this clearly indicates that Musa (peace be upon him) mentioned the bodily resurrection and that it was revealed to him in the Torah. The truth is that the Gospels are full of what apparently indicates that a human being will be resurrected with soul and body. As for the Torah, what is mentioned in it is not stated explicitly, according to what some knowledgeable Muslims from among the People of the Book related to me. The theistic philosophers (al-falasifa al-ilahiyyun) denied this and held only to the spiritual resurrection. This denial is based either on the claim that re-creating what has ceased to exist is impossible, which has its own problems, or on the claim that the infinity of dimensions is impossible. For some of them said: the human species is eternal, and rational souls are infinite like bodies. Therefore, if the bodily resurrection is affirmed, it would entail the gathering together in existence of infinite bodies, since every soul must have an independent body, and this would require an infinite extension in which those infinite bodies could be gathered. Another of them said: the individuals of the human species are infinite, while the elements are finite, so their parts are not sufficient for those bodies. How then can they be resurrected?

It has been objected that the eternity of the human species and the infinity of its individuals are things for which they cannot establish a proof.

Ibn al-Kamal said: To base the impossibility of bodily resurrection on the impossibility of the infinity of dimensions is an illusion that came to the mind of some eminent scholars. The matter is not as they imagined. For the resurrection of bodies that is necessary if the bodily resurrection occurs is the resurrection of those who are responsible (al-mukallafun), namely the obedient who deserve reward and the disobedient who deserve punishment. It is not the resurrection of all individuals of humankind, whether they were responsible or not. For this is not among the necessities of the religion (daruriyyat al-din), since the reports concerning it have not reached the level of mass transmission (tawatur), and consensus (ijma') has not been formed upon it. Al-Muhaqqiq al-Tusi has already drawn attention to this in *al-Tajrid*, where he said: "Revelation (al-sam') indicates it, and it is interpreted as referring to the responsible individuals through separation." The commentator (al-Sharih) said: That is, there is no problem regarding those who are not responsible, for it is possible that they will be completely annihilated and not restored. As for those who are responsible, their non-existence is interpreted as the dispersal of their parts.

Also in *Talkhis al-Muhassal*, where he said: Those who hold that it is possible to re-create what has ceased to exist said: God (exalted) annihilates the responsible persons and then restores them. Al-Amidi also drew attention to this in *Abkar al-Afkar*, where he established the disagreement regarding the restoration of the responsible person. There is no doubt that the infinity of all individuals of humankind does not entail the infinity of those among them who are responsible, such that the matter of their gathering would require infinite dimensions. End of quotation.

The truth is that one must challenge their claim of the eternity of the species and the infinity of its individuals. According to us, the argument of "application" (burhan al-tatbiq) is sufficient to refute the infinite, whether its parts have come together in existence or not, and whether they are ordered or unordered. As for limiting the gathering to the responsible rather than others, such as the insane, children, those who were not reached by the call, and the like, this is nothing. The reports concerning this are numerous, and perhaps they belong to the category of the meaning-wise mass transmission (al-mutawatir al-ma'nawi). Moreover, even if they were not so, there is no reason to disregard them or to hold a view contrary to what they indicate, as is not hidden.

The early natural philosophers (al-qudama' min al-falasifa al-tabi'iyyin) held that neither the bodily resurrection nor the spiritual resurrection is established. This is reported of the metempsychosists (al-tanasukhiyya), except the Jews. For them, metempsychosis is not continuous, but occurs to a single soul three times, as it is said.

It is related of Galen (Jalinus) that he suspended judgment on the matter of resurrection, for he said: "It has not become clear to me whether the soul is the temperament (al-mizaj) that ceases at death, so that its restoration is impossible, or whether it is a substance that remains after the structure has decayed, so that resurrection is possible." The polytheists are in grave doubt about it, which is why you find their statements about it confused. The Muslims are in agreement (*mujmi'un*) that it will occur, though they differ, as you have heard, regarding its manner. Likewise they differ regarding whether it is obligatory by revelation (sam'an) or by reason ('aqlan). The People of the Sunnah hold that it is obligatory by revelation absolutely. The Mu'tazila hold that for the responsible it is obligatory by reason, because according to them the reward for obedience and the punishment for disobedience are obligatory, and each of these two depends on the resurrection. There is consideration in this. And God (exalted) knows best.

This noble surah has included the establishment of lofty objectives and contained grand, manifest proofs. Do you not see that He (exalted) swore that the Prophet (ﷺ) is the most perfect of the messengers and that his way is the clearest of paths? He (glorified) indicated that the intended purpose is what was mentioned in His words "that you may warn" (*li-tunthira*), etc. Then He clarified it in summary: it is following the Reminder and fearing the Merciful in the unseen. He completed this by striking a parable, incorporating within it an exhortation to hold fast to the rope of the Book and what was sent down upon him, and an affirmation of their superiority over the other books and messengers. He also alluded to it again by stating that it is the worship of Him alone to whom is the return. Then He began to explain the premises by mentioning the signs, choosing from among them the most evident ones that indicate knowledge, power, wisdom, and mercy. He included within this that worship is the gratitude of the Benefactor and the receiving of blessing by spending it in His pleasure, and beware of leaning toward anyone other than Him. Then, in explaining the concluding matters, He mentioned the promise and the threat in terms of what will be attained in the Hereafter. He incorporated within this the hadith of "whoever travels the path and whoever abandons it," and mentioned their ultimate ends. He summarized within it that the straight path is the worship of God (exalted) with sincerity, free from the two impurities of desire and showing off, for He placed before the command to worship Him the avoidance of worshipping Satan. He included within it that its foundation is monotheism. Just as He mentioned the signs so that the discourse would not be rhetorical in the premises, He concluded with the proof of the return so that it would follow the same pattern in the concluding matters. He (glorified) made the conclusion of the conclusion that He, mighty and majestic, is not overwhelmed by anything, nor does His treasury diminish through giving, and that whoever is near Him with acceptance or far from Him with refusal does not escape His dominion. This confirms everything that preceded in the most complete manner. Since this is speech issuing from a station of greatness and majesty, it was necessary that the subtle point of *iltifat* (shift of address) be observed in His words "and to Him you will be returned," so that it would be a summary to clarify the detail. Thus the author of *al-Kashf* established it, and God (exalted) speaks the truth, and He guides to the way.

* * *

"By way of allusion" (*wa-min bab al-ishara*): It has been said that His words (glorified) "Ya-Sin" are an allusion (ishara) to the lordship of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) over all created beings. Thus the "sayyid" (lord) is the one who presides over the "sawad," meaning the great multitude, and here it is the whole of creation. It is as if it were said: "O Lord of creation!" His presiding over them (peace and blessings be upon him) is because he is the supreme intermediary in the outpouring of grace and aid. In a report: "God is the Giver, and I am the Distributor." Thus his station (ﷺ) in relation to the entire world is like the station of the heart in relation to the body. How delicate is the opening of the heart of the Qur'an with the heart of existence! In the letter *sin* there are clear signs and scriptures, secrets that cannot be counted. Likewise, in the combination "Ya-Sin, and the Qur'an" it may be an allusion to him (ﷺ). The Sufis have mentioned that by it is alluded to the Perfect Human (al-insan al-kamil). Likewise the Clear Book. Upon this is the saying of the Greatest Shaykh, may his secret be sanctified:

*I am the Qur'an and the seven oft-repeated, the spirit of spirits, not the spirit of vessels.*

And there is no one more perfect than the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace.

Some have applied the story of the people of Antioch to what is within the souls, by taking the town as an allusion to the heart, its people as an allusion to the self (nafs) and its qualities, the two as an allusion to the divine inspiration (al-khatir al-rahmani) and the lordly illumination (al-ilham al-rabbani), the third that was strengthened by them as an allusion to the attraction (al-jadhba), and the man who came from the farthest part of the city as an allusion to the spirit (al-ruh). Many of the verses of this surah have been applied in this manner. It has been said that in His words (glorified) "Your omen is with you," it is an allusion to their evil predisposition (isti'dad), which carried them off like the mythical phoenix (*anqa' mughriba*) to where Umm Qashʻam laid down her saddle-bag:

*To where Umm Qashʻam laid her saddle-bag.*

It has been said that in His words (exalted): "Indeed, the companions of the Garden today are busy in joy, they and their spouses, in shade upon couches, reclining," it is an allusion to a group of believers for whom the predominant concern in this world was seeking Paradise. Therefore they were attributed to it, though they are less than the people of God and His elite, who turned to nothing other than Him (mighty and majestic). Those are occupied with the delights of what they sought, while these are the companions of the Presence, occupied with their Master (exalted in majesty), enjoying His union and the contemplation of His beauty. Distinguish between the two states, for far apart are the two groups. That is why it is said: most of the people of Paradise are the simple-minded. Understand the allusion.

As for "Satan" in His words (exalted): "Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan," it is an allusion to everything that is obeyed and to which one submits other than God (mighty and majestic), whatever it may be, and his enmity is because he is the cause of the veil from the Lord of lords. In His words (exalted): "So let not their saying grieve you. Indeed, We know what they conceal and what they reveal," it is an allusion to the fact that one should not care about the harm of enemies nor give attention to it, for God (exalted) will requite them for it when He has made them stand before Him. This is it. We ask God (exalted) to protect us from the evil of the wicked, and to illuminate our hearts with His knowledge as He illuminated the hearts of His righteous servants. And we pray and send peace upon His beloved, the heart of the body of existences, and upon his family and companions, as long as Surah Ya-Sin is the heart of the Qur'an.
